Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verse 1–3:

(Surat Ibrahim - peace be upon him -)

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book which We have sent down to you, that you may bring mankind out of darkness into light, by the permission of their Lord, to the path of the All-Mighty, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿Allah, to Whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And woe to the disbelievers because of a severe punishment.﴾ ﴿Those who prefer the worldly life over the Hereafter, and avert [people] from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked. Those are in far error.﴾

(p-403) This surah is entirely Meccan according to the majority of scholars. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah that it is Meccan except for His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the favor of Allah for disbelief﴾ [Ibrahim: 28] up to His saying: ﴿into the Fire﴾ [Ibrahim: 30]. The connection of the beginning of this surah with the surah before it is very clear, for in that surah He mentioned: ﴿And even if a Quran had [been revealed] by which mountains would be moved﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31], then ﴿And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic judgment﴾ [al-Ra'd: 37], then ﴿And those with whom is knowledge of the Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43]. So His saying ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book which We have sent down to you﴾ is appropriate to this. Also, when they said, by way of demand, ﴿Why was there not sent down upon him a sign from his Lord?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 27], and it was said to him: ﴿Say, indeed Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back in repentance﴾ [al-Ra'd: 27], He sent down ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book which We have sent down to you﴾, as if it were said: Is it not sufficient for them among the signs a Book which We have sent down to you, that you may bring mankind out of darkness - which is misguidance - into light - which is guidance.

They permitted, in the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of "Alif, Lam, Ra" (al-Ra), that it be in a position of nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), with (kitab) as the predicate (khabar); or in a position of nominative case as the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "This is Alif, Lam, Ra"; or in a position of accusative case by an estimate of: "Hold to" or "Recite" ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾. And ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you﴾ is an explanatory clause in these two case analyses, and (kitab) is a subject (mubtada'). What permitted the beginning with it is that it is described in the estimate, i.e., "a great Book which We have sent down to you." They also permitted that (kitab) be the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "This is a Book," and (anzalnahu) is a clause in a position of description (sifah). In His saying (anzalnahu), and the attribution of the sending down to the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah), and His addressing Him, exalted is He, with His saying (ilayka), and the attribution of the bringing out to him, upon him be prayers and peace, is a great honoring and ennoblement of him, from the aspect of participation in attaining guidance: by the sending down of Him, exalted is He, and by his bringing out, upon him be prayers and peace; for he is the caller and the warner, though in reality the originator of guidance is Allah, exalted is He. (An-nas) is general, since he was sent to all creation, and "darkness" and "light" are metaphors for disbelief and faith. When He mentioned the cause of the sending down of the Book, which is His saying (li-tukhrija) - that is, the causing to come out - He said: "by the permission of their Lord"; that is, that bringing out is by the facilitation of their Owner, who watches over their interests, since they are His servants. So the mention of "the Lord" is appropriate here, as an alert to the favor of the Owner and to His being watchful over the state of His servants. (Bi-idhni) - its apparent connection is to His saying (li-tukhrija). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "by the permission of their Lord" be in a position of circumstantial state (hal), saying: that is, "permitted to you." Al-Zamakhshari said: "By the permission of their Lord" means by His facilitation and easing, borrowed from the permission which is the easing of a barrier, and that is what He grants them of gentleness and success. End. In it is a trace of Mu'tazilite doctrine.

It is apparent that His saying (ila sirat) is a substitute (badal) for His saying (ila al-nur). This interposition does not harm between the substituted-from and the substitute, because (bi-idhni) is an element governed by the governing word of the substituted-from, which is (li-tukhrija). Al-Zamakhshari permitted that "ila sirat" be by way of a resumptive statement (istithnaf), as if it were said: "To which light?" And it was said: "To the path of the All-Mighty, the Praiseworthy." It was read: (li-yakhruja), the imperfect of kharaja with a ya' with two dots beneath it, and (al-nas) is raised by it. Since His saying (ila al-nur) contained some vagueness, He clarified it with His saying (ila sirat). Since two things preceded: one of them, the attribution of the sending down of this Book to Him; and the second, the bringing out of mankind from darkness into light by the permission of their Lord, it was appropriate to mention these two attributes alongside the attribute of might, which includes power and dominance, from the aspect of the sending down of the Book; and the attribute of praise, which includes His being deserving of praise from the aspect of the bringing out from darkness into light, since guidance to faith is the blessing for which the servant must give praise and thanks. The attribute of (al-'Aziz) was placed first because of the preceding of what indicates it, and the attribute of (al-Hamid) follows it because of the following of what indicates it. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir (p-404) read "Allah" in the nominative case, and it was said: it is a subject (mubtada') omitted, i.e., "He is Allah." This i'rab is more suitable because of its clear connection to what precedes it, and its escape from the first estimate. The rest of the seven readers, and al-Asma'i from Nafi', read "Allahi" in the genitive case, as a substitute (badal) according to Ibn 'Atiyyah, al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa', and as an explanatory apposition ('atf al-bayan) according to al-Zamakhshari, who said: "Because it has come to function as a proper name due to its dominance and its specificity to the Worshipped One who deserves worship, just as al-Najm (the star) became dominant over al-Thurayya." End. This reasoning is not complete except on the assumption that its origin was "al-Ilah," then the vowel was transferred to the lam of definiteness, the hamzah was deleted, and transfer and deletion were obligatory in it; its root at that time being the hamzah, lam and ha'. The statements concerning this word have already been presented in the basmalah at the beginning of the Hamd. Ustadh Abu al-Hasan Ibn 'Asfur said: A description is not placed before the described noun except where it is heard, and that is rare; and the Arabs, regarding what is found of that, have two aspects. One of them: the description is placed first and kept as it was; and in the i'rab of such there are two views: one, that it be parsed as a placed-first adjective (na't muqaddam); and the second, that what follows the description be made a substitute. The second aspect: that the description be annexed to the described noun when it precedes it. End. Thus, according to what Ibn 'Asfur mentioned, it is permissible that (al-'Aziz al-Hamid) be parsed as two preceding adjectives, and the word (Allah) be parsed as the later-placed described noun. Among what has come in this respect, placing before what would have been an adjective if it were postponed, and postponing what would have been the described noun if it were placed first, is the statement of the poet:

And the believer who protects the birds, whom the riders of Makkah wipe between al-Ghayl and al-Sa'd.

If it had come in the common order, the construction would have been: "and the believer, the birds that seek protection."

(Waylun) is raised as a subject (mubtada'), and (lil-kafirin) is its predicate. When the mention of the (zulumat) had preceded, He invoked ruin upon those who did not come out of them. And (min 'adhabin shadid) is in the position of a description of (waylun). The interposition of the predicate between the description and the described noun does no harm, and it is not permissible that it be connected to (waylun), because it is a verbal noun (masdar), and interposing between the verbal noun and what is connected to it with the predicate is not permitted. And it appears from the words of al-Zamakhshari that it is not in the position of a description. He said: "If you say, what is the connection of His saying 'from a severe punishment' to 'woe'? I say: because the meaning is that they turn away from a severe punishment and cry out from it, saying 'Woe to us!' like His saying: ﴿They will call out there for destruction﴾ [al-Furqan: 13]." End. Its apparent meaning indicates an estimated governing word to which ﴿from a severe punishment﴾ is connected. This punishment may be understood as befalling them in the world, or as befalling them in the Hereafter.

Al-istihbab means preference and choice, and it is an (istif'al) form from love (mahabbah); because one who prefers a thing over another seeks, as it were, from himself that it be more beloved to him and more excellent in his estimation than the other. It is also permissible that (istafala) be in the meaning of (af'ala), like (istajaba) and (ajaba). And since it included the meaning of preference, it is governed by (ala). They permitted in the i'rab of (alladhina) that it be a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿Those are in far error﴾; and that it be coordinated to the vituperation (dhamm), either as the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "They are those who"; or accusative by an estimated verb, its estimate being "I vituperate"; or a substitute; or a description of "the disbelievers." The last of these aspects was explicitly stated by al-Hawfi, al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa', and it is not permissible; because in it there is interposition between the description and the described noun by a foreign element from both of them, which is His saying: ﴿from a severe punishment﴾, whether ﴿from a severe punishment﴾ is in the position of a description of (waylun), or connected to an omitted verb, i.e., "they cry out and wail from a severe punishment." Its parallel, if it is a description, is to say: "The house of Zayd the Qurashi, the good one," and this construction is not permissible, because you have interposed between Zayd and his description by a foreign element from both, which is the description of the house. The eloquent construction is to say: "The good house of Zayd the Qurashi," or "The house of Zayd the Qurashi, the good one." Al-Hasan read (wa-yusuddūna), the imperfect of asadda, with the hamzah of transitivity added to saddа - the intransitive - sududan. The discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and seek to make it crooked﴾ has already been presented in Al 'Imran, as well as the description of error with distance.

The statements concerning this word have already been presented in the basmalah at the beginning of the Hamd. Ustadh Abu al-Hasan Ibn 'Asfur said: A description is not placed before the described noun except where it is heard, and that is rare; and the Arabs, regarding what is found of that, have two aspects. One of them: the description is placed first and kept as it was; and in the i'rab of such there are two views: one, that it be parsed as a placed-first adjective (na't muqaddam); and the second, that what follows the description be made a substitute. The second aspect: that the description be annexed to the described noun when it precedes it. End. Thus, according to what Ibn 'Asfur mentioned, it is permissible that (al-'Aziz al-Hamid) be parsed as two preceding adjectives, and the word (Allah) be parsed as the later-placed described noun. Among what has come in this respect, placing before what would have been an adjective if it were postponed, and postponing what would have been the described noun if it were placed first, is the statement of the poet:

And the believer who protects the birds, whom the riders of Makkah wipe between al-Ghayl and al-Sa'd.

If it had come in the common order, the construction would have been: "and the believer, the birds that seek protection."

(Waylun) is raised as a subject (mubtada'), and (lil-kafirin) is its predicate. When the mention of the (zulumat) had preceded, He invoked ruin upon those who did not come out of them. And (min 'adhabin shadid) is in the position of a description of (waylun). The interposition of the predicate between the description and the described noun does no harm, and it is not permissible that it be connected to (waylun), because it is a verbal noun (masdar), and interposing between the verbal noun and what is connected to it with the predicate is not permitted. And it appears from the words of al-Zamakhshari that it is not in the position of a description. He said: "If you say, what is the connection of His saying 'from a severe punishment' to 'woe'? I say: because the meaning is that they turn away from a severe punishment and cry out from it, saying 'Woe to us!' like His saying: ﴿They will call out there for destruction﴾ [al-Furqan: 13]." End. Its apparent meaning indicates an estimated governing word to which ﴿from a severe punishment﴾ is connected. This punishment may be understood as befalling them in the world, or as befalling them in the Hereafter.

Al-istihbab means preference and choice, and it is an (istif'al) form from love (mahabbah); because one who prefers a thing over another seeks, as it were, from himself that it be more beloved to him and more excellent in his estimation than the other. It is also permissible that (istafala) be in the meaning of (af'ala), like (istajaba) and (ajaba). And since it included the meaning of preference, it is governed by (ala). They permitted in the i'rab of (alladhina) that it be a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿Those are in far error﴾; and that it be coordinated to the vituperation (dhamm), either as the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "They are those who"; or accusative by an estimated verb, its estimate being "I vituperate"; or a substitute; or a description of "the disbelievers." The last of these aspects was explicitly stated by al-Hawfi, al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa', and it is not permissible; because in it there is interposition between the description and the described noun by a foreign element from both of them, which is His saying: ﴿from a severe punishment﴾, whether ﴿from a severe punishment﴾ is in the position of a description of (waylun), or connected to an omitted verb, i.e., "they cry out and wail from a severe punishment." Its parallel, if it is a description, is to say: "The house of Zayd the Qurashi, the good one," and this construction is not permissible, because you have interposed between Zayd and his description by a foreign element from both, which is the description of the house. The eloquent construction is to say: "The good house of Zayd the Qurashi," or "The house of Zayd the Qurashi, the good one." Al-Hasan read (wa-yusuddūna), the imperfect of asadda, with the hamzah of transitivity added to saddа - the intransitive - sududan. The discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and seek to make it crooked﴾ has already been presented in Al 'Imran, as well as the description of error with distance.

(p-405) The occasion of its revelation: the Quraysh said, "Why are all the Books non-Arabic, while this one is Arabic?" So it was revealed. He then recounted the story of Musa (Moses), that God, exalted is He, sent him to his people in their own tongue, ﴿that you bring your people out of darkness into light﴾, just as He sent you to bring people out of darkness into light. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the tongue of his people﴾ is generality, so the Messenger, may blessings and peace be upon him, is included within it. If the call is general to all people, or if whoever is not of the messenger's people is included in following that messenger, then whoever's language is not the language of that Prophet must learn that language until he understands it, and must refer its interpretation to those who know it. It has also been said that there is an ellipsis in the speech, its implied meaning being: "And We did not send any messenger before you except in the tongue of his people, and We sent you to mankind entirely in the tongue of your people, and your people translate for others in their own tongues." The meaning of ﴿in the tongue of his people﴾ is in the language of his people.

Abu al-Sammal, Abu al-Jawza' and Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read (بِلِسْنِ) bi-lisn, with the sin pronounced sukun. They said it is like al-rish and al-riyash (both forms of the word for plumage). The author of al-Lawami' said: al-lisn is specific to language, whereas al-lisan may apply both to the organ (the tongue) and to speech. Ibn 'Atiyya said the same, saying: "The word lisan in this verse is meant to signify language, and it is said lisn and lisan in the sense of language; but as for the organ, lisn is not used for it."

Abu Raja', Abu al-Mutawakkil and al-Jahdari read (لُسُنِ) lusun, with damma on the lam and the sin, which is the plural of lisan, like 'imad and 'umud. It was also read with damma on the lam and sukun on the sin, lightened, like rusul and rusl. The pronoun in (قَوْمِهِ) qawmihi refers to (رَسُولٍ) rasul, that is, the people of that messenger. Al-Dahhak said: the pronoun in qawmihi refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), and he said: "All the Books were sent down in Arabic, then each Prophet conveyed them in the tongue of his people." Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is not correct, because His words ﴿in order that he might make clear to them﴾ refer to the people, who are the Arabs, so it would lead to the conclusion that God sent down the Torah from heaven in Arabic in order to make it clear to the Arabs; and this is a corrupt meaning." End of quote. Al-Kalbi said: all the Books were conveyed to Jibril in Arabic, and He commanded him to come to the messenger of every people in their language.

Al-Zamakhshari raised a question here, while Ibn 'Atiyya deferred both of them in their books. He says: The proof was established against mankind through the acknowledgment of eloquent speakers, who were presumed capable of producing a counter-challenge, and their admission of incapacity, just as it was established through the acknowledgment of the magicians to Musa and of the physicians to 'Isa, peace be upon them both. God, exalted is He, stated the reason why each messenger sent was in the language of his people, which is to make things clear to them. Then He mentioned that He leads astray whom He wills to be led astray, and guides whom He wills to be guided; so that messenger has no duty beyond conveying and making clear, and he was not charged to guide, but that is in the hand of God, according to what His decree has determined.

﴿And He is the All-Mighty﴾, who cannot be overcome. (﴿the All-Wise﴾), who places things according to what His wisdom and will require. Al-Zamakhshari said: By misguidance is meant leaving alone and withholding favour, and by guidance is meant success and favour; and this is a metaphor for disbelief and belief.

﴿And He is the All-Mighty﴾, so He is not overcome in His will; (﴿the All-Wise﴾), so He forsakes only those who deserve forsaking, and shows favour only to those deserving favour. End of quote. This is in the manner of al-i'tizal (Mu'tazilism, the rationalist school that holds that God's acts are bound by justice and wisdom).

Regarding His words (بِآياتِنا) bi-ayatina, the majority of commentators interpret them as the nine signs that God manifested at the hand of Musa, peace be upon him. It has been said that it is permissible to mean by them the verses of the Torah, and the implied meaning is: Just as We sent you, O Muhammad, with the Qur'an in clear Arabic, which is Our signs, so likewise We sent Musa with the Torah in the tongue of his people.

As for ﴿that bring out﴾ (أنْ أخْرِجْ) an, it is possible that "an" is explanatory (tafsiriyya, i.e., it introduces an explanation), and it is possible that it is verbal (masdariyya, i.e., it forms a verbal noun with the following verb). The claim of those who say it is superfluous (za'ida, i.e., an extra particle) is weak. In His words (قَوْمَكَ) qawmaka, there is a specification of his mission to his people, in contrast to ﴿so that you might bring out mankind﴾ [Ibrahim: 1]. The apparent meaning is that his people were the Children of Israel. It has been said: the Copts. If they were the Copts, then the darkness here is disbelief and the light is faith. If they were the Children of Israel and we say they were all believers, then the darkness is the humiliation of servitude, and the light is dignity through religion and the manifestation of God's command. If they were groups divided in religion, some of them with the Copts in worshipping Pharaoh and others on no basis at all, then the darkness is disbelief and the light is faith. It has been said: Musa was sent to the Copts (p-406) and the Children of Israel. It has been said: to the Copts, by acknowledging the oneness of God, that nothing be associated with Him, and by faith in Musa, and that he is a prophet from God; and to the Children of Israel, with the obligations and the details of his law, since they were believers. The phrase (وَذَكِّرْهُمْ) wa-dhakkirhum ("and remind them") may be a new command, or it may be coordinated with ﴿that bring out﴾, in which case it falls under the scope of "an".

As for (أَيَّامِ اللَّهِ) ayyam Allah ("the days of God"): Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada said: they are God's blessings upon them. Ubayy related it as a raised (marfu') hadith. From this is the poet's saying:

"And for us were bright, long days, in which we disobeyed the king, until we submitted."

It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd that they are His events and His punishments upon the past nations. It is said: so-and-so is knowledgeable about the days of the Arabs, meaning their battles, wars and great encounters, such as the Day of Dhi Qar, the Day of al-Fijar, the Day of Fiddah and others. Something similar was narrated from Malik, who said: they are His trials. The poet said:

"And our days are famous among our enemy."

Meaning: our battles. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: His bounties and His trials. Al-Tabari chose this. So His bounties are His shading them with the cloud, the sending down of manna and quails, and the splitting of the sea; and His trials are the enslavement of them by Pharaoh, the slaughter of their sons, and the destruction of the generations before them. In the hadith of Ubayy concerning the story of Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon them both: while Musa, peace be upon him, was among his people reminding them of the days of God, and the days of God are His trials and His bounties. Al-Tabari chose this second opinion. The word "days" encompasses both meanings, because the reminder occurs through both aspects together. In this word there is a magnification of the events that are being reminded of, and it is expressed through the time-frame in which they occurred. It is very common for an attribution to be made to a time-frame, while in reality the attribution is to something else, as in His words: ﴿Rather, the scheming of the night and the day﴾ [Saba': 33]. From this is their saying: "a gloomy day" (yawm 'abus), "a grim day" (yawm 'asib), and "a smiling day" (yawm bassam). The reality is a description of the severity or joy that occurred within it.

The indication in His words ﴿Indeed in that﴾ refers to the reminder of the days of God. (﴿patient, grateful﴾) are two intensive adjectives (sifatan mubalaghatan), and they both imply that the "days of God" [al-Jathiyah: 14] refer to His trials and His bounties; that is: patient under His trials, grateful for His bounties. So when he hears of the trials God sent down upon nations, or of the bounties He poured upon them, he becomes alert to what is incumbent upon him: patience when a trial befalls him, and gratitude when a blessing befalls him. He specified the patient and the grateful because they are the ones who benefit from reminding and alerting, and who are admonished by it. It has been said: he intended every believer who looks to his own soul, because patience and gratitude are among the innate qualities of the people of faith.

The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ʾidh ("when") in this type of construction has already been discussed in His saying: ﴿And remember the blessing of God upon you when you were enemies﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103], and the explanation of that verse applies here. However, here it is ﴿wa-yudhabbihūna﴾ with a waw, while in al-Baqarah it is without a waw, and in al-A'raf it is ﴿yaqtulūna﴾. Where the waw is absent, the verb is an explanation of His saying ﴿yasūmūnakum﴾ (they inflict upon you). Where the waw is present, it indicates a difference: the infliction of the evil punishment took the form of slaughter and other things, and where ﴿yaqtulūna﴾ appears, it uses the unrestricted term, which admits of slaughter and of other kinds of killing.

Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿wa-yadhbahūna﴾ as the present tense of the triliteral dhabaḥa, and Zayd ibn ʿAli read it likewise, except that he omitted the waw.

The explanation of taʾadhdhana (proclaimed) and its being followed by an oath has already been given in His saying in al-Aʿraf: ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed that He would surely send﴾ [al-A'raf: 167].

The ʾidh may be governed by ﴿udhkurū﴾ (remember), or it may be conjoined (maʿṭūf) to ﴿ʾidh anjākum﴾ (when He delivered you), since this announcement of an increase for gratitude is among His blessings. The apparent sense is that the object of the gratitude is the bestowal of favour, i.e. ﴿if you are grateful for My favour﴾. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Rabiʿ. Al-Hasan said: "I will increase you in My obedience." Al-Rabiʿ said: "I will increase you of My bounty." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "That is, if you affirm God's oneness and obey Him, I will surely increase you in reward." It seems he took into account the apparent contrast in His saying ﴿but if you disbelieve, indeed My punishment is severe﴾, where the apparent meaning of disbelief is polytheism; therefore he explained gratitude as monotheism, obedience, and so on.

He said ﴿but if you disbelieve﴾, that is, the blessing, so that you do not give thanks for it. He linked the severe punishment to the ingratitude for God's blessing, and He did not specify the place of the increase, so it may be in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both. The construction follows what is customary in the Qur'an: when good is mentioned, it is ascribed to Him, and when punishment is mentioned after it, He turns away from attributing it to Himself. Thus He ascribed the increase to Himself, saying ﴿I will surely increase you﴾, and said ﴿indeed My punishment is severe﴾. The construction did not come as ﴿I will surely punish you﴾. In ﴿I will surely increase you﴾ the object (mafʿūl) is expressed, but here it is not mentioned, although the meaning requires it, i.e. ﴿indeed My punishment for you is severe﴾.

ʿAbdullah read ﴿wa-ʾidh qāla rabbukum﴾ (and when your Lord said), as if he explained His saying ﴿taʾadhdhana﴾, since it means ʾadhina, that is, "informed," and informing can be by speech.

Then Moses, peace be upon him, alerted his people that the Creator, exalted is He, although He threatened severe punishment for disbelief, does not depend on their gratitude, because He, exalted is He, is the One free of need of your gratitude, the Praiseworthy who deserves praise for the abundant blessings He bestows, even if the praisers do not praise Him. The fruit of your gratitude returns only to you.

The ﴿antum﴾ (you) is addressed to his people. He said ﴿and whoever is on the earth﴾, meaning all people, because those in the higher world, the angels, are not included among "whoever is on the earth." The answer to ﴿in takfurū﴾ (if you disbelieve) is omitted, as the meaning indicates. The estimate is: "Indeed, the harm of your disbelief falls only upon you, while God, exalted is He, is characterised by absolute self-sufficiency and praiseworthiness, whether they disbelieve or give thanks." In His address to them there is a belittling of their status and a magnifying of God, exalted is He, and likewise in the mention of these two attributes.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "That is, if you affirm God's oneness and obey Him, I will surely increase you in reward." It seems he took into account the apparent contrast in His saying ﴿but if you disbelieve, indeed My punishment is severe﴾, where the apparent meaning of disbelief is polytheism; therefore he explained gratitude as monotheism, obedience, and so on.

He said ﴿but if you disbelieve﴾, that is, the blessing, so that you do not give thanks for it. He linked the severe punishment to the ingratitude for God's blessing, and He did not specify the place of the increase, so it may be in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both. The construction follows what is customary in the Qur'an: when good is mentioned, it is ascribed to Him, and when punishment is mentioned after it, He turns away from attributing it to Himself. Thus He ascribed the increase to Himself, saying ﴿I will surely increase you﴾, and said ﴿indeed My punishment is severe﴾. The construction did not come as ﴿I will surely punish you﴾. In ﴿I will surely increase you﴾ the object (mafʿūl) is expressed, but here it is not mentioned, although the meaning requires it, i.e. ﴿indeed My punishment for you is severe﴾.

ʿAbdullah read ﴿wa-ʾidh qāla rabbukum﴾ (and when your Lord said), as if he explained His saying ﴿taʾadhdhana﴾, since it means ʾadhina, that is, "informed," and informing can be by speech.

Then Moses, peace be upon him, alerted his people that the Creator, exalted is He, although He threatened severe punishment for disbelief, does not depend on their gratitude, because He, exalted is He, is the One free of need of your gratitude, the Praiseworthy who deserves praise for the abundant blessings He bestows, even if the praisers do not praise Him. The fruit of your gratitude returns only to you.

The ﴿antum﴾ (you) is addressed to his people. He said ﴿and whoever is on the earth﴾, meaning all people, because those in the higher world, the angels, are not included among "whoever is on the earth." The answer to ﴿in takfurū﴾ (if you disbelieve) is omitted, as the meaning indicates. The estimate is: "Indeed, the harm of your disbelief falls only upon you, while God, exalted is He, is characterised by absolute self-sufficiency and praiseworthiness, whether they disbelieve or give thanks." In His address to them there is a belittling of their status and a magnifying of God, exalted is He, and likewise in the mention of these two attributes.

When Moses' command from God, exalted is He, to remind them of the Days of God had preceded, he reminded them of the blessing God, exalted is He, had bestowed on them by delivering them from the people of Pharaoh, and within this is an enumeration of some of the punishments of God that befell them.

The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ʾidh ("when") in this type of construction has already been discussed in His saying: ﴿And remember the blessing of God upon you when you were enemies﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103], and the explanation of that verse applies here. However, here it is ﴿wa-yudhabbihūna﴾ with a waw, while in al-Baqarah it is without a waw, and in al-A'raf it is ﴿yaqtulūna﴾. Where the waw is absent, the verb is an explanation of His saying ﴿yasūmūnakum﴾ (they inflict upon you). Where the waw is present, it indicates a difference: the infliction of the evil punishment took the form of slaughter and other things, and where ﴿yaqtulūna﴾ appears, it uses the unrestricted term, which admits of slaughter and of other kinds of killing.

Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿wa-yadhbahūna﴾ as the present tense of the triliteral dhabaḥa, and Zayd ibn ʿAli read it likewise, except that he omitted the waw.

The explanation of taʾadhdhana (proclaimed) and its being followed by an oath has already been given in His saying in al-Aʿraf: ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed that He would surely send﴾ [al-A'raf: 167].

The ʾidh may be governed by ﴿udhkurū﴾ (remember), or it may be conjoined (maʿṭūf) to ﴿ʾidh anjākum﴾ (when He delivered you), since this announcement of an increase for gratitude is among His blessings. (p-408) The apparent reading is that this is part of Musa's address to his people. The hamzah in (ألم) (a-lam, "Has there not come to you...") is for confirmation (taqrir) and rebuke (tawbikh). The apparent reading is that (والذين) is in the genitive position, in coordination with what precedes it, either upon (الذين) or upon ﴿قوم نوح وعاد وثمود﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The clause "﴿لا يعلمهم إلا الله﴾" is an interjection (i'tiraD), and the meaning is that they are so numerous that none knows their number except God, end quote. But it is not an interjection clause, because an interjection clause occurs between two parts, one of which requires the other. Abu al-Baqa' said: this clause may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿من بعدهم﴾. If he means the pronoun in the genitive (بعدهم), then it is not permissible, because it is a circumstantial clause from what has been put in the genitive by annexation (idafah), and it has no place of i'rab, whether in the nominative or accusative. But if he means the pronoun resting in the prepositional phrase that stands in for the governing element, then it is possible. Abu al-Baqa' also said: it may be an independent resumptive clause (musta'nafah), and likewise "﴿جاءتهم﴾". Al-Zamakhshari permitted, and Abu al-Baqa' followed him, that (والذين) be a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is "﴿لا يعلمهم إلا الله﴾". Al-Zamakhshari said: the clause of subject and predicate occurred as an interjection, end quote. But it is not an interjection, because it did not occur between two parts, one of which requires the other.

The pronoun in (جاءتهم) refers to ﴿الذين من قبلكم﴾, and the clause is explanatory (tafsiriyyah) of the news (naba'). The apparent reading is that the aydi (أيدي, "hands") are the limbs, and that the pronoun in (أيديهم) and in (أفواههم) refers to those to whom the messengers came. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Zayd said: that is, they made the hands of themselves go into the mouths of themselves, so as to bite them out of rage at what the messengers brought. Ibn Zayd said: "﴿عضوا عليكم الأنامل من الغيظ﴾" [Al 'Imran: 119], and biting is a well-known human action. A poet said:

"His nails were consumed by the calluses, and he came to bite upon me the wadhifa."

(And another said):

"If only Salma had seen my emaciation,
and the thinness of my shin and my hand,
and the distance of my family and the harshness of my kin,
she would have bitten, from grief, the tips of her hand."

Ibn 'Abbas said: when they heard the Book of God they wondered and returned their hands to their mouths. Abu Salih said: when the Messenger of God ﷺ said to them, "I am the Messenger of God to you," they pointed with their fingers to their mouths, saying "be silent," rejecting him, dismissing his words, and finding what he brought repugnant. It has been said: they put their hands in their mouths laughing and mocking, like one overcome by laughter who places his hand over his mouth. It has been said: they pointed with their hands to their tongues and to what their tongues uttered of their saying "﴿إنا كفرنا بما أرسلتم به﴾", that is, this is our answer to you, and we have no other, despairing them of assent. It has been said: the two pronouns refer to the messengers, as Muqatil said; he said: they took the hands of the messengers and placed them upon the mouths of the messengers, to silence them and cut off their speech. Al-Hasan and others said: they put the hands of themselves into the mouths of the messengers, rejecting their words, and this is more abominable in rejection and more effective in presumption over the messengers and in harming them; on this view the pronoun in (أيديهم) refers to the messengers. It has been said: the meaning of "hands" here is blessings, the plural of yad meaning blessing; that is, they rejected the blessings of the prophets, which are the greatest blessings, namely their admonitions and advice, and what was revealed to them of laws and signs, into the mouths of the prophets; for when they denied these and did not accept them, it was as if they had returned them into their mouths, and sent them back to where they came from, as an idiom. It has been said: on this view the pronoun in (أفواههم) refers to the disbelievers, and "fi" has the meaning of "bi"; that is, "with their mouths," and the meaning is: they denied them with their mouths. Regarding "fi" meaning "bi", one says: "jalastu fi al-bayt" and "bi al-bayt" (I sat in the house). 

(p-409) Al-Farra' said: we have found among the Arabs those who put "fi" in the place of "bi", so they say: "adkhalaka Allahu al-jannata" and "fi al-jannah" (God made you enter the Garden). He recited:

"And I desire in them more than Laqit and his kin, but I do not desire Shinbis."

He means: "arghabu biha" (I desire in/with them). Abu 'Ubaydah said: this is a figure of speech (darb mathal), meaning they did not believe and did not respond. The Arabs say of a man who falls silent from answering and holds back: "radda yadahu fi fihi" (he returned his hand into his mouth), and al-Akhfash also said this. Al-Qutabi said: no one from the Arabs has been heard to say "radda yadahu fi fihi" when he abandons what he was commanded, end quote. But one who heard is proof against one who did not hear; Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash related this from the Arabs. So on what Abu 'Ubaydah said, this is from the metaphorical figure of representation (majaz al-tamthil), as if the one who holds back from answering and keeps silent placed his hand over his mouth. Al-Tabari rejected Abu 'Ubaydah's view and said: they had answered with denial, because they said: "﴿إنا كفرنا بما أرسلتم به﴾". But what al-Tabari said does not refute Abu 'Ubaydah, for Abu 'Ubaydah means that they held back and fell silent from the satisfactory answer which the coming of the messengers with clear proofs requires, namely acknowledging faith and affirming the messengers. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is possible that the word "hands" is used figuratively, that is, they rejected their strength, their resistance, and their confrontation in what they said with their mouths of denial, so the meaning is: they returned all their resistance into their mouths, that is, into their statements; and he expressed all resistance by "hands", since the hands are the place of greatest resistance and opposition, end quote. First they hastened to disbelief, which is pure denial, then they informed that they were in doubt (shakk), which is hesitation; as if they looked at it with some look which led them to move from pure denial to hesitation. Or these are two statements from two groups: a group that hastened to denial and disbelief, and a group that doubted; and doubt regarding the like of what the messengers brought is disbelief. Talhah recited "(مما تدعونا)" with the assimilation of the nun of the nominative into the pronoun, as it is assimilated into the nun of protection (nun al-wiqayah) in such as "(أتحاجوني)". The meaning is: "مما تدعونا إليه" (of that to which you call us), namely faith in God. "(مريب)" is a confirmatory adjective (sifah tawkidiyyah). The interrogative hamzah whose meaning is denial entered upon the adverbial phrase which is the predicate of the subject, because the speech is not about doubt itself but about that which is doubted, and that it does not admit doubt because of the manifestness of the proofs and their testimony to it. A noun is understood to be omitted (mudaf), so it is said: "أفي ألوهية الله" (is there doubt about the divinity of God?). It is said: "أفي وحدانيته" (about His oneness). Then He alerted them to the attribute which requires that doubt never occur about it, which is His being the originator and creator of the world, so He said: "﴿فاطر السماوات والأرض﴾". "(فاطر)" is an attribute of God, and there is no harm in separating the described from its attribute by such a subject as this, so one may say: "في الدار زيد الحسنة" though the original structure is "في الدار الحسنة زيد". Zayd ibn 'Ali recited "فاطرَ" in the accusative as praise. When He mentioned that He is the originator of the world, and alerted to the attribute which is not appropriate to accompany doubt, He mentioned what He is upon of kindness to them and benevolence toward them, saying: "﴿يدعوكم لیغفر لكم﴾", that is, He calls you to faith, as He said: "﴿إذ تدعون إلى الإيمان﴾" [Ghafir: 10], or He calls you for the sake of forgiveness, like: "دعوته لينصرني" (I called him so that he would help me). The poet said:

"I called upon Miswar for what befell me, and he answered, so the answer of Miswar's two hands."

As for "﴿من ذنوبكم﴾", Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash went to the view that "من" is superfluous, meaning "ليغفر لكم ذنوبكم" (that He may forgive you your sins). The majority of the Basrans do not permit its superfluity in an affirmative statement, nor when a definite noun is in the genitive, and partition (tab'id) is valid in it, since what is forgiven is what is between them and God, unlike what is between them and the servants of injustices. By another way partition is valid, namely that Islam erases what came before it, and what is committed after faith of sins remains left unmentioned, is in God's will, and the promise is only of forgiveness of what preceded, not of what is incurred afterward. Al-Zamakhshari said something to the effect: the custom in addressing disbelievers is to say "من ذنوبكم", and in addressing believers "ذنوبكم", and this was to distinguish between the two addresses and so as not to equate the two groups, end quote. It is said: what is the benefit of the distinction in address when the meaning is shared, since the disbeliever when he believes and the believer when he repents are both sharers in forgiveness, (p-410) and what you imagined in it, the forgiveness of some sins for the disbeliever who believed, is present in the believer who repented. Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: as for the statement of the author of the Kashshaf, that the purpose is to distinguish the address to the believer from the address to the disbeliever, it is of the category of "tamamat" (absurdities); for if this partition occurs, there is no need to mention this answer, and if it does not occur, this statement is corrupt.

He said: "﴿إلى أجل مسمى﴾": until a time which we have specified, or we have specified its measure, if you believe; otherwise He will hasten you to destruction before that time, end quote. This is based on the view of the two terms (ajalayn), which is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah. The discussion of part of this was mentioned in Surat al-A'raf in His saying: "﴿ولكل أمة أجل﴾" [al-A'raf: 34]. It is said here: "ويؤخركم إلى أجل مسمى" before death, so He will not hasten the punishment upon you. "إن أنتم إلا بشر مثلنا" (You are only human beings like us), with no superiority between us and you, nor any superiority for you over us; so why are you singled out for prophethood to the exclusion of us? Al-Zamakhshari said: if God had sent messengers to humans, He would have made them of a nobler kind than them, namely angels, end quote. This is according to the Mu'tazilite doctrine of the preference of angels over others. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: in their saying there is a proposition of the improbability of sending humans. Some people said: rather they intended its impossibility, and they followed the path of the Barahimah, or of those among the philosophers who say that the genera do not admit this analogy. The apparent meaning of their words does not require that they went to this extreme, and what I have mentioned is indicated by their asking them for proof; and it is possible that their demand from them of a manifest authority was only by way of challenge, meaning: your sending is impossible; otherwise, bring a manifest authority, that is, you will never do that; so by this possibility their tendency toward the view of the philosophers is strengthened, end quote.

What appears is that their demand for a manifest authority, although the messengers had come to them with clear proofs, was only by way of obstinacy and contrivance; otherwise what they were brought of proofs and signs is sufficient for one who seeks insight. But they imitated their fathers in what they were upon of error. Do you not see that when they stated that they were like them, they said: "﴿تريدون أن تصدونا عما كان يعبد آباؤنا﴾", that is, your only aim is that we become followers of you and leave what we were raised upon, the religion of our fathers. Talhah recited "﴿أن تصدونا﴾" with the nun doubled, making "أن" the lightened form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), and supposing a separation between it and the verb, and the original was "تصدوننا", so the nun of the nominative was assimilated into the pronoun. The preferable reading is that "أن" is the binary particle which puts the imperfect in the subjunctive, but here it did not govern, rather it was made inoperative, just as those who read "﴿لمن أراد أن يتم الرضاعة﴾" [al-Baqarah: 233] with "يُتِمُّ" in the nominative did so, taking it as analogous to its sister "ما" (the verbal-masdar particle).

Then He alerted them to the attribute which requires that doubt never occur about it, which is His being the originator and creator of the world, so He said: "﴿فاطر السماوات والأرض﴾". "(فاطر)" is an attribute of God, and there is no harm in separating the described from its attribute by such a subject as this, so one may say: "في الدار زيد الحسنة" though the original structure is "في الدار الحسنة زيد". Zayd ibn 'Ali recited "فاطرَ" in the accusative as praise. When He mentioned that He is the originator of the world, and alerted to the attribute which is not appropriate to accompany doubt, He mentioned what He is upon of kindness to them and benevolence toward them, saying: "﴿يدعوكم لیغفر لكم﴾", that is, He calls you to faith, as He said: "﴿إذ تدعون إلى الإيمان﴾" [Ghafir: 10], or He calls you for the sake of forgiveness, like: "دعوته لينصرني" (I called him so that he would help me). The poet said:

"I called upon Miswar for what befell me, and he answered, so the answer of Miswar's two hands."

As for "﴿من ذنوبكم﴾", Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash went to the view that "من" is superfluous, meaning "ليغفر لكم ذنوبكم" (that He may forgive you your sins). The majority of the Basrans do not permit its superfluity in an affirmative statement, nor when a definite noun is in the genitive, and partition (tab'id) is valid in it, since what is forgiven is what is between them and God, unlike what is between them and the servants of injustices. By another way partition is valid, namely that Islam erases what came before it, and what is committed after faith of sins remains left unmentioned, is in God's will, and the promise is only of forgiveness of what preceded, not of what is incurred afterward. Al-Zamakhshari said something to the effect: the custom in addressing disbelievers is to say "من ذنوبكم", and in addressing believers "ذنوبكم", and this was to distinguish between the two addresses and so as not to equate the two groups, end quote. It is said: what is the benefit of the distinction in address when the meaning is shared, since the disbeliever when he believes and the believer when he repents are both sharers in forgiveness, (p-410) and what you imagined in it, the forgiveness of some sins for the disbeliever who believed, is present in the believer who repented. Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: as for the statement of the author of the Kashshaf, that the purpose is to distinguish the address to the believer from the address to the disbeliever, it is of the category of "tamamat" (absurdities); for if this partition occurs, there is no need to mention this answer, and if it does not occur, this statement is corrupt.

He said: "﴿إلى أجل مسمى﴾": until a time which we have specified, or we have specified its measure, if you believe; otherwise He will hasten you to destruction before that time, end quote. This is based on the view of the two terms (ajalayn), which is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah. The discussion of part of this was mentioned in Surat al-A'raf in His saying: "﴿ولكل أمة أجل﴾" [al-A'raf: 34]. It is said here: "ويؤخركم إلى أجل مسمى" before death, so He will not hasten the punishment upon you. "إن أنتم إلا بشر مثلنا" (You are only human beings like us), with no superiority between us and you, nor any superiority for you over us; so why are you singled out for prophethood to the exclusion of us? Al-Zamakhshari said: if God had sent messengers to humans, He would have made them of a nobler kind than them, namely angels, end quote. This is according to the Mu'tazilite doctrine of the preference of angels over others. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: in their saying there is a proposition of the improbability of sending humans. Some people said: rather they intended its impossibility, and they followed the path of the Barahimah, or of those among the philosophers who say that the genera do not admit this analogy. The apparent meaning of their words does not require that they went to this extreme, and what I have mentioned is indicated by their asking them for proof; and it is possible that their demand from them of a manifest authority was only by way of challenge, meaning: your sending is impossible; otherwise, bring a manifest authority, that is, you will never do that; so by this possibility their tendency toward the view of the philosophers is strengthened, end quote.

What appears is that their demand for a manifest authority, although the messengers had come to them with clear proofs, was only by way of obstinacy and contrivance; otherwise what they were brought of proofs and signs is sufficient for one who seeks insight. But they imitated their fathers in what they were upon of error. Do you not see that when they stated that they were like them, they said: "﴿تريدون أن تصدونا عما كان يعبد آباؤنا﴾", that is, your only aim is that we become followers of you and leave what we were raised upon, the religion of our fathers. Talhah recited "﴿أن تصدونا﴾" with the nun doubled, making "أن" the lightened form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), and supposing a separation between it and the verb, and the original was "تصدوننا", so the nun of the nominative was assimilated into the pronoun. The preferable reading is that "أن" is the binary particle which puts the imperfect in the subjunctive, but here it did not govern, rather it was made inoperative, just as those who read "﴿لمن أراد أن يتم الرضاعة﴾" [al-Baqarah: 233] with "يُتِمُّ" in the nominative did so, taking it as analogous to its sister "ما" (the verbal-masdar particle).

﴿They said to them, their messengers: "We are only humans like you, but God bestows His favour upon whomever He wills of His servants. It was not for us to bring you an authority except by God's leave. And upon God let the believers rely."﴾ ﴿"And why should we not rely upon God, when He has guided us to our paths? We will surely bear patiently what you inflict upon us. And upon God let those who rely (upon Him) rely."﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieved said to their messengers: "We will surely expel you from our land, or you will return to our religion." So their Lord revealed to them: "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿"And We will surely make you dwell in the land after them. That is for whoever fears My standing (before Me) and fears My threat."﴾ ﴿They sought victory, and every obstinate tyrant failed.﴾ ﴿Behind him is Hell, and he is given to drink of pus-water.﴾ ﴿He gulps it down and can barely swallow it; death comes to him from every place, yet he will not die; and behind him is a harsh punishment.﴾

(p-411) They (the disbelievers) conceded to the messengers that they resemble them in humanity alone. As for the other attributes in which the messengers were singled out, they were not like them in these. They did not mention the attribute by which they were distinguished, out of humility on their part and in attributing it to God. They did not explicitly mention God's favour upon them alone, but they expressed it generally, in "upon whomever He wills of His servants." The meaning is: He bestows prophethood upon whomever He wills to make a prophet. The meaning of "by God's leave" is: by His permission and will. That is, the sign you have proposed is not something we can bring, nor is it within our power; for this reason the construction is "it was not for us" (wa-ma kana lana), since it is a matter dependent upon God's will.

"Then let them rely" (fa-l-yatawakkal) is a command from them to the believers to rely (upon God). They intended by it themselves first, primarily, and commanded themselves with it, as if they said: "It is incumbent upon us to rely upon God in patience toward your opposition and enmity and what befalls us from you." Do you not see their saying: "And why should we not rely upon God?" Its meaning: "What excuse do we have for not relying upon God, when He has guided us, having done for us what necessitates our reliance upon Him, which is granting us success in being guided, each one of us, to the path that requires him to follow it in religion?" The first command, namely His saying "Then let the believers rely" (fa-l-yatawakkal al-mu'minun), is for initiating reliance, and the second is for steadfastness upon what they have newly undertaken of their reliance.

"We will surely bear patiently" (wa-la-nasbiranna) is the answer to an oath, and it indicates a prior mention of that which requires patience, which is harm. The "ma" (here) is verbal (masdariyyah, i.e., it forms a verbal noun with what follows), and they permitted that it be in the sense of "alladhi" (which). The pronoun is elided, that is: "what you have inflicted upon us" (ma adhaytumuhu-na, with the object pronoun omitted). Its original form was "bihi" (with it), so there are two opinions: has "bihi" been elided, or the preposition "bi", so that the verb reaches the pronoun? Al-Hasan read "li-yatawakkal" with a kasra on the lam of the imperative, which is the original form. "Aw" (or) is for one of the two matters: they swore that there was no escape from their expulsion of them or their return to their religion, as if they said: "One of these two will surely come to pass."

Interpreting "aw" here in the sense of "hatta" (until), or in the sense of "illa an" (except that), is the view of one who has not examined closely what follows it, because the construction "hatta" does not work, nor does the construction "illa an" with His saying "you will surely return" (la-ta'udunna), unlike "la-alzamanna-ka" (I will surely hold you to it) or "taqdiyyanni haqqi" (you shall pay me my due). The "return" (al-'awd) here means "becoming." Alternatively, it may be an address to the messengers and those who believed in them. The ruling of those who believed in them prevailed, because they had been in their religion before that, so it is correct to keep "la-ta'udunna" (you will return) applied to what is understood from it initially, since it had preceded that they had been in their religion. As for the messengers, they had never been in their religion at all. Or the meaning of their return to their religion is their silence about them and their being neglectful of them, not demanding of them belief in God and what the messengers brought.

Abu Hayyan notes that Abu Hayyah read "la-yuhlikanna al-zalimin" and "li-yuskinannakum" with the yā' of third-person address, taking into account His saying "So their Lord revealed to them," since its wording is that of the absent party. "And We will surely make you dwell" (wa-la-nuskinannakumu) came with the second-person pronoun, honouring them with direct address, and did not come with the third-person pronoun, as in His saying "So their Lord revealed to them." When they swore by them to expel the messengers and to return to their religion, God, exalted is He, swore to destroy them. What expulsion is greater than destruction, such that there is no return to it ever? And [the promise includes] the settling of the messengers and those who believed in them and their offspring in the land of those who swore to expel the messengers.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He specified "the wrongdoers" from among those who disbelieved, since it is possible that some of the disbelievers who uttered that statement might believe; He threatened the destruction only of those who were purely committed to wrongdoing. Others said: he meant by "the wrongdoers" the polytheists; God, exalted is He, said: "Indeed, polytheism is a tremendous wrong" (Luqman 13). The reference by "that" is to the inheritance of the land by the prophets and those who believed in them after the destruction of the wrongdoers, as in His saying, exalted is He, "And the good end is for the God-fearing" (al-A'raf 128).

"Maqam" can be a verbal noun or a place. Al-Farra' said: "maqami" is a verbal noun attributed to the agent, meaning: My standing over him with the preservation of his deeds and My watching over him, as in His saying: "Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned?" (al-Ra'd 33). Al-Zajjaj said: it is the place where he stands before Me for reckoning, and it is the standing place of God at which He makes His servants stand on the Day of Resurrection, as in His saying, exalted is He: "And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens" (al-Rahman 46). And (it is) with an inserted "maqam" (i.e., the word is in apposition or elided), meaning: for whoever fears Me.

The apparent view is that the pronoun in "wa-istaftahu" (they sought victory) refers to the prophets, meaning: they sought God's help against their enemies, as in His saying: "If you seek a decision, then the decision has come to you" (al-Anfal 19). It may also be from "al-futahah", which means judgement, i.e., they sought God's judgement and asked Him to decide between them. The seeking of victory by the messengers is frequent in the Qur'an, as in Noah's saying: "So judge between me and them with a judgement and save me" (al-Shu'ara' 118); Lot's saying: "My Lord, save me and my family from what they do" (al-Shu'ara' 169); Shu'ayb's saying: "Our Lord, judge between us and our people with truth" (al-A'raf 89); and Moses' saying: "Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh..." (Yunus 88), the verse.

Ibn Zayd said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, meaning: the disbelievers sought victory, in the manner of what Quraysh said: "Hasten to us our share" (Sad 16); and Abu Jahl's saying: "O God, if this is the truth from You, rain down stones upon us from the sky or bring us a painful punishment," and his saying: "O God, sever us from kinship and bring us what is unknown, so destroy him this morning." It seems that when their denial and harm became strong, and they were not hastened with punishment, they thought that what they had brought was false; so they sought victory in the manner of mockery and derision, like the people of Noah's saying: "Bring us what you threaten us with" (Hud 32); the people of Shu'ayb: "Then drop upon us fragments from the sky" (al-Shu'ara' 187); 'Ad: "We will not be punished" (al-Shu'ara' 138); and some of Quraysh: "Then rain down upon us stones from the sky" (al-Anfal 32).

It was said: the pronoun refers to both groups: the prophets and their deniers, because they all asked that the one in the right be helped and the one in the wrong be defeated. What strengthens the return of the pronoun to the messengers specifically is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Muhaysin: "wa-istaftihu" with a kasra on the ta', as an imperative addressed to the messengers, coordinated with "la-yuhlikanna" (He will surely destroy), meaning: their Lord revealed to them and said to them, "He will surely destroy," and He said to them, "Seek victory," i.e., ask for help, and ask it of your Lord.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that the people of Makkah sought victory, i.e., asked for rain, and "al-fath" means rain in the years of drought that were sent upon them by the prayer of the Messenger, and they were not watered. So He, glorified is He, mentioned that, and that He disappointed the hope of every obstinate tyrant, and that he is given to drink in Hell instead of his drink another water, which is the pus of the people of the Fire.

"Wa-istaftahu" according to this interpretation is a resumptive, independent statement, disconnected from the account of the messengers and their peoples; end of quotation.

"Wa-khaba" (and failed) is coordinated with an elided element whose estimate is: "So they were helped and triumphed. And every obstinate tyrant failed," and they are the people of the messengers. The explanation of "jabbar" has already been given. "'Anid" means one who persists in opposition, like "khalit" in the sense of "mukhalit" (one who mixes), according to the view of those who made the pronoun refer to the disbelievers, as if "wa-khaba" is coordinated with "wa-istaftahu."

"Min wara'ihi" (behind him): Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn al-Anbari said: it means "from after him." The poet said:
I swore, leaving you no doubt; and there is no refuge for a man from God.
Abu 'Ubaydah also said, as did Qutrub, al-Tabari and a group: "min wara'ihi" means "from in front of him," which is the meaning of al-Zamakhshari's saying: "from between his hands." And [a poet] recited:
Perhaps the distress in which I am will be followed by a near relief.

This is a description of his state in this world, because he is set in readiness for Hell, so it is as if it is before him while he is on its brink; or it is a description of his state in the Hereafter, when he is raised and made to stand. The poet said:
Do the Banu Marwan hope for my hearing and obedience, while the people of Tamim and the wilderness lie behind me?
Another said:
Is it not that behind me, if my death is delayed, lies the staff that the fingers bend around?

Wara' (behind, beyond) is said by Abu 'Ubayda and al-Azhari to be one of the words with contrary meanings (adداد, al-addad). It was also said that it is not among the addad. Tha'lab said: it is a name for whatever is hidden from you, whether it is in front of you or behind you. It was also said: it means "from behind him," that is, in pursuit of him, as you say "the matter is behind you," meaning it will come to you.

"Yusqa" (and he is given to drink) is coordinated with an omitted element whose implied sense is: "he is cast into it and given to drink," or it is coordinated with the governing element in "min wara'ihi," which occupies the position of a qualifier (sifa). The word "Jahannam" is in the nominative as the subject of the verb (fa'iliyya), and the apparent meaning is that "ma'" (water) is literal, and "sadid" (pus) is as well.

(p-413) Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Sadid" is a qualifier (na't) of "ma'" (water), as you say, "this is an iron ring," though it is not water. But since it has taken the place of water in our customary usage, it is called water. It was also said: it is a qualifier with the particle of comparison omitted, as you say, "I passed by a lion-like man" (rijulin asad), the implied sense being "like pus." According to Ibn 'Atiyya's view, it is the pus itself and not literally water; according to this view it is not pus, but that which is compared to pus.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Sadid" is an explicative apposition (atf bayan) to "ma'"; he said: "He is given to drink from water," so he made it vague, then clarified it with his saying "sadid." End of quotation. The Basrans do not permit explicative apposition in indefinite nouns, but the Kufans permitted it, and al-Farisi followed them, parsing "zaytunatin" (Q. 24:35) as an explicative apposition to "shajaratin mubarakatin" (Q. 24:35). Thus, according to the view of the Basrans, it is not permissible for "sadid" to be an explicative apposition.

Al-Hawfi said: "Sadid" is a qualifier of "ma'." Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak said: it is what flows from the bodies of the people of the Fire. Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Rabi' said: it is the washing-water of the people of the Fire in the Fire. It was also said: it is what flows from the private parts of fornicators, male and female. It was also said: "sadid" in the sense of "masdud 'anhu" (turned away from), that is, because of its loathsomeness one turns away from it, so it is derived from "sadd" (turning away).

Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned from the hadith of Abu Umama, from the Messenger (ﷺ), that he said concerning His saying: ﴿And he is given to drink of water like pus﴾ ﴿which he gulps﴾: "It is brought near to him, and he dislikes it. When it is brought close to him, it scorches his face and his scalp falls off. When he drinks it, it cuts his intestines until it comes out from his anus." "Yatajarra'uhu" means he strains to gulp it down.

"Wa la yakadu yusighuhu": that is, he does not nearly swallow it, so how could swallowing occur? The apparent sense here is the negation of his nearly swallowing it, and when nearness is negated, swallowing is negated too, as in His saying: ﴿he could hardly see it﴾ (Q. 24:40), meaning he came nowhere near seeing it, so how could he see it? As for the hadith: "it is brought to us, then he drinks it." If the hadith is sound, the meaning is: "he nearly does not swallow it before he drinks it, then he drinks it," as in: ﴿So they slaughtered her, though they nearly did not do it﴾ (Q. 2:71), meaning they nearly did not do it before the slaughter.

"Tajarra'a" is of the form "tafa''ala." It may carry several senses here: it may be reflexive (lil-mutawa'a), meaning "he made him gulp, so he gulped," like "I taught him, so he learned"; it may denote effort (lil-takallluf), like "tahallama" (he pretended to dream); it may denote continuing the action over a period of time (lil-muwasala), like "tafahhama" (he understood gradually), meaning he takes it little by little; or it may agree with the bare form, meaning "tajarra'ahu" (he gulped it), as you say "'adā al-shay'" and "ta'adahu" (he passed beyond it).

"Yatajarra'uhu" is either a qualifier of what precedes it, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yusqa," or a new independent sentence (isti'naf).

"Wa ya'tihi al-mawt": that is, its causes. The apparent sense of His saying "from every place" is "from the six directions," because of the dreadfulness of the pains he suffers. Ibrahim al-Taymi said: "from every place" means from his body, even from the ends of his hair. It was also said: even from the tips of his toes. The apparent sense is that this is in the Hereafter.

Al-Akhfash said: it means the afflictions that befall the disbeliever in this world, which he called "death," but this is far-fetched, because the context of the discourse indicates that this is among the conditions of the disbeliever in Jahannam.

His saying "wa ma huwa bi-mayyit" (and he is not dead) is because of the prolonged severity of death and the extension of its agonies.

"Min wara'ihi": the disagreement over "min wara'ihi" is like the disagreement over "min wara'ihi Jahannam" (Q. 14:16). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Wa min wara'ihi 'adhabun ghalizun" (and behind him is severe punishment): that is, at every moment he faces, he receives a punishment harsher and more severe than what came before. It is related from al-Fudayl: it is the cutting off of breaths and their confinement within the bodies. It was also said: the pronoun in "wara'ihi" refers to the previously mentioned punishment, not to every tyrant.

﴿They said to them, their messengers: "We are only humans like you, but God bestows His favour upon whomever He wills of His servants. It was not for us to bring you an authority except by God's leave. And upon God let the believers rely."﴾ ﴿"And why should we not rely upon God, when He has guided us to our paths? We will surely bear patiently what you inflict upon us. And upon God let those who rely (upon Him) rely."﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieved said to their messengers: "We will surely expel you from our land, or you will return to our religion." Al-Zajjaj said: it is the place where he stands before Me for reckoning, and it is the standing place of God at which He makes His servants stand on the Day of Resurrection, as in His saying, exalted is He: "And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens" (al-Rahman 46). And (it is) with an inserted "maqam" (i.e., the word is in apposition or elided), meaning: for whoever fears Me.

The apparent view is that the pronoun in "wa-istaftahu" (they sought victory) refers to the prophets, meaning: they sought God's help against their enemies, as in His saying: "If you seek a decision, then the decision has come to you" (al-Anfal 19). It may also be from "al-futahah", which means judgement, i.e., they sought God's judgement and asked Him to decide between them. The seeking of victory by the messengers is frequent in the Qur'an, as in Noah's saying: "So judge between me and them with a judgement and save me" (al-Shu'ara' 118); Lot's saying: "My Lord, save me and my family from what they do" (al-Shu'ara' 169); Shu'ayb's saying: "Our Lord, judge between us and our people with truth" (al-A'raf 89); and Moses' saying: "Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh..." (Yunus 88), the verse.

It seems that when their denial and harm became strong, and they were not hastened with punishment, they thought that what they had brought was false; so they sought victory in the manner of mockery and derision, like the people of Noah's saying: "Bring us what you threaten us with" (Hud 32); the people of Shu'ayb: "Then drop upon us fragments from the sky" (al-Shu'ara' 187); 'Ad: "We will not be punished" (al-Shu'ara' 138); and some of Quraysh: "Then rain down upon us stones from the sky" (al-Anfal 32).

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that the people of Makkah sought victory, i.e., asked for rain, and "al-fath" means rain in the years of drought that were sent upon them by the prayer of the Messenger, and they were not watered. So He, glorified is He, mentioned that, and that He disappointed the hope of every obstinate tyrant, and that he is given to drink in Hell instead of his drink another water, which is the pus of the people of the Fire.

"Wa-istaftahu" according to this interpretation is a resumptive, independent statement, disconnected from the account of the messengers and their peoples; end of quotation.

"Wa-khaba" (and failed) is coordinated with an elided element whose estimate is: "So they were helped and triumphed. And every obstinate tyrant failed," and they are the people of the messengers. The explanation of "jabbar" has already been given. "Min wara'ihi" (behind him): Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn al-Anbari said: it means "from after him." The poet said:
I swore, leaving you no doubt; and there is no refuge for a man from God.
Abu 'Ubaydah also said, as did Qutrub, al-Tabari and a group: "min wara'ihi" means "from in front of him," which is the meaning of al-Zamakhshari's saying: "from between his hands." And [a poet] recited:
Perhaps the distress in which I am will be followed by a near relief.

This is a description of his state in this world, because he is set in readiness for Hell, so it is as if it is before him while he is on its brink; or it is a description of his state in the Hereafter, when he is raised and made to stand. The poet said:
Do the Banu Marwan hope for my hearing and obedience, while the people of Tamim and the wilderness lie behind me?
Another said:
Is it not that behind me, if my death is delayed, lies the staff that the fingers bend around?

Wara' (behind, beyond) is said by Abu 'Ubayda and al-Azhari to be one of the words with contrary meanings (adداد, al-addad). It was also said that it is not among the addad. The word "Jahannam" is in the nominative as the subject of the verb (fa'iliyya), and the apparent meaning is that "ma'" (water) is literal, and "sadid" (pus) is as well.

"Yatajarra'uhu" means he strains to gulp it down.

"Wa la yakadu yusighuhu": that is, he does not nearly swallow it, so how could swallowing occur? The apparent sense here is the negation of his nearly swallowing it, and when nearness is negated, swallowing is negated too, as in His saying: ﴿he could hardly see it﴾ (Q. 24:40), meaning he came nowhere near seeing it, so how could he see it? "Yatajarra'uhu" is either a qualifier of what precedes it, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yusqa," or a new independent sentence (isti'naf).

﴿They said to them, their messengers: "We are only humans like you, but God bestows His favour upon whomever He wills of His servants. It was not for us to bring you an authority except by God's leave. And upon God let the believers rely."﴾ ﴿"And why should we not rely upon God, when He has guided us to our paths? We will surely bear patiently what you inflict upon us. And upon God let those who rely (upon Him) rely."﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieved said to their messengers: "We will surely expel you from our land, or you will return to our religion." So their Lord revealed to them: "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿"And We will surely make you dwell in the land after them. That is for whoever fears My standing (before Me) and fears My threat."﴾ ﴿They sought victory, and every obstinate tyrant failed.﴾ ﴿Behind him is Hell, and he is given to drink of pus-water.﴾ ﴿He gulps it down and can barely swallow it; death comes to him from every place, yet he will not die; and behind him is a harsh punishment.﴾

(p-411) They (the disbelievers) conceded to the messengers that they resemble them in humanity alone. As for the other attributes in which the messengers were singled out, they were not like them in these. They did not mention the attribute by which they were distinguished, out of humility on their part and in attributing it to God. They did not explicitly mention God's favour upon them alone, but they expressed it generally, in "upon whomever He wills of His servants." The meaning is: He bestows prophethood upon whomever He wills to make a prophet. The meaning of "by God's leave" is: by His permission and will. That is, the sign you have proposed is not something we can bring, nor is it within our power; for this reason the construction is "it was not for us" (wa-ma kana lana), since it is a matter dependent upon God's will.

"Then let them rely" (fa-l-yatawakkal) is a command from them to the believers to rely (upon God). They intended by it themselves first, primarily, and commanded themselves with it, as if they said: "It is incumbent upon us to rely upon God in patience toward your opposition and enmity and what befalls us from you." Do you not see their saying: "And why should we not rely upon God?" Its meaning: "What excuse do we have for not relying upon God, when He has guided us, having done for us what necessitates our reliance upon Him, which is granting us success in being guided, each one of us, to the path that requires him to follow it in religion?" The first command, namely His saying "Then let the believers rely" (fa-l-yatawakkal al-mu'minun), is for initiating reliance, and the second is for steadfastness upon what they have newly undertaken of their reliance.

"We will surely bear patiently" (wa-la-nasbiranna) is the answer to an oath, and it indicates a prior mention of that which requires patience, which is harm. The "ma" (here) is verbal (masdariyyah, i.e., it forms a verbal noun with what follows), and they permitted that it be in the sense of "alladhi" (which). The pronoun is elided, that is: "what you have inflicted upon us" (ma adhaytumuhu-na, with the object pronoun omitted). Its original form was "bihi" (with it), so there are two opinions: has "bihi" been elided, or the preposition "bi", so that the verb reaches the pronoun? Al-Hasan read "li-yatawakkal" with a kasra on the lam of the imperative, which is the original form. "Aw" (or) is for one of the two matters: they swore that there was no escape from their expulsion of them or their return to their religion, as if they said: "One of these two will surely come to pass."

Interpreting "aw" here in the sense of "hatta" (until), or in the sense of "illa an" (except that), is the view of one who has not examined closely what follows it, because the construction "hatta" does not work, nor does the construction "illa an" with His saying "you will surely return" (la-ta'udunna), unlike "la-alzamanna-ka" (I will surely hold you to it) or "taqdiyyanni haqqi" (you shall pay me my due). The "return" (al-'awd) here means "becoming." Alternatively, it may be an address to the messengers and those who believed in them. The ruling of those who believed in them prevailed, because they had been in their religion before that, so it is correct to keep "la-ta'udunna" (you will return) applied to what is understood from it initially, since it had preceded that they had been in their religion. As for the messengers, they had never been in their religion at all. Or the meaning of their return to their religion is their silence about them and their being neglectful of them, not demanding of them belief in God and what the messengers brought.

Abu Hayyan notes that Abu Hayyah read "la-yuhlikanna al-zalimin" and "li-yuskinannakum" with the yā' of third-person address, taking into account His saying "So their Lord revealed to them," since its wording is that of the absent party. "And We will surely make you dwell" (wa-la-nuskinannakumu) came with the second-person pronoun, honouring them with direct address, and did not come with the third-person pronoun, as in His saying "So their Lord revealed to them." When they swore by them to expel the messengers and to return to their religion, God, exalted is He, swore to destroy them. What expulsion is greater than destruction, such that there is no return to it ever? And [the promise includes] the settling of the messengers and those who believed in them and their offspring in the land of those who swore to expel the messengers.
