They did not explicitly mention God's favour upon them alone, but they expressed it generally, in "upon whomever He wills of His servants." The meaning is: He bestows prophethood upon whomever He wills to make a prophet. The meaning of "by God's leave" is: by His permission and will. That is, the sign you have proposed is not something we can bring, nor is it within our power; for this reason the construction is "it was not for us" (wa-ma kana lana), since it is a matter dependent upon God's will.

"Then let them rely" (fa-l-yatawakkal) is a command from them to the believers to rely (upon God). They intended by it themselves first, primarily, and commanded themselves with it, as if they said: "It is incumbent upon us to rely upon God in patience toward your opposition and enmity and what befalls us from you." Do you not see their saying: "And why should we not rely upon God?" Its meaning: "What excuse do we have for not relying upon God, when He has guided us, having done for us what necessitates our reliance upon Him, which is granting us success in being guided, each one of us, to the path that requires him to follow it in religion?" The first command, namely His saying "Then let the believers rely" (fa-l-yatawakkal al-mu'minun), is for initiating reliance, and the second is for steadfastness upon what they have newly undertaken of their reliance.

"We will surely bear patiently" (wa-la-nasbiranna) is the answer to an oath, and it indicates a prior mention of that which requires patience, which is harm. The "ma" (here) is verbal (masdariyyah, i.e., it forms a verbal noun with what follows), and they permitted that it be in the sense of "alladhi" (which). The pronoun is elided, that is: "what you have inflicted upon us" (ma adhaytumuhu-na, with the object pronoun omitted). Its original form was "bihi" (with it), so there are two opinions: has "bihi" been elided, or the preposition "bi", so that the verb reaches the pronoun? Al-Hasan read "li-yatawakkal" with a kasra on the lam of the imperative, which is the original form. "Aw" (or) is for one of the two matters: they swore that there was no escape from their expulsion of them or their return to their religion, as if they said: "One of these two will surely come to pass."

Interpreting "aw" here in the sense of "hatta" (until), or in the sense of "illa an" (except that), is the view of one who has not examined closely what follows it, because the construction "hatta" does not work, nor does the construction "illa an" with His saying "you will surely return" (la-ta'udunna), unlike "la-alzamanna-ka" (I will surely hold you to it) or "taqdiyyanni haqqi" (you shall pay me my due). The "return" (al-'awd) here means "becoming." Alternatively, it may be an address to the messengers and those who believed in them. The ruling of those who believed in them prevailed, because they had been in their religion before that, so it is correct to keep "la-ta'udunna" (you will return) applied to what is understood from it initially, since it had preceded that they had been in their religion. As for the messengers, they had never been in their religion at all. Or the meaning of their return to their religion is their silence about them and their being neglectful of them, not demanding of them belief in God and what the messengers brought.

Abu Hayyan notes that Abu Hayyah read "la-yuhlikanna al-zalimin" and "li-yuskinannakum" with the yā' of third-person address, taking into account His saying "So their Lord revealed to them," since its wording is that of the absent party. "And We will surely make you dwell" (wa-la-nuskinannakumu) came with the second-person pronoun, honouring them with direct address, and did not come with the third-person pronoun, as in His saying "So their Lord revealed to them." When they swore by them to expel the messengers and to return to their religion, God, exalted is He, swore to destroy them. What expulsion is greater than destruction, such that there is no return to it ever? And [the promise includes] the settling of the messengers and those who believed in them and their offspring in the land of those who swore to expel the messengers.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He specified "the wrongdoers" from among those who disbelieved, since it is possible that some of the disbelievers who uttered that statement might believe; He threatened the destruction only of those who were purely committed to wrongdoing. Others said: he meant by "the wrongdoers" the polytheists; God, exalted is He, said: "Indeed, polytheism is a tremendous wrong" (Luqman 13). The reference by "that" is to the inheritance of the land by the prophets and those who believed in them after the destruction of the wrongdoers, as in His saying, exalted is He, "And the good end is for the God-fearing" (al-A'raf 128).

"Maqam" can be a verbal noun or a place. Al-Farra' said: "maqami" is a verbal noun attributed to the agent, meaning: My standing over him with the preservation of his deeds and My watching over him, as in His saying: "Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned?" Al-Zajjaj said: it is the place where he stands before Me for reckoning, and it is the standing place of God at which He makes His servants stand on the Day of Resurrection, as in His saying, exalted is He: "And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens" (al-Rahman 46). And (it is) with an inserted "maqam" (i.e., the word is in apposition or elided), meaning: for whoever fears Me.

The apparent view is that the pronoun in "wa-istaftahu" (they sought victory) refers to the prophets, meaning: they sought God's help against their enemies, as in His saying: "If you seek a decision, then the decision has come to you" (al-Anfal 19). It may also be from "al-futahah", which means judgement, i.e., they sought God's judgement and asked Him to decide between them. The seeking of victory by the messengers is frequent in the Qur'an, as in Noah's saying: "So judge between me and them with a judgement and save me" (al-Shu'ara' 118); Lot's saying: "My Lord, save me and my family from what they do" (al-Shu'ara' 169); Shu'ayb's saying: "Our Lord, judge between us and our people with truth" (al-A'raf 89); and Moses' saying: "Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh..." (Yunus 88), the verse.

It seems that when their denial and harm became strong, and they were not hastened with punishment, they thought that what they had brought was false; so they sought victory in the manner of mockery and derision, like the people of Noah's saying: "Bring us what you threaten us with" (Hud 32); the people of Shu'ayb: "Then drop upon us fragments from the sky" (al-Shu'ara' 187); 'Ad: "We will not be punished" (al-Shu'ara' 138); and some of Quraysh: "Then rain down upon us stones from the sky" (al-Anfal 32).

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that the people of Makkah sought victory, i.e., asked for rain, and "al-fath" means rain in the years of drought that were sent upon them by the prayer of the Messenger, and they were not watered. So He, glorified is He, mentioned that, and that He disappointed the hope of every obstinate tyrant, and that he is given to drink in Hell instead of his drink another water, which is the pus of the people of the Fire.

"Wa-istaftahu" according to this interpretation is a resumptive, independent statement, disconnected from the account of the messengers and their peoples; end of quotation.

"Wa-khaba" (and failed) is coordinated with an elided element whose estimate is: "So they were helped and triumphed. And every obstinate tyrant failed," and they are the people of the messengers. The explanation of "jabbar" has already been given. "'Anid" means one who persists in opposition, like "khalit" in the sense of "mukhalit" (one who mixes), according to the view of those who made the pronoun refer to the disbelievers, as if "wa-khaba" is coordinated with "wa-istaftahu."

"Min wara'ihi" (behind him): Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn al-Anbari said: it means "from after him." The poet said:
I swore, leaving you no doubt; and there is no refuge for a man from God.
Abu 'Ubaydah also said, as did Qutrub, al-Tabari and a group: "min wara'ihi" means "from in front of him," which is the meaning of al-Zamakhshari's saying: "from between his hands." And [a poet] recited:
Perhaps the distress in which I am will be followed by a near relief.

This is a description of his state in this world, because he is set in readiness for Hell, so it is as if it is before him while he is on its brink; or it is a description of his state in the Hereafter, when he is raised and made to stand. The poet said:
Do the Banu Marwan hope for my hearing and obedience, while the people of Tamim and the wilderness lie behind me?
Another said:
Is it not that behind me, if my death is delayed, lies the staff that the fingers bend around?

Wara' (behind, beyond) is said by Abu 'Ubayda and al-Azhari to be one of the words with contrary meanings (adداد, al-addad). It was also said that it is not among the addad. It was also said: it means "from behind him," that is, in pursuit of him, as you say "the matter is behind you," meaning it will come to you.

The word "Jahannam" is in the nominative as the subject of the verb (fa'iliyya), and the apparent meaning is that "ma'" (water) is literal, and "sadid" (pus) is as well.

It was also said: "sadid" in the sense of "masdud 'anhu" (turned away from), that is, because of its loathsomeness one turns away from it, so it is derived from "sadd" (turning away).

Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned from the hadith of Abu Umama, from the Messenger (ﷺ), that he said concerning His saying: ﴿And he is given to drink of water like pus﴾ ﴿which he gulps﴾: "It is brought near to him, and he dislikes it. When it is brought close to him, it scorches his face and his scalp falls off. When he drinks it, it cuts his intestines until it comes out from his anus." "Yatajarra'uhu" means he strains to gulp it down.

"Wa la yakadu yusighuhu": that is, he does not nearly swallow it, so how could swallowing occur? The apparent sense here is the negation of his nearly swallowing it, and when nearness is negated, swallowing is negated too, as in His saying: ﴿he could hardly see it﴾ (Q. 24:40), meaning he came nowhere near seeing it, so how could he see it? As for the hadith: "it is brought to us, then he drinks it." If the hadith is sound, the meaning is: "he nearly does not swallow it before he drinks it, then he drinks it," as in: ﴿So they slaughtered her, though they nearly did not do it﴾ (Q. 2:71), meaning they nearly did not do it before the slaughter.

"Tajarra'a" is of the form "tafa''ala." It may carry several senses here: it may be reflexive (lil-mutawa'a), meaning "he made him gulp, so he gulped," like "I taught him, so he learned"; it may denote effort (lil-takallluf), like "tahallama" (he pretended to dream); it may denote continuing the action over a period of time (lil-muwasala), like "tafahhama" (he understood gradually), meaning he takes it little by little; or it may agree with the bare form, meaning "tajarra'ahu" (he gulped it), as you say "'adā al-shay'" and "ta'adahu" (he passed beyond it).

"Yatajarra'uhu" is either a qualifier of what precedes it, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yusqa," or a new independent sentence (isti'naf).

"Wa ya'tihi al-mawt": that is, its causes. The apparent sense of His saying "from every place" is "from the six directions," because of the dreadfulness of the pains he suffers. Ibrahim al-Taymi said: "from every place" means from his body, even from the ends of his hair. It was also said: even from the tips of his toes. The apparent sense is that this is in the Hereafter.

Al-Akhfash said: it means the afflictions that befall the disbeliever in this world, which he called "death," but this is far-fetched, because the context of the discourse indicates that this is among the conditions of the disbeliever in Jahannam.

His saying "wa ma huwa bi-mayyit" (and he is not dead) is because of the prolonged severity of death and the extension of its agonies.

"Min wara'ihi": the disagreement over "min wara'ihi" is like the disagreement over "min wara'ihi Jahannam" (Q. 14:16). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Wa min wara'ihi 'adhabun ghalizun" (and behind him is severe punishment): that is, at every moment he faces, he receives a punishment harsher and more severe than what came before. It is related from al-Fudayl: it is the cutting off of breaths and their confinement within the bodies. It was also said: the pronoun in "wara'ihi" refers to the previously mentioned punishment, not to every tyrant.

﴿They said to them, their messengers: "We are only humans like you, but God bestows His favour upon whomever He wills of His servants. It was not for us to bring you an authority except by God's leave. And upon God let the believers rely."﴾ ﴿"And why should we not rely upon God, when He has guided us to our paths? We will surely bear patiently what you inflict upon us. And upon God let those who rely (upon Him) rely."﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieved said to their messengers: "We will surely expel you from our land, or you will return to our religion." So their Lord revealed to them: "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿"And We will surely make you dwell in the land after them. That is for whoever fears My standing (before Me) and fears My threat."﴾ ﴿They sought victory, and every obstinate tyrant failed.﴾ ﴿Behind him is Hell, and he is given to drink of pus-water.﴾ ﴿He gulps it down and can barely swallow it; death comes to him from every place, yet he will not die; and behind him is a harsh punishment.﴾

It was also said: "sadid" in the sense of "masdud 'anhu" (turned away from), that is, because of its loathsomeness one turns away from it, so it is derived from "sadd" (turning away).

Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned from the hadith of Abu Umama, from the Messenger (ﷺ), that he said concerning His saying: ﴿And he is given to drink of water like pus﴾ ﴿which he gulps﴾: "It is brought near to him, and he dislikes it. When it is brought close to him, it scorches his face and his scalp falls off. When he drinks it, it cuts his intestines until it comes out from his anus." "Yatajarra'uhu" means he strains to gulp it down.

"Wa la yakadu yusighuhu": that is, he does not nearly swallow it, so how could swallowing occur? The apparent sense here is the negation of his nearly swallowing it, and when nearness is negated, swallowing is negated too, as in His saying: ﴿he could hardly see it﴾ (Q. 24:40), meaning he came nowhere near seeing it, so how could he see it? As for the hadith: "it is brought to us, then he drinks it." If the hadith is sound, the meaning is: "he nearly does not swallow it before he drinks it, then he drinks it," as in: ﴿So they slaughtered her, though they nearly did not do it﴾ (Q. 2:71), meaning they nearly did not do it before the slaughter.

"Tajarra'a" is of the form "tafa''ala." It may carry several senses here: it may be reflexive (lil-mutawa'a), meaning "he made him gulp, so he gulped," like "I taught him, so he learned"; it may denote effort (lil-takallluf), like "tahallama" (he pretended to dream); it may denote continuing the action over a period of time (lil-muwasala), like "tafahhama" (he understood gradually), meaning he takes it little by little; or it may agree with the bare form, meaning "tajarra'ahu" (he gulped it), as you say "'adā al-shay'" and "ta'adahu" (he passed beyond it).

"Yatajarra'uhu" is either a qualifier of what precedes it, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yusqa," or a new independent sentence (isti'naf).

"Wa ya'tihi al-mawt": that is, its causes. The apparent sense of His saying "from every place" is "from the six directions," because of the dreadfulness of the pains he suffers. Ibrahim al-Taymi said: "from every place" means from his body, even from the ends of his hair. It was also said: even from the tips of his toes. The apparent sense is that this is in the Hereafter.

Al-Akhfash said: it means the afflictions that befall the disbeliever in this world, which he called "death," but this is far-fetched, because the context of the discourse indicates that this is among the conditions of the disbeliever in Jahannam.

His saying "wa ma huwa bi-mayyit" (and he is not dead) is because of the prolonged severity of death and the extension of its agonies.

"Min wara'ihi": the disagreement over "min wara'ihi" is like the disagreement over "min wara'ihi Jahannam" (Q. 14:16). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Wa min wara'ihi 'adhabun ghalizun" (and behind him is severe punishment): that is, at every moment he faces, he receives a punishment harsher and more severe than what came before. It is related from al-Fudayl: it is the cutting off of breaths and their confinement within the bodies. It was also said: the pronoun in "wara'ihi" refers to the previously mentioned punishment, not to every tyrant.

﴿They said to them, their messengers: "We are only humans like you, but God bestows His favour upon whomever He wills of His servants. It was not for us to bring you an authority except by God's leave. And upon God let the believers rely."﴾ ﴿"And why should we not rely upon God, when He has guided us to our paths? We will surely bear patiently what you inflict upon us. And upon God let those who rely (upon Him) rely."﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieved said to their messengers: "We will surely expel you from our land, or you will return to our religion." So their Lord revealed to them: "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿"And We will surely make you dwell in the land after them. That is for whoever fears My standing (before Me) and fears My threat."﴾ ﴿They sought victory, and every obstinate tyrant failed.﴾ ﴿Behind him is Hell, and he is given to drink of pus-water.﴾ ﴿He gulps it down and can barely swallow it; death comes to him from every place, yet he will not die; and behind him is a harsh punishment.﴾

(p-411) They (the disbelievers) conceded to the messengers that they resemble them in humanity alone. As for the other attributes in which the messengers were singled out, they were not like them in these. They did not mention the attribute by which they were distinguished, out of humility on their part and in attributing it to God. They did not explicitly mention God's favour upon them alone, but they expressed it generally, in "upon whomever He wills of His servants." The meaning is: He bestows prophethood upon whomever He wills to make a prophet. The meaning of "by God's leave" is: by His permission and will. That is, the sign you have proposed is not something we can bring, nor is it within our power; for this reason the construction is "it was not for us" (wa-ma kana lana), since it is a matter dependent upon God's will.

"Then let them rely" (fa-l-yatawakkal) is a command from them to the believers to rely (upon God). They intended by it themselves first, primarily, and commanded themselves with it, as if they said: "It is incumbent upon us to rely upon God in patience toward your opposition and enmity and what befalls us from you." Do you not see their saying: "And why should we not rely upon God?" Its meaning: "What excuse do we have for not relying upon God, when He has guided us, having done for us what necessitates our reliance upon Him, which is granting us success in being guided, each one of us, to the path that requires him to follow it in religion?" The first command, namely His saying "Then let the believers rely" (fa-l-yatawakkal al-mu'minun), is for initiating reliance, and the second is for steadfastness upon what they have newly undertaken of their reliance.

"We will surely bear patiently" (wa-la-nasbiranna) is the answer to an oath, and it indicates a prior mention of that which requires patience, which is harm. The "ma" (here) is verbal (masdariyyah, i.e., it forms a verbal noun with what follows), and they permitted that it be in the sense of "alladhi" (which). The pronoun is elided, that is: "what you have inflicted upon us" (ma adhaytumuhu-na, with the object pronoun omitted). Its original form was "bihi" (with it), so there are two opinions: has "bihi" been elided, or the preposition "bi", so that the verb reaches the pronoun? Al-Hasan read "li-yatawakkal" with a kasra on the lam of the imperative, which is the original form. "Aw" (or) is for one of the two matters: they swore that there was no escape from their expulsion of them or their return to their religion, as if they said: "One of these two will surely come to pass."

Interpreting "aw" here in the sense of "hatta" (until), or in the sense of "illa an" (except that), is the view of one who has not examined closely what follows it, because the construction "hatta" does not work, nor does the construction "illa an" with His saying "you will surely return" (la-ta'udunna), unlike "la-alzamanna-ka" (I will surely hold you to it) or "taqdiyyanni haqqi" (you shall pay me my due). The "return" (al-'awd) here means "becoming." Alternatively, it may be an address to the messengers and those who believed in them. The ruling of those who believed in them prevailed, because they had been in their religion before that, so it is correct to keep "la-ta'udunna" (you will return) applied to what is understood from it initially, since it had preceded that they had been in their religion. As for the messengers, they had never been in their religion at all. Or the meaning of their return to their religion is their silence about them and their being neglectful of them, not demanding of them belief in God and what the messengers brought.

Abu Hayyan notes that Abu Hayyah read "la-yuhlikanna al-zalimin" and "li-yuskinannakum" with the yā' of third-person address, taking into account His saying "So their Lord revealed to them," since its wording is that of the absent party. "And We will surely make you dwell" (wa-la-nuskinannakumu) came with the second-person pronoun, honouring them with direct address, and did not come with the third-person pronoun, as in His saying "So their Lord revealed to them." When they swore by them to expel the messengers and to return to their religion, God, exalted is He, swore to destroy them. What expulsion is greater than destruction, such that there is no return to it ever? And [the promise includes] the settling of the messengers and those who believed in them and their offspring in the land of those who swore to expel the messengers.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He specified "the wrongdoers" from among those who disbelieved, since it is possible that some of the disbelievers who uttered that statement might believe; He threatened the destruction only of those who were purely committed to wrongdoing. Others said: he meant by "the wrongdoers" the polytheists; God, exalted is He, said: "Indeed, polytheism is a tremendous wrong" (Luqman 13). The reference by "that" is to the inheritance of the land by the prophets and those who believed in them after the destruction of the wrongdoers, as in His saying, exalted is He, "And the good end is for the God-fearing" (al-A'raf 128).

"Maqam" can be a verbal noun or a place. Al-Farra' said: "maqami" is a verbal noun attributed to the agent, meaning: My standing over him with the preservation of his deeds and My watching over him, as in His saying: "Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned?" (al-Ra'd 33). Al-Zajjaj said: it is the place where he stands before Me for reckoning, and it is the standing place of God at which He makes His servants stand on the Day of Resurrection, as in His saying, exalted is He: "And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens" (al-Rahman 46). And (it is) with an inserted "maqam" (i.e., the word is in apposition or elided), meaning: for whoever fears Me.

The apparent view is that the pronoun in "wa-istaftahu" (they sought victory) refers to the prophets, meaning: they sought God's help against their enemies, as in His saying: "If you seek a decision, then the decision has come to you" (al-Anfal 19). It may also be from "al-futahah", which means judgement, i.e., they sought God's judgement and asked Him to decide between them. The seeking of victory by the messengers is frequent in the Qur'an, as in Noah's saying: "So judge between me and them with a judgement and save me" (al-Shu'ara' 118); Lot's saying: "My Lord, save me and my family from what they do" (al-Shu'ara' 169); Shu'ayb's saying: "Our Lord, judge between us and our people with truth" (al-A'raf 89); and Moses' saying: "Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh..." (Yunus 88), the verse.

Ibn Zayd said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, meaning: the disbelievers sought victory, in the manner of what Quraysh said: "Hasten to us our share" (Sad 16); and Abu Jahl's saying: "O God, if this is the truth from You, rain down stones upon us from the sky or bring us a painful punishment," and his saying: "O God, sever us from kinship and bring us what is unknown, so destroy him this morning." It seems that when their denial and harm became strong, and they were not hastened with punishment, they thought that what they had brought was false; so they sought victory in the manner of mockery and derision, like the people of Noah's saying: "Bring us what you threaten us with" (Hud 32); the people of Shu'ayb: "Then drop upon us fragments from the sky" (al-Shu'ara' 187); 'Ad: "We will not be punished" (al-Shu'ara' 138); and some of Quraysh: "Then rain down upon us stones from the sky" (al-Anfal 32).

It was said: the pronoun refers to both groups: the prophets and their deniers, because they all asked that the one in the right be helped and the one in the wrong be defeated. What strengthens the return of the pronoun to the messengers specifically is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Muhaysin: "wa-istaftihu" with a kasra on the ta', as an imperative addressed to the messengers, coordinated with "la-yuhlikanna" (He will surely destroy), meaning: their Lord revealed to them and said to them, "He will surely destroy," and He said to them, "Seek victory," i.e., ask for help, and ask it of your Lord.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that the people of Makkah sought victory, i.e., asked for rain, and "al-fath" means rain in the years of drought that were sent upon them by the prayer of the Messenger, and they were not watered. So He, glorified is He, mentioned that, and that He disappointed the hope of every obstinate tyrant, and that he is given to drink in Hell instead of his drink another water, which is the pus of the people of the Fire.

"Wa-istaftahu" according to this interpretation is a resumptive, independent statement, disconnected from the account of the messengers and their peoples; end of quotation.

"Wa-khaba" (and failed) is coordinated with an elided element whose estimate is: "So they were helped and triumphed. And every obstinate tyrant failed," and they are the people of the messengers. The explanation of "jabbar" has already been given. "'Anid" means one who persists in opposition, like "khalit" in the sense of "mukhalit" (one who mixes), according to the view of those who made the pronoun refer to the disbelievers, as if "wa-khaba" is coordinated with "wa-istaftahu."

"Min wara'ihi" (behind him): Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn al-Anbari said: it means "from after him." The poet said:
I swore, leaving you no doubt; and there is no refuge for a man from God.
Abu 'Ubaydah also said, as did Qutrub, al-Tabari and a group: "min wara'ihi" means "from in front of him," which is the meaning of al-Zamakhshari's saying: "from between his hands." And [a poet] recited:
Perhaps the distress in which I am will be followed by a near relief.

This is a description of his state in this world, because he is set in readiness for Hell, so it is as if it is before him while he is on its brink; or it is a description of his state in the Hereafter, when he is raised and made to stand. The poet said:
Do the Banu Marwan hope for my hearing and obedience, while the people of Tamim and the wilderness lie behind me?
Another said:
Is it not that behind me, if my death is delayed, lies the staff that the fingers bend around?

Wara' (behind, beyond) is said by Abu 'Ubayda and al-Azhari to be one of the words with contrary meanings (adداد, al-addad). It was also said that it is not among the addad. Tha'lab said: it is a name for whatever is hidden from you, whether it is in front of you or behind you. It was also said: it means "from behind him," that is, in pursuit of him, as you say "the matter is behind you," meaning it will come to you.

"Yusqa" (and he is given to drink) is coordinated with an omitted element whose implied sense is: "he is cast into it and given to drink," or it is coordinated with the governing element in "min wara'ihi," which occupies the position of a qualifier (sifa). The word "Jahannam" is in the nominative as the subject of the verb (fa'iliyya), and the apparent meaning is that "ma'" (water) is literal, and "sadid" (pus) is as well.

(p-413) Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Sadid" is a qualifier (na't) of "ma'" (water), as you say, "this is an iron ring," though it is not water. But since it has taken the place of water in our customary usage, it is called water. It was also said: it is a qualifier with the particle of comparison omitted, as you say, "I passed by a lion-like man" (rijulin asad), the implied sense being "like pus." According to Ibn 'Atiyya's view, it is the pus itself and not literally water; according to this view it is not pus, but that which is compared to pus.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Sadid" is an explicative apposition (atf bayan) to "ma'"; he said: "He is given to drink from water," so he made it vague, then clarified it with his saying "sadid." End of quotation. The Basrans do not permit explicative apposition in indefinite nouns, but the Kufans permitted it, and al-Farisi followed them, parsing "zaytunatin" (Q. 24:35) as an explicative apposition to "shajaratin mubarakatin" (Q. 24:35). Thus, according to the view of the Basrans, it is not permissible for "sadid" to be an explicative apposition.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that the people of Makkah sought victory, i.e., asked for rain, and "al-fath" means rain in the years of drought that were sent upon them by the prayer of the Messenger, and they were not watered. So He, glorified is He, mentioned that, and that He disappointed the hope of every obstinate tyrant, and that he is given to drink in Hell instead of his drink another water, which is the pus of the people of the Fire.

"Wa-istaftahu" according to this interpretation is a resumptive, independent statement, disconnected from the account of the messengers and their peoples; end of quotation.

"Wa-khaba" (and failed) is coordinated with an elided element whose estimate is: "So they were helped and triumphed. And every obstinate tyrant failed," and they are the people of the messengers. I swore, leaving you no doubt; and there is no refuge for a man from God.
Abu 'Ubaydah also said, as did Qutrub, al-Tabari and a group: "min wara'ihi" means "from in front of him," which is the meaning of al-Zamakhshari's saying: "from between his hands." And [a poet] recited:

﴿They said to them, their messengers: "We are only humans like you, but God bestows His favour upon whomever He wills of His servants. And upon God let those who rely (upon Him) rely."﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieved said to their messengers: "We will surely expel you from our land, or you will return to our religion." That is, the sign you have proposed is not something we can bring, nor is it within our power; for this reason the construction is "it was not for us" (wa-ma kana lana), since it is a matter dependent upon God's will.

Al-Hasan read "li-yatawakkal" with a kasra on the lam of the imperative, which is the original form. "Aw" (or) is for one of the two matters: they swore that there was no escape from their expulsion of them or their return to their religion, as if they said: "One of these two will surely come to pass."

Interpreting "aw" here in the sense of "hatta" (until), or in the sense of "illa an" (except that), is the view of one who has not examined closely what follows it, because the construction "hatta" does not work, nor does the construction "illa an" with His saying "you will surely return" (la-ta'udunna), unlike "la-alzamanna-ka" (I will surely hold you to it) or "taqdiyyanni haqqi" (you shall pay me my due). The "return" (al-'awd) here means "becoming." Alternatively, it may be an address to the messengers and those who believed in them. The ruling of those who believed in them prevailed, because they had been in their religion before that, so it is correct to keep "la-ta'udunna" (you will return) applied to what is understood from it initially, since it had preceded that they had been in their religion. As for the messengers, they had never been in their religion at all. Or the meaning of their return to their religion is their silence about them and their being neglectful of them, not demanding of them belief in God and what the messengers brought.

Abu Hayyan notes that Abu Hayyah read "la-yuhlikanna al-zalimin" and "li-yuskinannakum" with the yā' of third-person address, taking into account His saying "So their Lord revealed to them," since its wording is that of the absent party. "And We will surely make you dwell" (wa-la-nuskinannakumu) came with the second-person pronoun, honouring them with direct address, and did not come with the third-person pronoun, as in His saying "So their Lord revealed to them." When they swore by them to expel the messengers and to return to their religion, God, exalted is He, swore to destroy them. What expulsion is greater than destruction, such that there is no return to it ever? And [the promise includes] the settling of the messengers and those who believed in them and their offspring in the land of those who swore to expel the messengers.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He specified "the wrongdoers" from among those who disbelieved, since it is possible that some of the disbelievers who uttered that statement might believe; He threatened the destruction only of those who were purely committed to wrongdoing. Others said: he meant by "the wrongdoers" the polytheists; God, exalted is He, said: "Indeed, polytheism is a tremendous wrong" (Luqman 13). The reference by "that" is to the inheritance of the land by the prophets and those who believed in them after the destruction of the wrongdoers, as in His saying, exalted is He, "And the good end is for the God-fearing" (al-A'raf 128).

"Maqam" can be a verbal noun or a place. Al-Farra' said: "maqami" is a verbal noun attributed to the agent, meaning: My standing over him with the preservation of his deeds and My watching over him, as in His saying: "Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned?" (al-Ra'd 33). Al-Zajjaj said: it is the place where he stands before Me for reckoning, and it is the standing place of God at which He makes His servants stand on the Day of Resurrection, as in His saying, exalted is He: "And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens" (al-Rahman 46). And (it is) with an inserted "maqam" (i.e., the word is in apposition or elided), meaning: for whoever fears Me.

I swore, leaving you no doubt; and there is no refuge for a man from God.

Perhaps the distress in which I am will be followed by a near relief.

Al-Akhfash said: it means the afflictions that befall the disbeliever in this world, which he called "death," but this is far-fetched, because the context of the discourse indicates that this is among the conditions of the disbeliever in Jahannam.

﴿They said to them, their messengers: "We are only humans like you, but God bestows His favour upon whomever He wills of His servants. It was not for us to bring you an authority except by God's leave. And upon God let the believers rely."﴾ ﴿"And why should we not rely upon God, when He has guided us to our paths? We will surely bear patiently what you inflict upon us. And upon God let those who rely (upon Him) rely."﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieved said to their messengers: "We will surely expel you from our land, or you will return to our religion." So their Lord revealed to them: "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿"And We will surely make you dwell in the land after them. That is for whoever fears My standing (before Me) and fears My threat."﴾ ﴿They sought victory, and every obstinate tyrant failed.﴾ ﴿Behind him is Hell, and he is given to drink of pus-water.﴾ ﴿He gulps it down and can barely swallow it; death comes to him from every place, yet he will not die; and behind him is a harsh punishment.﴾

It may carry several senses here: it may be reflexive (lil-mutawa'a), meaning "he made him gulp, so he gulped," like "I taught him, so he learned"; it may denote effort (lil-takallluf), like "tahallama" (he pretended to dream); it may denote continuing the action over a period of time (lil-muwasala), like "tafahhama" (he understood gradually), meaning he takes it little by little; or it may agree with the bare form, meaning "tajarra'ahu" (he gulped it), as you say "'adā al-shay'" and "ta'adahu" (he passed beyond it).

"Yatajarra'uhu" is either a qualifier of what precedes it, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yusqa," or a new independent sentence (isti'naf).

"Wa ya'tihi al-mawt": that is, its causes. The apparent sense of His saying "from every place" is "from the six directions," because of the dreadfulness of the pains he suffers. Ibrahim al-Taymi said: "from every place" means from his body, even from the ends of his hair. It was also said: even from the tips of his toes. The apparent sense is that this is in the Hereafter.

Al-Akhfash said: it means the afflictions that befall the disbeliever in this world, which he called "death," but this is far-fetched, because the context of the discourse indicates that this is among the conditions of the disbeliever in Jahannam.

His saying "wa ma huwa bi-mayyit" (and he is not dead) is because of the prolonged severity of death and the extension of its agonies.

"Min wara'ihi": the disagreement over "min wara'ihi" is like the disagreement over "min wara'ihi Jahannam" (Q. 14:16). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Wa min wara'ihi 'adhabun ghalizun" (and behind him is severe punishment): that is, at every moment he faces, he receives a punishment harsher and more severe than what came before. It is related from al-Fudayl: it is the cutting off of breaths and their confinement within the bodies. It was also said: the pronoun in "wara'ihi" refers to the previously mentioned punishment, not to every tyrant.

﴿They said to them, their messengers: "We are only humans like you, but God bestows His favour upon whomever He wills of His servants. It was not for us to bring you an authority except by God's leave. And upon God let the believers rely."﴾ ﴿"And why should we not rely upon God, when He has guided us to our paths? We will surely bear patiently what you inflict upon us. And upon God let those who rely (upon Him) rely."﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieved said to their messengers: "We will surely expel you from our land, or you will return to our religion." So their Lord revealed to them: "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿"And We will surely make you dwell in the land after them. That is for whoever fears My standing (before Me) and fears My threat."﴾ ﴿They sought victory, and every obstinate tyrant failed.﴾ ﴿Behind him is Hell, and he is given to drink of pus-water.﴾ ﴿He gulps it down and can barely swallow it; death comes to him from every place, yet he will not die; and behind him is a harsh punishment.﴾

(p-411) They (the disbelievers) conceded to the messengers that they resemble them in humanity alone. As for the other attributes in which the messengers were singled out, they were not like them in these. They did not mention the attribute by which they were distinguished, out of humility on their part and in attributing it to God. They did not explicitly mention God's favour upon them alone, but they expressed it generally, in "upon whomever He wills of His servants." The meaning is: He bestows prophethood upon whomever He wills to make a prophet. The meaning of "by God's leave" is: by His permission and will. That is, the sign you have proposed is not something we can bring, nor is it within our power; for this reason the construction is "it was not for us" (wa-ma kana lana), since it is a matter dependent upon God's will.

"Then let them rely" (fa-l-yatawakkal) is a command from them to the believers to rely (upon God). They intended by it themselves first, primarily, and commanded themselves with it, as if they said: "It is incumbent upon us to rely upon God in patience toward your opposition and enmity and what befalls us from you." Do you not see their saying: "And why should we not rely upon God?" Its meaning: "What excuse do we have for not relying upon God, when He has guided us, having done for us what necessitates our reliance upon Him, which is granting us success in being guided, each one of us, to the path that requires him to follow it in religion?" The first command, namely His saying "Then let the believers rely" (fa-l-yatawakkal al-mu'minun), is for initiating reliance, and the second is for steadfastness upon what they have newly undertaken of their reliance.

"We will surely bear patiently" (wa-la-nasbiranna) is the answer to an oath, and it indicates a prior mention of that which requires patience, which is harm. The "ma" (here) is verbal (masdariyyah, i.e., it forms a verbal noun with what follows), and they permitted that it be in the sense of "alladhi" (which). The pronoun is elided, that is: "what you have inflicted upon us" (ma adhaytumuhu-na, with the object pronoun omitted). Its original form was "bihi" (with it), so there are two opinions: has "bihi" been elided, or the preposition "bi", so that the verb reaches the pronoun? Al-Hasan read "li-yatawakkal" with a kasra on the lam of the imperative, which is the original form. "Aw" (or) is for one of the two matters: they swore that there was no escape from their expulsion of them or their return to their religion, as if they said: "One of these two will surely come to pass."

Interpreting "aw" here in the sense of "hatta" (until), or in the sense of "illa an" (except that), is the view of one who has not examined closely what follows it, because the construction "hatta" does not work, nor does the construction "illa an" with His saying "you will surely return" (la-ta'udunna), unlike "la-alzamanna-ka" (I will surely hold you to it) or "taqdiyyanni haqqi" (you shall pay me my due). The "return" (al-'awd) here means "becoming." Alternatively, it may be an address to the messengers and those who believed in them. The ruling of those who believed in them prevailed, because they had been in their religion before that, so it is correct to keep "la-ta'udunna" (you will return) applied to what is understood from it initially, since it had preceded that they had been in their religion. As for the messengers, they had never been in their religion at all. Or the meaning of their return to their religion is their silence about them and their being neglectful of them, not demanding of them belief in God and what the messengers brought.

Abu Hayyan notes that Abu Hayyah read "la-yuhlikanna al-zalimin" and "li-yuskinannakum" with the yā' of third-person address, taking into account His saying "So their Lord revealed to them," since its wording is that of the absent party. "And We will surely make you dwell" (wa-la-nuskinannakumu) came with the second-person pronoun, honouring them with direct address, and did not come with the third-person pronoun, as in His saying "So their Lord revealed to them." When they swore by them to expel the messengers and to return to their religion, God, exalted is He, swore to destroy them. What expulsion is greater than destruction, such that there is no return to it ever? And [the promise includes] the settling of the messengers and those who believed in them and their offspring in the land of those who swore to expel the messengers.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He specified "the wrongdoers" from among those who disbelieved, since it is possible that some of the disbelievers who uttered that statement might believe; He threatened the destruction only of those who were purely committed to wrongdoing. Others said: he meant by "the wrongdoers" the polytheists; God, exalted is He, said: "Indeed, polytheism is a tremendous wrong" (Luqman 13). The reference by "that" is to the inheritance of the land by the prophets and those who believed in them after the destruction of the wrongdoers, as in His saying, exalted is He, "And the good end is for the God-fearing" (al-A'raf 128).

"Maqam" can be a verbal noun or a place. Al-Farra' said: "maqami" is a verbal noun attributed to the agent, meaning: My standing over him with the preservation of his deeds and My watching over him, as in His saying: "Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned?" (al-Ra'd 33). Al-Zajjaj said: it is the place where he stands before Me for reckoning, and it is the standing place of God at which He makes His servants stand on the Day of Resurrection, as in His saying, exalted is He: "And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens" (al-Rahman 46). And (it is) with an inserted "maqam" (i.e., the word is in apposition or elided), meaning: for whoever fears Me.

The apparent view is that the pronoun in "wa-istaftahu" (they sought victory) refers to the prophets, meaning: they sought God's help against their enemies, as in His saying: "If you seek a decision, then the decision has come to you" (al-Anfal 19). It may also be from "al-futahah", which means judgement, i.e., they sought God's judgement and asked Him to decide between them. The seeking of victory by the messengers is frequent in the Qur'an, as in Noah's saying: "So judge between me and them with a judgement and save me" (al-Shu'ara' 118); Lot's saying: "My Lord, save me and my family from what they do" (al-Shu'ara' 169); Shu'ayb's saying: "Our Lord, judge between us and our people with truth" (al-A'raf 89); and Moses' saying: "Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh..." (Yunus 88), the verse.

Ibn Zayd said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, meaning: the disbelievers sought victory, in the manner of what Quraysh said: "Hasten to us our share" (Sad 16); and Abu Jahl's saying: "O God, if this is the truth from You, rain down stones upon us from the sky or bring us a painful punishment," and his saying: "O God, sever us from kinship and bring us what is unknown, so destroy him this morning." It seems that when their denial and harm became strong, and they were not hastened with punishment, they thought that what they had brought was false; so they sought victory in the manner of mockery and derision, like the people of Noah's saying: "Bring us what you threaten us with" (Hud 32); the people of Shu'ayb: "Then drop upon us fragments from the sky" (al-Shu'ara' 187); 'Ad: "We will not be punished" (al-Shu'ara' 138); and some of Quraysh: "Then rain down upon us stones from the sky" (al-Anfal 32).

It was said: the pronoun refers to both groups: the prophets and their deniers, because they all asked that the one in the right be helped and the one in the wrong be defeated. What strengthens the return of the pronoun to the messengers specifically is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Muhaysin: "wa-istaftihu" with a kasra on the ta', as an imperative addressed to the messengers, coordinated with "la-yuhlikanna" (He will surely destroy), meaning: their Lord revealed to them and said to them, "He will surely destroy," and He said to them, "Seek victory," i.e., ask for help, and ask it of your Lord.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that the people of Makkah sought victory, i.e., asked for rain, and "al-fath" means rain in the years of drought that were sent upon them by the prayer of the Messenger, and they were not watered. So He, glorified is He, mentioned that, and that He disappointed the hope of every obstinate tyrant, and that he is given to drink in Hell instead of his drink another water, which is the pus of the people of the Fire.

"Wa-istaftahu" according to this interpretation is a resumptive, independent statement, disconnected from the account of the messengers and their peoples; end of quotation.

"Wa-khaba" (and failed) is coordinated with an elided element whose estimate is: "So they were helped and triumphed. And every obstinate tyrant failed," and they are the people of the messengers. The explanation of "jabbar" has already been given. "'Anid" means one who persists in opposition, like "khalit" in the sense of "mukhalit" (one who mixes), according to the view of those who made the pronoun refer to the disbelievers, as if "wa-khaba" is coordinated with "wa-istaftahu."

"Min wara'ihi" (behind him): Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn al-Anbari said: it means "from after him." The poet said:
I swore, leaving you no doubt; and there is no refuge for a man from God.
Abu 'Ubaydah also said, as did Qutrub, al-Tabari and a group: "min wara'ihi" means "from in front of him," which is the meaning of al-Zamakhshari's saying: "from between his hands." And [a poet] recited:
Perhaps the distress in which I am will be followed by a near relief.

This is a description of his state in this world, because he is set in readiness for Hell, so it is as if it is before him while he is on its brink; or it is a description of his state in the Hereafter, when he is raised and made to stand. The poet said:
Do the Banu Marwan hope for my hearing and obedience, while the people of Tamim and the wilderness lie behind me?
Another said:
Is it not that behind me, if my death is delayed, lies the staff that the fingers bend around?

Wara' (behind, beyond) is said by Abu 'Ubayda and al-Azhari to be one of the words with contrary meanings (adداد, al-addad). It was also said that it is not among the addad. Tha'lab said: it is a name for whatever is hidden from you, whether it is in front of you or behind you. It was also said: it means "from behind him," that is, in pursuit of him, as you say "the matter is behind you," meaning it will come to you.

"Yusqa" (and he is given to drink) is coordinated with an omitted element whose implied sense is: "he is cast into it and given to drink," or it is coordinated with the governing element in "min wara'ihi," which occupies the position of a qualifier (sifa). The word "Jahannam" is in the nominative as the subject of the verb (fa'iliyya), and the apparent meaning is that "ma'" (water) is literal, and "sadid" (pus) is as well.

(p-413) Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Sadid" is a qualifier (na't) of "ma'" (water), as you say, "this is an iron ring," though it is not water. But since it has taken the place of water in our customary usage, it is called water. It was also said: it is a qualifier with the particle of comparison omitted, as you say, "I passed by a lion-like man" (rijulin asad), the implied sense being "like pus." According to Ibn 'Atiyya's view, it is the pus itself and not literally water; according to this view it is not pus, but that which is compared to pus.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Sadid" is an explicative apposition (atf bayan) to "ma'"; he said: "He is given to drink from water," so he made it vague, then clarified it with his saying "sadid." End of quotation. The Basrans do not permit explicative apposition in indefinite nouns, but the Kufans permitted it, and al-Farisi followed them, parsing "zaytunatin" (Q. 24:35) as an explicative apposition to "shajaratin mubarakatin" (Q. 24:35). Thus, according to the view of the Basrans, it is not permissible for "sadid" to be an explicative apposition.

Al-Hawfi said: "Sadid" is a qualifier of "ma'." Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak said: it is what flows from the bodies of the people of the Fire. Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Rabi' said: it is the washing-water of the people of the Fire in the Fire. It was also said: it is what flows from the private parts of fornicators, male and female. It was also said: "sadid" in the sense of "masdud 'anhu" (turned away from), that is, because of its loathsomeness one turns away from it, so it is derived from "sadd" (turning away).

Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned from the hadith of Abu Umama, from the Messenger (ﷺ), that he said concerning His saying: ﴿And he is given to drink of water like pus﴾ ﴿which he gulps﴾: "It is brought near to him, and he dislikes it. When it is brought close to him, it scorches his face and his scalp falls off. When he drinks it, it cuts his intestines until it comes out from his anus." "Yatajarra'uhu" means he strains to gulp it down.

"Wa la yakadu yusighuhu": that is, he does not nearly swallow it, so how could swallowing occur? The apparent sense here is the negation of his nearly swallowing it, and when nearness is negated, swallowing is negated too, as in His saying: ﴿he could hardly see it﴾ (Q. 24:40), meaning he came nowhere near seeing it, so how could he see it? As for the hadith: "it is brought to us, then he drinks it." If the hadith is sound, the meaning is: "he nearly does not swallow it before he drinks it, then he drinks it," as in: ﴿So they slaughtered her, though they nearly did not do it﴾ (Q. 2:71), meaning they nearly did not do it before the slaughter.

"Tajarra'a" is of the form "tafa''ala." It may carry several senses here: it may be reflexive (lil-mutawa'a), meaning "he made him gulp, so he gulped," like "I taught him, so he learned"; it may denote effort (lil-takallluf), like "tahallama" (he pretended to dream); it may denote continuing the action over a period of time (lil-muwasala), like "tafahhama" (he understood gradually), meaning he takes it little by little; or it may agree with the bare form, meaning "tajarra'ahu" (he gulped it), as you say "'adā al-shay'" and "ta'adahu" (he passed beyond it).

"Yatajarra'uhu" is either a qualifier of what precedes it, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yusqa," or a new independent sentence (isti'naf).

"Wa ya'tihi al-mawt": that is, its causes. The apparent sense of His saying "from every place" is "from the six directions," because of the dreadfulness of the pains he suffers. Ibrahim al-Taymi said: "from every place" means from his body, even from the ends of his hair. It was also said: even from the tips of his toes. The apparent sense is that this is in the Hereafter.

Al-Akhfash said: it means the afflictions that befall the disbeliever in this world, which he called "death," but this is far-fetched, because the context of the discourse indicates that this is among the conditions of the disbeliever in Jahannam.

His saying "wa ma huwa bi-mayyit" (and he is not dead) is because of the prolonged severity of death and the extension of its agonies.

"Min wara'ihi": the disagreement over "min wara'ihi" is like the disagreement over "min wara'ihi Jahannam" (Q. 14:16). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Wa min wara'ihi 'adhabun ghalizun" (and behind him is severe punishment): that is, at every moment he faces, he receives a punishment harsher and more severe than what came before. It is related from al-Fudayl: it is the cutting off of breaths and their confinement within the bodies. It was also said: the pronoun in "wara'ihi" refers to the previously mentioned punishment, not to every tyrant.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verses 22–23 (part 1 of 3):

﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord: their deeds are like ashes, upon which the wind blows violently on a stormy day. They have no power over anything of what they earned. That is the far-reaching error.﴾ [Ibrahim: 18] ﴿Have you not seen that God created the heavens and the earth with truth? If He wills, He can remove you and bring a new creation.﴾ [Ibrahim: 19] ﴿And that is not difficult for God.﴾ [Ibrahim: 20] ﴿And they will all come forth before God, and the weak will say to those who were arrogant: "We were indeed your followers. Can you then avert from us anything of God's punishment?" They will say: "If God had guided us, we would have guided you. It is all the same for us, whether we panic or endure patiently; for us there is no escape."﴾ [Ibrahim: 21] ﴿And Satan will say, when the matter has been decided: "God promised you a true promise, and I promised you, but I broke my promise to you. I had no authority over you, except that I called you and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves. I cannot help you, nor can you help me. I disowned your associating me with God before." Indeed, for the wrongdoers there is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds will be admitted into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein by the permission of their Lord. Their greeting therein will be: "Peace."﴾ ﴿Have you not seen how God struck a parable: a good word like a good tree, whose root is firm and whose branches are in the sky,﴾ [Ibrahim: 24] ﴿giving its fruit every season by the permission of its Lord. God strikes parables for people, so that they may take heed.﴾ [Ibrahim: 25] ﴿And the parable of an evil word is like an evil tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability.﴾ [Ibrahim: 26]

(p. 414) Al-ramad (ashes) is well known. Ibn Isa said: it is a substance that burning reduces to dust like powder. Its plural in quantity is rumud, and in paucity armidah. Its plural in the pattern af'ila' (armida') is rare. They say: ramad ramadad when it becomes the finest dust, the finest it can be.

Al-jaza' (distress) is the failure to bear hardship, and it is the opposite of patience. The poet said:

"I was distressed, yet I did not grow distressed at the parting with a [true] distress, and I consoled a heart enamored of the maidens."

Al-musrikh (the helper) is the one who relieves. The poet said:

"So do not despair; indeed I am not a helper for you, and there is no aid or victory from me for you."

Al-sarikh is the one who cries for help, from sarakha, yasrukhu, sarkhan, surakhan and sarkhatan. Salamah ibn Jandal said:

"Whenever a frightened crier came to us, the cry for him was the clatter of shins."

Istarkha' means to cry out, and tasarrakha means to force oneself to cry out. He said: "He called me for help and I answered his cry." Al-sarikh is a verbal noun like al-tarih, and it is applied to both the helper and the one seeking help, as one of the contronyms (words with opposite meanings).

Al-far' is a branch of a tree. It is also applied to what is born from a thing. Al-far' also means hair; one says: a man with abundant hair is afra', and a woman is far'a'. Imru' al-Qays ibn Hujr said:

"And a branch covering the back, jet-black and dark."

Ijtatta al-shay' means he uprooted it, and jatta al-shay' means he pulled it out. Al-juththa is the person's form, whether sitting or standing. Laqit al-Iyadi said:

"He is the expulsion that uproots your root; whoever has seen the like of this coming, and whoever has heard of it."

Al-bawar means destruction. The poet said:

"I have not seen their like, champions in war, on the morning of battle when ruin was feared."

(p. 415) Regarding ﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord: their deeds are like ashes﴾ [Ibrahim: 18]: "mathalu" is in the nominative as a mubtada' (inceptive subject, the topic of the sentence), and its predicate (khabar) is omitted. Its estimated form according to Sibawayh is: "what is recited to you" or "what is related." Al-mathal (likeness) is used figuratively for a description that is strange. The clause ﴿their deeds are like ashes﴾ [Ibrahim: 18] is a resumptive clause (jumla musta'anafa) on an implied question, as if it were said: "What is their likeness?" and then it was answered: "their deeds are like ashes," just as you say: "The description of Zayd: his honour is protected and his wealth is spent freely."

Ibn Atiyyah said: the view of al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' is that "mathal" is annulled (i.e., treated as not governing), and the meaning is: "those who disbelieved, their deeds are like ashes." Al-Hufi said: "mathal" is in the nominative by inception, and "a'maluhum" is a badal (substitution, specifically badal al-ishtimal, substitution of inclusion) for "mathal," and "ka-ramad" is the predicate. Al-Zamakhshari said: or "a'maluhum" may be a substitution for "mathal alladhina kafaru," with the estimated form "the likeness of their deeds," and "ka-ramad" is the predicate. Ibn Atiyyah said: it is also said that it is an inceptive subject, and "a'maluhum" is a second inceptive subject, and "ka-ramad" is the predicate of the second, and the whole clause is the predicate of the first. This is, in my view, the most preponderant of the opinions. It is as if you said: "The likeness established in the soul for those who disbelieved is this clause mentioned, namely their deeds in their corruption at the time of need and their dissolution like ashes that the wind scatters and disperses with its force, so that no trace of it remains and nothing of it is gathered." End quote.

This view that Ibn Atiyyah preferred was said by al-Hufi, and it is not permissible, because the clause that occurs as a predicate of the first inceptive subject, which is "mathal," lacks a pronoun referring back to the likeness, and it is not the same as the subject in meaning, so it does not need a pronoun.

The deeds of the disbelievers were the noble acts they used to do: keeping ties of kinship, freeing slaves, ransoming captives, slaughtering camels for guests, relieving the distressed, granting protection, and other such things. He likened their nullification and passing away to scattered dust, because they were built on no foundation of knowledge of God and belief in Him, and because they were done for His sake with the ashes that the violent wind blows away.

Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read "al-riyah" (the winds) in the plural, while the majority read it in the singular. The description of the day as "a stormy day" [Ibrahim: 18], though it is an attribute of the wind, is figurative, as they say: "the day when the agent (wakil) came down was sleeping." Al-Harawi said: the estimated form is "on a day of a stormy wind," and it was omitted because the wind had already been mentioned, as the poet said:

"When there comes a day whose sun is darkened and eclipsed."

He means: "the sun is eclipsed." It is also said that "stormy" is an attribute of the wind, but when it came after "day" it took the case-ending of "day" by adjacency (ittiba' i'rabihi), as it is said: "the lizard's hole, ruined" (juhru dabbin kharibin), meaning that it was put in the genitive by proximity (khafd 'ala al-jiwar).

Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibrahim ibn Abi Bakr from al-Hasan read "fi yawmin 'asifin" [Ibrahim: 18] with the genitive construction (idafa) of "day" to "stormy," and it is a case of the omission of the qualified noun and the placing of the attribute in its position, its estimated form being "on a day of stormy wind." The explanation of "al-'usuf" (stormy blowing) has already been given in Yunus in the words of His saying: ﴿A stormy wind came upon them﴾ [Yunus: 22]. According to the opinion of one who permitted the idafa of a noun to its attribute, the reading may be: "They will have no power on the Day of Resurrection over what they earned of their deeds, meaning they will see no trace of reward for it, just as nothing can be made of ashes scattered by the wind." It is also said: "They will have no power over the reward of what they earned," with an omitted genitive (mudaf) understood.

In the Sahih (of al-Bukhari and Muslim) from Aisha, may God be pleased with her, she said: "O Messenger of God, Ibn Jud'an used to keep ties of kinship and feed the poor in the Jahiliyyah. Does that benefit him?" He said: "It will not benefit him, because he never said: 'My Lord, forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgment.'" Also in the Sahih: "Indeed the disbeliever is fed in this world for the good deeds he did for God." That is an indication of their being in this state.

The phrase "on such a far-reaching error" refers to the deep abyss into which its person plunges, and which is far removed from the path of salvation, and far from the truth or the reward.

In al-Baqarah: ﴿They have no power over anything of what they earned﴾ [Ibrahim: 18] has various stylistic refinements in eloquence and differences in word order, while the meaning is one.

﴿Have you not seen that God created the heavens and the earth with truth? If He wills, He can remove you and bring a new creation﴾ [Ibrahim: 19] ﴿And that is not difficult for God﴾ [Ibrahim: 20].

﴿And they will all come forth before God, and the weak will say to those who were arrogant: "We were indeed your followers. Can you then avert from us anything of God's punishment?" They will say: "If God had guided us, we would have guided you. It is all the same for us, whether we panic or endure patiently; for us there is no escape."﴾ [Ibrahim: 21]: al-Sulami read "alam tar" (have you not seen) with the sukun on the ra'. Its basis is that he applied the pausal form to the connected reading. Another explanation is that the Arabs dropped the alif of "tara" in their saying: "qama al-qawmu, wa law tara ma Zayd" (the people stood, and if you did not see what Zayd was), just as the ya' of "la ubali" (I do not care) was dropped to become "la ubal." When the jussive particle entered, it was imagined that the ra' was the last letter of the word, so it was given sukun for the jussive, just as they say of "la ubali": "lam ubal," imagining the lam as the final letter of the word. The seeing here means knowing, and so it is a seeing of the heart.

Al-Akhawan read "khaliqu" as an active participle (ism al-fa'il), and "al-ard" in the genitive. The rest of the seven read "khalaqa" as a past verb, and "al-ard" in the accusative. As for "bi-l-haqq," al-Zamakhshari said: with wisdom, with a sound purpose and a great matter; He did not create them in vain or in play. Ibn Atiyyah said: with truth, that is, with what is right in terms of the interests of His servants, and the carrying out of His prior decree, and to show that this is evidence of Him and of His power. It is also said: with His word and speech. It is also said: "bi-l-haqq" is a circumstantial (hal) clause, meaning "truly." The apparent meaning of His saying "He can remove you" [Ibrahim: 19] is that it is a general address to people. From Ibn Abbas: it is an address to the disbelievers. As for "and bring a new creation" [Ibrahim: 19], it may mean: "if He wills, He can remove you, O people, and bring other people of your kind, human beings, or it may mean of other than your kind." The first is the view of the majority of the exegetes. Similar to these two possibilities was mentioned by the exegetes regarding His saying in al-Nisa': ﴿If He wills, He can remove you, O people, and bring others﴾ [al-Nisa: 133], and we explained there that it allows only the first interpretation.

"And that" means: your removal and the bringing of a new creation are neither impossible nor difficult for Him, may He be exalted, because He is the one capable of what He wills. Al-Zamakhshari said: because He is capable by His essence; there is no particular restriction for Him to one thing rather than another. When the motive for something is fully present for Him and no obstacle stands in the way, it happens without hesitation, like the movement of your finger. When a motive calls Him to something and no hindrance stands in its way, [it happens]. End quote.

In this there is a trace of Mu'tazilism in his saying "the capable" (al-qadir), because they affirm a "capability" (qadiriyya) and deny "power" (qudra); and in his likening His action, may He be exalted, to the action of a servant in his saying "like the movement of your finger." In our view, the movement of our finger is only by the power of God, may He be exalted, and what is attributed to us of power has no effect in bringing anything into existence.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: this verse explains how far they have strayed into error, and the enormity of their disbelief in God, given the clarity of His signs that testify to Him, which indicate His dazzling power and His far-reaching wisdom, and that He is the one worthy of being worshipped, feared for His punishment, and hoped for His reward in the abode of recompense. End quote.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verse 22–23 (part 2 of 3):

﴿And they came forth﴾ [Ibrahim: 21]: That is, they emerged from their graves to face Allah's recompense and reckoning. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of their coming forth before Allah, when Allah, exalted is He, nothing is hidden from Him until it is brought out, is that they used to hide from people's eyes when committing indecencies, thinking that this was concealed from Allah. When the Day of Resurrection comes, they will be exposed to Allah in their own selves, and they will know that nothing hidden is concealed from Him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "And they came forth" means they came to the open ground (al-baraz), which is the wide open land, and this was borrowed to describe the gathering on the Day of Resurrection. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: The interpretation of the philosophers (al-hukama') is that when the soul departs from the body, it is as if the covering is removed, and it remains stripped in its own essence, bare of everything other than itself, and that is the "coming forth" before Allah, exalted is He. This man (al-Razi) often cites the words of the philosophers, and they differ from the people of the revealed laws (ahl al-shara'i') in interpreting the speech of Allah, exalted is He, revealed in the language of the Arabs, and the Arabs do not understand any of the concepts of the people of philosophy. Their interpretation is like a riddle and enigmas, and this man calls them "philosophers," though they are among the most ignorant of the disbelievers in Allah, exalted is He, and in His prophets. The pronoun in ﴿And they came forth﴾ [Ibrahim: 21] refers to the created beings who are being reckoned, and the past tense was used to express the certainty of the one who reports it, as though it had already happened. Zayd ibn 'Ali recited (wa-baraza) in the passive voice and with a doubled ra'. Al-du'afa' (the weak) are the followers and the common people. In the Mushaf it was written with a waw before the hamza (in the word al-du'afa'? no, in the word for the "ulama' of the Children of Israel"), following the pronunciation of those who enlarge the alif before the hamza, inclining it toward the waw. Similar is 'ulama' Bani Isra'il (the scholars of the Children of Israel). Al-ladhina istakbaru (those who were arrogant) are their leaders and chiefs, who sought to be followed by the weak and to make them follow them. Istakbaru and takabbaru mean they showed the magnification of themselves, or they were arrogant against following the messengers and worshipping Allah. Taba'an (followers): it may be a collective noun for tabi', like khadim and khuddam, and ghaib and ghuyyab. It may also be a verbal noun (masdar), like the saying 'adlun wa-ridan. ﴿Are you going to avail us anything?﴾: this is an interrogative whose meaning is their rebuke and reproach of them, though they knew that they would not avail them. The meaning is: We followed you in the misguidance you were in, just as you commanded us, and you did not avail us anything. Therefore their answer came (p-417): ﴿If Allah had guided us, we would have guided you﴾. They answered this way as an excuse and out of shame, and as a rejection of guidance to Allah, exalted is He, and this is a true statement in itself. Al-Zamakhshari said: The first min is for specification (li-l-tabyin), and the second is for partition (li-l-tab'id), as though it were said: "Are you going to avail us some part of that thing which is the punishment of Allah?" It is also permissible that both are for partition together, meaning: "Are you going to avail us some part of a thing which is part of the punishment of Allah," that is, part of a part of the punishment of Allah. End of quotation. These two interpretations that al-Zamakhshari gave for min in the two places: the first requires that ﴿of anything﴾ [Ibrahim: 21] be placed before ﴿of the punishment of Allah﴾ [Ibrahim: 21], because he made ﴿of anything﴾ the thing specified by ﴿of the punishment of Allah﴾. The specifying min is preceded by what it specifies, and does not come after it. The second interpretation, that "part of a thing" is "part of the punishment," requires that it be an apposition (badal), which would be the substitution of a general for a particular, because "of anything" is more general than "of the punishment of Allah." If by "thing" he means a thing from the punishment, then the meaning returns to what was estimated, namely "part of a part of the punishment of Allah." This is not acceptable, because the partitive quality of a thing is absolute, so it cannot have a part. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' stated that min in His saying "of anything" is extra (za'ida). Al-Hawfi said: ﴿of the punishment of Allah﴾ [Ibrahim: 21] is connected to ﴿are you going to avail﴾ [Ibrahim: 21], and min in ﴿of anything﴾ [Ibrahim: 21] is for the generalization of the genus, extra for emphasis. Abu al-Baqa' said: min is extra, meaning a thing that is from the punishment of Allah, and it is construed in terms of meaning, its estimate being: "Are you going to prevent from us anything?" It is also permissible that "thing" stands in the position of a verbal noun, meaning "sufficiency," so that "of the punishment of Allah" is connected to ﴿are you going to avail﴾ [Ibrahim: 21]. End of quotation. The justification for the extra min is that the predicate is in the context of interrogation, as if the interrogative particle entered upon it and governed it, and the extra min here is like the extra min in the construction: "So are you going to avail?" Al-Zamakhshari said: They answered them, making excuses for what they had done to them, that if Allah had guided them to faith, they would have guided them, and they did not misguide them, either perceiving their sin in their misguidance and their misguiding of them as being against Allah, as Allah related about them: They said: ﴿If Allah had willed, we would not have associated, nor would our fathers﴾ [al-An'am: 148], and ﴿If Allah had willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him﴾ [al-Nahl: 35]. They say this in the Hereafter as they used to say it in this world. What indicates this is His saying, relating about the hypocrites: ﴿On the Day when Allah resurrects them all, and they swear to Him as they swear to you, and they think they are on something﴾ [al-Mujadila: 18]. End of quotation. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi related from al-Zamakhshari that they said this while lying in it, and what indicates this is the Exalted One's saying about the hypocrites: ﴿On the Day when Allah resurrects them all, and they swear to Him as they swear to you, and they think they are on something﴾ [al-Mujadila: 18]. Al-Razi said: Know that the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school, who hold that human reason and justice are binding on God) do not permit the occurrence of lying among the people of the Resurrection, so this statement from him contradicts the principles of his shaykhs, and it is not accepted from him. Al-Zamakhshari also said: It is permissible that the meaning is: "If we had been among the people of grace (al-lutf), and our Lord had shown us grace, and we had been guided, we would have guided you to faith." Al-Razi said: Al-Qadi mentioned this view and rejected it, saying: It is not permissible to interpret this as grace, because Allah has already done that. It was also said: If Allah had delivered us from the punishment and guided us to the path of Paradise, we would have guided you. Al-Zamakhshari, expanding on this statement, said: If Allah had guided us to the way of salvation from the punishment, we would have guided you, that is, we would have freed you from it and led you on the path of salvation, just as we led you on the path of destruction. End of quotation. It was also said: What indicates that the intended guidance is guidance to the path of Paradise is that it is what they sought and asked for, so it must be what is meant. Ibn 'Abbas said: If Allah had guided us, we would have guided you. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿It is the same for us whether we protest or endure﴾ [Ibrahim: 21] to its end falls under the speech of the arrogant, and its clauses came without the conjunction waw, as though each clause were created independent and not conjoined, even though they are linked to one another in meaning, because their question "Are you going to avail us?" was only because of their distress at their condition. So they said that, equating themselves with them in that, since they were united in the punishment of the misguidance in which they had been united. They are saying: What is this distress and reproach? There is no benefit in distress, just as there is no benefit in patience. When they said "If Allah had guided us," they followed that with despair of salvation, so they said: ﴿We have no escape﴾ [Ibrahim: 21]: that is, no refuge and no place of flight, whether we protest or endure. It was also said: "It is the same for us" is part of the speech of the weak and of those who were arrogant (p-418), and the estimate is: They all said, "It is the same for us," informing about their state. The discussion of this kind of equalizing was mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqara. The apparent meaning is that this dialogue between the weak and the leaders takes place at the time of the exposure before Allah. It is related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Ibn Zayd that their saying ﴿It is the same for us whether we protest or endure﴾ [Ibrahim: 21] was after they had endured in the Fire for five hundred years, and after they had protested for an equal period.

﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided: Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I broke it to you. I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves. I cannot help you, nor can you help me. Indeed, I disbelieve in your associating me with Allah before. Indeed, for the wrongdoers there is a painful punishment﴾: The connection of this verse to what came before is that when He mentioned the dialogue of the followers with their disbelieving leaders, He mentioned the dialogue of Satan with his followers among mankind, because the leaders and the devils share in being involved in misguidance. Satan here is Iblis, and he is the chief of the devils. In the hadith of intercession from the hadith of 'Uqba ibn 'Amir: "The disbelievers will say: The believers have found someone to intercede for them, so who will intercede for us? They will say: None but Iblis, for he is the one who misguided us. They will come to him and say: The believers have found someone to intercede for them, so stand up and intercede for us, for you misguided us. He will stand up, and from his assembly there will rise the foulest smell anyone has ever smelled. And at that point he will say: ﴿Indeed Allah promised you﴾, the verse." It is related from al-Hasan: Iblis will stand as a preacher in Hell, on a pulpit of fire, and all creatures will hear him, and he will say: Indeed Allah promised you the promise of truth, meaning the Resurrection, Paradise, the Fire, the reward of the obedient and the punishment of the disobedient, and He fulfilled His promise to you.
