I promised you that there would be no Resurrection, no Paradise, no Fire, no reward and no punishment, and I broke it to you. "The matter has been decided": a group has been appointed for Paradise and a group for the Fire, and all of that happens at the place of standing (al-mawqif). This is indicated by the hadith of intercession, or it is after the people of Paradise have entered Paradise and the people of the Fire have entered the Fire. This is also indicated by what we have mentioned from al-Hasan, and it is the interpretation of al-Tabari. It was also said: "The matter has been decided" means it has been cut off and completed, and that is the reckoning, and the two groups have been sent off to their abodes. The "promise of truth" may be understood as an attributive construction, meaning "the true promise." It may be that "truth" is an attribute of Allah, meaning His promise. It may also be that "truth" refers to the established thing, which is the Resurrection and the recompense for deeds, meaning: He fulfilled for you what He promised you, and I promised you the opposite of that, so I broke it to you. As for ﴿but I had no authority over you except that I called you﴾, the apparent meaning is that this is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), because his calling them to misguidance and his whispering is not of the kind of authority, which is clear proof. It was said: It is possible that by authority he means dominance, control and power, meaning: I did not compel you or frighten you with force, but I presented something to you, and your opinion accepted it. It was also said: It is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), because the power to move a person toward something is sometimes by force from the mover, and sometimes by strengthening the motive in his heart, and this is done by casting whispers into him, so this is a kind of control. It was also said: The apparent meaning of this speech indicates that Satan has no power to strike a person down, distort his limbs and organs, or remove his reason. So ﴿do not blame me﴾. It was recited as ﴿so let them not blame me﴾ with the ya', in the third person, and this is a shift (iltifat). He means: concerning what you were given of misguidance, and blame yourselves for your bad judgment and for your responding to my call without deliberation or proof. Al-Zamakhshari said: And blame yourselves, since you were deceived and obeyed me when I called you, and you did not obey your Lord when He called you. This is evidence that the human being is the one who chooses wretchedness and happiness and acquires them for himself, and from Allah there is only enabling, and from Satan only adornment. If the matter were as the determinists (al-Mujbira, those who hold that human actions are wholly predetermined) claim, he would have said: "So do not blame me, nor yourselves, for Allah has decreed disbelief for you and compelled you to it." End of quotation. This is on the path of the Mu'tazila.

﴿Mā anā bimuṣrikhikum﴾ (I cannot help you). Ibn ʿAbbas said: "by benefiting you." Ibn Jubayr said: "by rescuing you." al-Rabiʿ said: "by saving you." Mujahid said: "by aiding you." All of these statements are close in meaning.

Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-Aʿmash, and Hamza read: ﴿bimuṣrikhiyya﴾, with a kasra on the ya. Many grammarians criticized this reading. al-Farraʾ said: "It may be a mistake of the reciters, for few of them are free from error. He probably thought that the ba' in ﴿bimuṣrikhiyya﴾ governs the whole word, while the ba' is separate from the first person (ya') ending." Abu ʿUbayd said: "We think they erred. They assumed that the ba' takes a kasra because of what follows it." al-Akhfash said: "I have not heard this from any Arab or from any grammarian." al-Zajjaj said: "This reading is, according to all grammarians, poor and rejected, and it has no justification except a weak one." al-Nahhas said: "This has become a consensus, and the Book of God may not be interpreted as an anomaly." al-Zamakhshari said: "It is weak, and they cited for it an anonymous line of verse:

*Qāla lahā: hal laki yā tāfiyyi*
*Qālat lahu: mā anta bil-marḍiyyi*

(He said to her: "Do you have any [desire], O Tafi?" She said to him: "You are not the one who is pleasing.")

It seems that he considered the ya' of possession (ya' al-idafa) to be silent, and before it a silent ya', so he vocalized it with a kasra, according to the principle of resolving two silent letters meeting. But this is not sound, because the ya' of possession is only ever pronounced with a fatha when it is preceded by an alif, as in ʿaṣāya (my staff), fa-mā bāluhā (what is its matter), and when it is preceded by a ya'." (Objection): "The first ya' is treated like a true, sound letter because of the idgham (assimilation), as if it were a ya' that came silent after a silent sound consonant, so it is vocalized with a kasra according to the original rule." (Answer): "This is a good analogy, but the widespread usage, which is like a mutawatir report (a report transmitted by so many chains that it cannot be doubted), overrides analogies." End of quote. As for his statement "and they cited for it an anonymous line of verse," another source has mentioned that it belongs to al-Aghlab al-ʿIjli, and this dialect still survives on the lips of many people today; one says: *mā fiyyi afʿalu kadhā* ("I will not do this"), with a kasra on the ya'. As for the vocalization he mentioned, it is the interpretation of al-Farraʾ, which al-Zajjaj reported from him. As for his remark in the course of his speech, "where it is preceded by an alif," I do not know of any case where ḥayth is added to a clause introduced by an adverb, such as *qaʿada Zaydun ḥaythu amāma ʿUmar wa Bakr*, so this construction needs to be heard from authority. As for his statement "because the ya' of possession is at its end," it has been transmitted that the ya' after an alif is silent, and the readers recited so in words like *maḥyāya* (my life), and what those grammarians we mentioned have said should not be paid attention to. Later scholars have followed their footsteps in this, so it is not permissible to say of it that it is an error, or ugly, or poor. Some scholars of language have reported that it is a dialect, but its use is rare. Quṭrub explicitly stated that it is a dialect of the Banu Yarbuʿ. al-Qasim ibn Maʿn, one of the leaders of the Kufan grammarians, said: "It is correct." Husayn al-Juʿfi asked Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla' about it, and when the grammarians' criticism of the reading was mentioned, he said: "It is permissible." He also said: "Do not mind whether its vowel is lower or higher." And it is reported from him that he said: "With the khafḍ (kasra) it is good." And it is also reported from him that he said: "It is permissible." It is not, in terms of i'rab (grammatical inflection), like that, and no attention should be paid to Abu Hatim's denial of Abu ʿAmr's approval of it, for Abu ʿAmr is an imam of language, an imam of grammar, an imam of recitation, and a pure Arab; he permitted it and considered it good. They have also transmitted the line of al-Nabigha:

*ʿAlayya li-ʿAmrin niʿmatun baʿda niʿmatin*
*li-wālidihi laysat bi-dhāti ʿaqārib*

(Upon me, for ʿAmr, is a favor after a favor, for his father; it is not one of the stinging kind.)

with the ya' of ʿalayya vocalized with a kasra.

﴿Wa-mā ashrakatumūni min qabl﴾: the ma here is verbal-masdariyya (it forms a verbal noun), and ﴿min qabl﴾ is connected to ﴿ashrakatumūni﴾, meaning: "I disbelieve today in your associating me [with God] before this day, i.e., in the world, as in His saying: ﴿Innā burā'u minkum wa-mimmā taʿbudūna min dūnillāhi kafarnā bikum﴾ ("We are free of you and of what you worship besides God; we have rejected you") [al-Mumtahana 60:4], and He said: ﴿Wa-yawma al-qiyāmati yakfurūna bi-shirkikum﴾ ("On the Day of Resurrection they will deny your associating") [Fatir 35:14]." It has also been said: ma is relative, in the sense of alladhi (which), and the estimate is: "I disbelieved in the idol which you associated with me," so the returning pronoun was omitted. It has also been said: ﴿min qabl﴾ is connected to ﴿kafartu﴾, and ma is in the sense of alladhi: "I disbelieved before, when I refused to prostrate to Adam, in that which you associated with me, namely God, glorified and exalted be He." One says: "I associated Zayd," and when the hamzat al-naql (causative hamza) is added, one says: "I made Zayd associate ʿAmr," i.e., I made him a partner for him. However, this view entails applying ma to God, the Exalted, and the more correct view regarding ma is that it is not applied to any individual of those who have knowledge. al-Zamakhshari said: "Similar to this ma, meaning in its application to God, is the ma in their saying: ﴿Subḥāna mā sakhkhara lanā kunna﴾ (Glory be to Him who subjected these to us)." Whoever prohibits this takes Subḥān as a proper name for the meaning of glorification, just as barra is used as a proper name for piety. The ma is a temporal verbal-masdariyya, and this would be a statement by Iblis confessing his former disbelief against himself, meaning: "My sin came before your sin." ﴿Fa-lā istikhāra ʿindī anna al-ẓālimīna lahum ʿadhābun alīm﴾ (So there is no fault in me, that the wrongdoers have a painful punishment): the apparent view is that this is part of Iblis's speech; God related what he will say at that time, so that it would be a warning to the listeners, that they should consider their end and prepare for what is inevitable, and that they should imagine in themselves that situation in which Satan will say what he says, so that they may fear, act to deliver themselves from it, and be saved. It has also been said: it is from the speech of the guardians of Hell on that day. It has also been said: it is from the speech of God, the Exalted. Abu ʿAbdillah al-Razi has a discussion here about Satan and the angels, which can be found in his tafsir.

﴿Wa-udkhila alladhīna āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāti jannātin tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhāru khālidīna fīhā bi-idhni rabbihim taḥiyyatuhum fīhā salām﴾ (And those who believed and did righteous deeds will be admitted into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein by the permission of their Lord; their greeting therein will be "Peace"): when He gathered both groups in His saying: ﴿Wa-barazū lillāhi jamīʿan﴾ ("And they will all come forth before God") [Ibrahim 14:21], and mentioned some of the states of the disbelievers, He mentioned what the affair of the believers culminated in, namely their admission into Paradise. The majority of readers recited ﴿wa-udkhila﴾ as a past passive verb. al-Hasan and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd recited ﴿wa-udkhilu﴾ with the first-person hamza, the present tense of adkhala, meaning: "And I will admit [them]." According to the majority's reading, the agent may be the angels. The apparent sense is that ﴿bi-idhni rabbihim﴾ is connected to ﴿udkhila﴾. al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: with what is it connected, in the other reading, and your saying 'and I will admit them' [with the phrase] 'by the permission of their Lord' is not a complete statement?" I answer: "The correct way in this reading is that the phrase ﴿bi-idhni rabbihim﴾ is connected to what follows it, meaning: ﴿taḥiyyatuhum fīhā salām﴾ (their greeting therein is 'Peace') by the permission of their Lord; i.e., the angels greet them by the permission of their Lord." End of quote. The apparent meaning of his statement is that ﴿bi-idhni rabbihim﴾ is the object-complement of ﴿taḥiyyatuhum﴾, and that is why he said: "i.e., the angels greet them by the permission of their Lord." This is not permissible, because it entails placing the complement of a verbal noun (masdar) that is dissolved into a masdariyya particle and verb before it, which is not allowed. Abu al-Fadl ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Ahmad al-Razi al-Hasan said: "Udkhilu" with a raised lam, in the future tense, by God's report about Himself, so that the phrase "by the permission of their Lord" becomes more gentle toward them and more tender to them. The explanation of ﴿taḥiyyatuhum fīhā salām﴾ was given at the beginning of Surat Yunus.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verses 22–23 (part 1 of 3):

﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord: their deeds are like ashes, upon which the wind blows violently on a stormy day. They have no power over anything of what they earned. That is the far-reaching error.﴾ [Ibrahim: 18] ﴿Have you not seen that God created the heavens and the earth with truth? If He wills, He can remove you and bring a new creation.﴾ [Ibrahim: 19] ﴿And that is not difficult for God.﴾ [Ibrahim: 20] ﴿And they will all come forth before God, and the weak will say to those who were arrogant: "We were indeed your followers. Can you then avert from us anything of God's punishment?" They will say: "If God had guided us, we would have guided you. It is all the same for us, whether we panic or endure patiently; for us there is no escape."﴾ [Ibrahim: 21] ﴿And Satan will say, when the matter has been decided: "God promised you a true promise, and I promised you, but I broke my promise to you. I had no authority over you, except that I called you and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves. I cannot help you, nor can you help me. I disowned your associating me with God before." Indeed, for the wrongdoers there is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds will be admitted into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein by the permission of their Lord. Their greeting therein will be: "Peace."﴾ ﴿Have you not seen how God struck a parable: a good word like a good tree, whose root is firm and whose branches are in the sky,﴾ [Ibrahim: 24] ﴿giving its fruit every season by the permission of its Lord. God strikes parables for people, so that they may take heed.﴾ [Ibrahim: 25] ﴿And the parable of an evil word is like an evil tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability.﴾ [Ibrahim: 26]

(p. 414) Al-ramad (ashes) is well known. Ibn Isa said: it is a substance that burning reduces to dust like powder. Its plural in quantity is rumud, and in paucity armidah. Its plural in the pattern af'ila' (armida') is rare. They say: ramad ramadad when it becomes the finest dust, the finest it can be.

Al-jaza' (distress) is the failure to bear hardship, and it is the opposite of patience. The poet said:

"I was distressed, yet I did not grow distressed at the parting with a [true] distress, and I consoled a heart enamored of the maidens."

Al-musrikh (the helper) is the one who relieves. The poet said:

"So do not despair; indeed I am not a helper for you, and there is no aid or victory from me for you."

Al-sarikh is the one who cries for help, from sarakha, yasrukhu, sarkhan, surakhan and sarkhatan. Salamah ibn Jandal said:

"Whenever a frightened crier came to us, the cry for him was the clatter of shins."

Istarkha' means to cry out, and tasarrakha means to force oneself to cry out. He said: "He called me for help and I answered his cry." Al-sarikh is a verbal noun like al-tarih, and it is applied to both the helper and the one seeking help, as one of the contronyms (words with opposite meanings).

Al-far' is a branch of a tree. It is also applied to what is born from a thing. Al-far' also means hair; one says: a man with abundant hair is afra', and a woman is far'a'. Imru' al-Qays ibn Hujr said:

"And a branch covering the back, jet-black and dark."

Ijtatta al-shay' means he uprooted it, and jatta al-shay' means he pulled it out. Al-juththa is the person's form, whether sitting or standing. Laqit al-Iyadi said:

"He is the expulsion that uproots your root; whoever has seen the like of this coming, and whoever has heard of it."

Al-bawar means destruction. The poet said:

"I have not seen their like, champions in war, on the morning of battle when ruin was feared."

(p. 415) Regarding ﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord: their deeds are like ashes﴾ [Ibrahim: 18]: "mathalu" is in the nominative as a mubtada' (inceptive subject, the topic of the sentence), and its predicate (khabar) is omitted. Its estimated form according to Sibawayh is: "what is recited to you" or "what is related." Al-mathal (likeness) is used figuratively for a description that is strange. The clause ﴿their deeds are like ashes﴾ [Ibrahim: 18] is a resumptive clause (jumla musta'anafa) on an implied question, as if it were said: "What is their likeness?" and then it was answered: "their deeds are like ashes," just as you say: "The description of Zayd: his honour is protected and his wealth is spent freely."

Ibn Atiyyah said: the view of al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' is that "mathal" is annulled (i.e., treated as not governing), and the meaning is: "those who disbelieved, their deeds are like ashes." Al-Hufi said: "mathal" is in the nominative by inception, and "a'maluhum" is a badal (substitution, specifically badal al-ishtimal, substitution of inclusion) for "mathal," and "ka-ramad" is the predicate. Al-Zamakhshari said: or "a'maluhum" may be a substitution for "mathal alladhina kafaru," with the estimated form "the likeness of their deeds," and "ka-ramad" is the predicate. Ibn Atiyyah said: it is also said that it is an inceptive subject, and "a'maluhum" is a second inceptive subject, and "ka-ramad" is the predicate of the second, and the whole clause is the predicate of the first. This is, in my view, the most preponderant of the opinions. It is as if you said: "The likeness established in the soul for those who disbelieved is this clause mentioned, namely their deeds in their corruption at the time of need and their dissolution like ashes that the wind scatters and disperses with its force, so that no trace of it remains and nothing of it is gathered." End quote.

This view that Ibn Atiyyah preferred was said by al-Hufi, and it is not permissible, because the clause that occurs as a predicate of the first inceptive subject, which is "mathal," lacks a pronoun referring back to the likeness, and it is not the same as the subject in meaning, so it does not need a pronoun.

The deeds of the disbelievers were the noble acts they used to do: keeping ties of kinship, freeing slaves, ransoming captives, slaughtering camels for guests, relieving the distressed, granting protection, and other such things. He likened their nullification and passing away to scattered dust, because they were built on no foundation of knowledge of God and belief in Him, and because they were done for His sake with the ashes that the violent wind blows away.

Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read "al-riyah" (the winds) in the plural, while the majority read it in the singular. The description of the day as "a stormy day" [Ibrahim: 18], though it is an attribute of the wind, is figurative, as they say: "the day when the agent (wakil) came down was sleeping." Al-Harawi said: the estimated form is "on a day of a stormy wind," and it was omitted because the wind had already been mentioned, as the poet said:

"When there comes a day whose sun is darkened and eclipsed."

He means: "the sun is eclipsed." It is also said that "stormy" is an attribute of the wind, but when it came after "day" it took the case-ending of "day" by adjacency (ittiba' i'rabihi), as it is said: "the lizard's hole, ruined" (juhru dabbin kharibin), meaning that it was put in the genitive by proximity (khafd 'ala al-jiwar).

Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibrahim ibn Abi Bakr from al-Hasan read "fi yawmin 'asifin" [Ibrahim: 18] with the genitive construction (idafa) of "day" to "stormy," and it is a case of the omission of the qualified noun and the placing of the attribute in its position, its estimated form being "on a day of stormy wind." The explanation of "al-'usuf" (stormy blowing) has already been given in Yunus in the words of His saying: ﴿A stormy wind came upon them﴾ [Yunus: 22]. According to the opinion of one who permitted the idafa of a noun to its attribute, the reading may be: "They will have no power on the Day of Resurrection over what they earned of their deeds, meaning they will see no trace of reward for it, just as nothing can be made of ashes scattered by the wind." It is also said: "They will have no power over the reward of what they earned," with an omitted genitive (mudaf) understood.

In the Sahih (of al-Bukhari and Muslim) from Aisha, may God be pleased with her, she said: "O Messenger of God, Ibn Jud'an used to keep ties of kinship and feed the poor in the Jahiliyyah. Does that benefit him?" He said: "It will not benefit him, because he never said: 'My Lord, forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgment.'" Also in the Sahih: "Indeed the disbeliever is fed in this world for the good deeds he did for God." That is an indication of their being in this state.

The phrase "on such a far-reaching error" refers to the deep abyss into which its person plunges, and which is far removed from the path of salvation, and far from the truth or the reward.

In al-Baqarah: ﴿They have no power over anything of what they earned﴾ [Ibrahim: 18] has various stylistic refinements in eloquence and differences in word order, while the meaning is one.

﴿Have you not seen that God created the heavens and the earth with truth? If He wills, He can remove you and bring a new creation﴾ [Ibrahim: 19] ﴿And that is not difficult for God﴾ [Ibrahim: 20].

﴿And they will all come forth before God, and the weak will say to those who were arrogant: "We were indeed your followers. Can you then avert from us anything of God's punishment?" They will say: "If God had guided us, we would have guided you. It is all the same for us, whether we panic or endure patiently; for us there is no escape."﴾ [Ibrahim: 21]: al-Sulami read "alam tar" (have you not seen) with the sukun on the ra'. Its basis is that he applied the pausal form to the connected reading. Another explanation is that the Arabs dropped the alif of "tara" in their saying: "qama al-qawmu, wa law tara ma Zayd" (the people stood, and if you did not see what Zayd was), just as the ya' of "la ubali" (I do not care) was dropped to become "la ubal." When the jussive particle entered, it was imagined that the ra' was the last letter of the word, so it was given sukun for the jussive, just as they say of "la ubali": "lam ubal," imagining the lam as the final letter of the word. The seeing here means knowing, and so it is a seeing of the heart.

Al-Akhawan read "khaliqu" as an active participle (ism al-fa'il), and "al-ard" in the genitive. The rest of the seven read "khalaqa" as a past verb, and "al-ard" in the accusative. As for "bi-l-haqq," al-Zamakhshari said: with wisdom, with a sound purpose and a great matter; He did not create them in vain or in play. Ibn Atiyyah said: with truth, that is, with what is right in terms of the interests of His servants, and the carrying out of His prior decree, and to show that this is evidence of Him and of His power. It is also said: with His word and speech. It is also said: "bi-l-haqq" is a circumstantial (hal) clause, meaning "truly." The apparent meaning of His saying "He can remove you" [Ibrahim: 19] is that it is a general address to people. From Ibn Abbas: it is an address to the disbelievers. As for "and bring a new creation" [Ibrahim: 19], it may mean: "if He wills, He can remove you, O people, and bring other people of your kind, human beings, or it may mean of other than your kind." The first is the view of the majority of the exegetes. Similar to these two possibilities was mentioned by the exegetes regarding His saying in al-Nisa': ﴿If He wills, He can remove you, O people, and bring others﴾ [al-Nisa: 133], and we explained there that it allows only the first interpretation.

"And that" means: your removal and the bringing of a new creation are neither impossible nor difficult for Him, may He be exalted, because He is the one capable of what He wills. Al-Zamakhshari said: because He is capable by His essence; there is no particular restriction for Him to one thing rather than another. When the motive for something is fully present for Him and no obstacle stands in the way, it happens without hesitation, like the movement of your finger. When a motive calls Him to something and no hindrance stands in its way, [it happens]. End quote.

In this there is a trace of Mu'tazilism in his saying "the capable" (al-qadir), because they affirm a "capability" (qadiriyya) and deny "power" (qudra); and in his likening His action, may He be exalted, to the action of a servant in his saying "like the movement of your finger." In our view, the movement of our finger is only by the power of God, may He be exalted, and what is attributed to us of power has no effect in bringing anything into existence.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: this verse explains how far they have strayed into error, and the enormity of their disbelief in God, given the clarity of His signs that testify to Him, which indicate His dazzling power and His far-reaching wisdom, and that He is the one worthy of being worshipped, feared for His punishment, and hoped for His reward in the abode of recompense. End quote.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verse 22–23 (part 2 of 3):

﴿And they came forth﴾ [Ibrahim: 21]: That is, they emerged from their graves to face Allah's recompense and reckoning. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of their coming forth before Allah, when Allah, exalted is He, nothing is hidden from Him until it is brought out, is that they used to hide from people's eyes when committing indecencies, thinking that this was concealed from Allah. When the Day of Resurrection comes, they will be exposed to Allah in their own selves, and they will know that nothing hidden is concealed from Him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "And they came forth" means they came to the open ground (al-baraz), which is the wide open land, and this was borrowed to describe the gathering on the Day of Resurrection. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: The interpretation of the philosophers (al-hukama') is that when the soul departs from the body, it is as if the covering is removed, and it remains stripped in its own essence, bare of everything other than itself, and that is the "coming forth" before Allah, exalted is He. This man (al-Razi) often cites the words of the philosophers, and they differ from the people of the revealed laws (ahl al-shara'i') in interpreting the speech of Allah, exalted is He, revealed in the language of the Arabs, and the Arabs do not understand any of the concepts of the people of philosophy. Their interpretation is like a riddle and enigmas, and this man calls them "philosophers," though they are among the most ignorant of the disbelievers in Allah, exalted is He, and in His prophets. The pronoun in ﴿And they came forth﴾ [Ibrahim: 21] refers to the created beings who are being reckoned, and the past tense was used to express the certainty of the one who reports it, as though it had already happened. Zayd ibn 'Ali recited (wa-baraza) in the passive voice and with a doubled ra'. Al-du'afa' (the weak) are the followers and the common people. In the Mushaf it was written with a waw before the hamza (in the word al-du'afa'? no, in the word for the "ulama' of the Children of Israel"), following the pronunciation of those who enlarge the alif before the hamza, inclining it toward the waw. Similar is 'ulama' Bani Isra'il (the scholars of the Children of Israel). Al-ladhina istakbaru (those who were arrogant) are their leaders and chiefs, who sought to be followed by the weak and to make them follow them. Istakbaru and takabbaru mean they showed the magnification of themselves, or they were arrogant against following the messengers and worshipping Allah. Taba'an (followers): it may be a collective noun for tabi', like khadim and khuddam, and ghaib and ghuyyab. It may also be a verbal noun (masdar), like the saying 'adlun wa-ridan. ﴿Are you going to avail us anything?﴾: this is an interrogative whose meaning is their rebuke and reproach of them, though they knew that they would not avail them. The meaning is: We followed you in the misguidance you were in, just as you commanded us, and you did not avail us anything. Therefore their answer came (p-417): ﴿If Allah had guided us, we would have guided you﴾. They answered this way as an excuse and out of shame, and as a rejection of guidance to Allah, exalted is He, and this is a true statement in itself. Al-Zamakhshari said: The first min is for specification (li-l-tabyin), and the second is for partition (li-l-tab'id), as though it were said: "Are you going to avail us some part of that thing which is the punishment of Allah?" It is also permissible that both are for partition together, meaning: "Are you going to avail us some part of a thing which is part of the punishment of Allah," that is, part of a part of the punishment of Allah. End of quotation. These two interpretations that al-Zamakhshari gave for min in the two places: the first requires that ﴿of anything﴾ [Ibrahim: 21] be placed before ﴿of the punishment of Allah﴾ [Ibrahim: 21], because he made ﴿of anything﴾ the thing specified by ﴿of the punishment of Allah﴾. The specifying min is preceded by what it specifies, and does not come after it. The second interpretation, that "part of a thing" is "part of the punishment," requires that it be an apposition (badal), which would be the substitution of a general for a particular, because "of anything" is more general than "of the punishment of Allah." If by "thing" he means a thing from the punishment, then the meaning returns to what was estimated, namely "part of a part of the punishment of Allah." This is not acceptable, because the partitive quality of a thing is absolute, so it cannot have a part. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' stated that min in His saying "of anything" is extra (za'ida). Al-Hawfi said: ﴿of the punishment of Allah﴾ [Ibrahim: 21] is connected to ﴿are you going to avail﴾ [Ibrahim: 21], and min in ﴿of anything﴾ [Ibrahim: 21] is for the generalization of the genus, extra for emphasis. Abu al-Baqa' said: min is extra, meaning a thing that is from the punishment of Allah, and it is construed in terms of meaning, its estimate being: "Are you going to prevent from us anything?" It is also permissible that "thing" stands in the position of a verbal noun, meaning "sufficiency," so that "of the punishment of Allah" is connected to ﴿are you going to avail﴾ [Ibrahim: 21]. End of quotation. The justification for the extra min is that the predicate is in the context of interrogation, as if the interrogative particle entered upon it and governed it, and the extra min here is like the extra min in the construction: "So are you going to avail?" Al-Zamakhshari said: They answered them, making excuses for what they had done to them, that if Allah had guided them to faith, they would have guided them, and they did not misguide them, either perceiving their sin in their misguidance and their misguiding of them as being against Allah, as Allah related about them: They said: ﴿If Allah had willed, we would not have associated, nor would our fathers﴾ [al-An'am: 148], and ﴿If Allah had willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him﴾ [al-Nahl: 35]. They say this in the Hereafter as they used to say it in this world. What indicates this is His saying, relating about the hypocrites: ﴿On the Day when Allah resurrects them all, and they swear to Him as they swear to you, and they think they are on something﴾ [al-Mujadila: 18]. End of quotation. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi related from al-Zamakhshari that they said this while lying in it, and what indicates this is the Exalted One's saying about the hypocrites: ﴿On the Day when Allah resurrects them all, and they swear to Him as they swear to you, and they think they are on something﴾ [al-Mujadila: 18]. Al-Razi said: Know that the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school, who hold that human reason and justice are binding on God) do not permit the occurrence of lying among the people of the Resurrection, so this statement from him contradicts the principles of his shaykhs, and it is not accepted from him. Al-Zamakhshari also said: It is permissible that the meaning is: "If we had been among the people of grace (al-lutf), and our Lord had shown us grace, and we had been guided, we would have guided you to faith." Al-Razi said: Al-Qadi mentioned this view and rejected it, saying: It is not permissible to interpret this as grace, because Allah has already done that. It was also said: If Allah had delivered us from the punishment and guided us to the path of Paradise, we would have guided you. Al-Zamakhshari, expanding on this statement, said: If Allah had guided us to the way of salvation from the punishment, we would have guided you, that is, we would have freed you from it and led you on the path of salvation, just as we led you on the path of destruction. End of quotation. It was also said: What indicates that the intended guidance is guidance to the path of Paradise is that it is what they sought and asked for, so it must be what is meant. Ibn 'Abbas said: If Allah had guided us, we would have guided you. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿It is the same for us whether we protest or endure﴾ [Ibrahim: 21] to its end falls under the speech of the arrogant, and its clauses came without the conjunction waw, as though each clause were created independent and not conjoined, even though they are linked to one another in meaning, because their question "Are you going to avail us?" was only because of their distress at their condition. So they said that, equating themselves with them in that, since they were united in the punishment of the misguidance in which they had been united. They are saying: What is this distress and reproach? There is no benefit in distress, just as there is no benefit in patience. When they said "If Allah had guided us," they followed that with despair of salvation, so they said: ﴿We have no escape﴾ [Ibrahim: 21]: that is, no refuge and no place of flight, whether we protest or endure. It was also said: "It is the same for us" is part of the speech of the weak and of those who were arrogant (p-418), and the estimate is: They all said, "It is the same for us," informing about their state. The discussion of this kind of equalizing was mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqara. The apparent meaning is that this dialogue between the weak and the leaders takes place at the time of the exposure before Allah. It is related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Ibn Zayd that their saying ﴿It is the same for us whether we protest or endure﴾ [Ibrahim: 21] was after they had endured in the Fire for five hundred years, and after they had protested for an equal period.

﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided: Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I broke it to you. I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves. I cannot help you, nor can you help me. Indeed, I disbelieve in your associating me with Allah before. Indeed, for the wrongdoers there is a painful punishment﴾: The connection of this verse to what came before is that when He mentioned the dialogue of the followers with their disbelieving leaders, He mentioned the dialogue of Satan with his followers among mankind, because the leaders and the devils share in being involved in misguidance. Satan here is Iblis, and he is the chief of the devils. In the hadith of intercession from the hadith of 'Uqba ibn 'Amir: "The disbelievers will say: The believers have found someone to intercede for them, so who will intercede for us? They will say: None but Iblis, for he is the one who misguided us. They will come to him and say: The believers have found someone to intercede for them, so stand up and intercede for us, for you misguided us. He will stand up, and from his assembly there will rise the foulest smell anyone has ever smelled. And at that point he will say: ﴿Indeed Allah promised you﴾, the verse." It is related from al-Hasan: Iblis will stand as a preacher in Hell, on a pulpit of fire, and all creatures will hear him, and he will say: Indeed Allah promised you the promise of truth, meaning the Resurrection, Paradise, the Fire, the reward of the obedient and the punishment of the disobedient, and He fulfilled His promise to you. I promised you that there would be no Resurrection, no Paradise, no Fire, no reward and no punishment, and I broke it to you. "The matter has been decided": a group has been appointed for Paradise and a group for the Fire, and all of that happens at the place of standing (al-mawqif). This is indicated by the hadith of intercession, or it is after the people of Paradise have entered Paradise and the people of the Fire have entered the Fire. This is also indicated by what we have mentioned from al-Hasan, and it is the interpretation of al-Tabari. It was also said: "The matter has been decided" means it has been cut off and completed, and that is the reckoning, and the two groups have been sent off to their abodes. The "promise of truth" may be understood as an attributive construction, meaning "the true promise." It may be that "truth" is an attribute of Allah, meaning His promise. It may also be that "truth" refers to the established thing, which is the Resurrection and the recompense for deeds, meaning: He fulfilled for you what He promised you, and I promised you the opposite of that, so I broke it to you. As for ﴿but I had no authority over you except that I called you﴾, the apparent meaning is that this is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), because his calling them to misguidance and his whispering is not of the kind of authority, which is clear proof. It was said: It is possible that by authority he means dominance, control and power, meaning: I did not compel you or frighten you with force, but I presented something to you, and your opinion accepted it. It was also said: It is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), because the power to move a person toward something is sometimes by force from the mover, and sometimes by strengthening the motive in his heart, and this is done by casting whispers into him, so this is a kind of control. It was also said: The apparent meaning of this speech indicates that Satan has no power to strike a person down, distort his limbs and organs, or remove his reason. So ﴿do not blame me﴾. It was recited as ﴿so let them not blame me﴾ with the ya', in the third person, and this is a shift (iltifat). He means: concerning what you were given of misguidance, and blame yourselves for your bad judgment and for your responding to my call without deliberation or proof. Al-Zamakhshari said: And blame yourselves, since you were deceived and obeyed me when I called you, and you did not obey your Lord when He called you. This is evidence that the human being is the one who chooses wretchedness and happiness and acquires them for himself, and from Allah there is only enabling, and from Satan only adornment. If the matter were as the determinists (al-Mujbira, those who hold that human actions are wholly predetermined) claim, he would have said: "So do not blame me, nor yourselves, for Allah has decreed disbelief for you and compelled you to it." End of quotation. This is on the path of the Mu'tazila.

﴿Mā anā bimuṣrikhikum﴾ (I cannot help you). Ibn ʿAbbas said: "by benefiting you." Ibn Jubayr said: "by rescuing you." al-Rabiʿ said: "by saving you." Mujahid said: "by aiding you." All of these statements are close in meaning.

Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-Aʿmash, and Hamza read: ﴿bimuṣrikhiyya﴾, with a kasra on the ya. Many grammarians criticized this reading. al-Farraʾ said: "It may be a mistake of the reciters, for few of them are free from error. He probably thought that the ba' in ﴿bimuṣrikhiyya﴾ governs the whole word, while the ba' is separate from the first person (ya') ending." Abu ʿUbayd said: "We think they erred. They assumed that the ba' takes a kasra because of what follows it." al-Akhfash said: "I have not heard this from any Arab or from any grammarian." al-Zajjaj said: "This reading is, according to all grammarians, poor and rejected, and it has no justification except a weak one." al-Nahhas said: "This has become a consensus, and the Book of God may not be interpreted as an anomaly." al-Zamakhshari said: "It is weak, and they cited for it an anonymous line of verse:

*Qāla lahā: hal laki yā tāfiyyi*
*Qālat lahu: mā anta bil-marḍiyyi*

(He said to her: "Do you have any [desire], O Tafi?" She said to him: "You are not the one who is pleasing.")

It seems that he considered the ya' of possession (ya' al-idafa) to be silent, and before it a silent ya', so he vocalized it with a kasra, according to the principle of resolving two silent letters meeting. But this is not sound, because the ya' of possession is only ever pronounced with a fatha when it is preceded by an alif, as in ʿaṣāya (my staff), fa-mā bāluhā (what is its matter), and when it is preceded by a ya'." (Objection): "The first ya' is treated like a true, sound letter because of the idgham (assimilation), as if it were a ya' that came silent after a silent sound consonant, so it is vocalized with a kasra according to the original rule." (Answer): "This is a good analogy, but the widespread usage, which is like a mutawatir report (a report transmitted by so many chains that it cannot be doubted), overrides analogies." End of quote. As for his statement "and they cited for it an anonymous line of verse," another source has mentioned that it belongs to al-Aghlab al-ʿIjli, and this dialect still survives on the lips of many people today; one says: *mā fiyyi afʿalu kadhā* ("I will not do this"), with a kasra on the ya'. As for the vocalization he mentioned, it is the interpretation of al-Farraʾ, which al-Zajjaj reported from him. As for his remark in the course of his speech, "where it is preceded by an alif," I do not know of any case where ḥayth is added to a clause introduced by an adverb, such as *qaʿada Zaydun ḥaythu amāma ʿUmar wa Bakr*, so this construction needs to be heard from authority. As for his statement "because the ya' of possession is at its end," it has been transmitted that the ya' after an alif is silent, and the readers recited so in words like *maḥyāya* (my life), and what those grammarians we mentioned have said should not be paid attention to. Later scholars have followed their footsteps in this, so it is not permissible to say of it that it is an error, or ugly, or poor. Some scholars of language have reported that it is a dialect, but its use is rare. Quṭrub explicitly stated that it is a dialect of the Banu Yarbuʿ. al-Qasim ibn Maʿn, one of the leaders of the Kufan grammarians, said: "It is correct." Husayn al-Juʿfi asked Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla' about it, and when the grammarians' criticism of the reading was mentioned, he said: "It is permissible." He also said: "Do not mind whether its vowel is lower or higher." And it is reported from him that he said: "With the khafḍ (kasra) it is good." And it is also reported from him that he said: "It is permissible." It is not, in terms of i'rab (grammatical inflection), like that, and no attention should be paid to Abu Hatim's denial of Abu ʿAmr's approval of it, for Abu ʿAmr is an imam of language, an imam of grammar, an imam of recitation, and a pure Arab; he permitted it and considered it good. They have also transmitted the line of al-Nabigha:

*ʿAlayya li-ʿAmrin niʿmatun baʿda niʿmatin*
*li-wālidihi laysat bi-dhāti ʿaqārib*

(Upon me, for ʿAmr, is a favor after a favor, for his father; it is not one of the stinging kind.)

with the ya' of ʿalayya vocalized with a kasra.

﴿Wa-mā ashrakatumūni min qabl﴾: the ma here is verbal-masdariyya (it forms a verbal noun), and ﴿min qabl﴾ is connected to ﴿ashrakatumūni﴾, meaning: "I disbelieve today in your associating me [with God] before this day, i.e., in the world, as in His saying: ﴿Innā burā'u minkum wa-mimmā taʿbudūna min dūnillāhi kafarnā bikum﴾ ("We are free of you and of what you worship besides God; we have rejected you") [al-Mumtahana 60:4], and He said: ﴿Wa-yawma al-qiyāmati yakfurūna bi-shirkikum﴾ ("On the Day of Resurrection they will deny your associating") [Fatir 35:14]." It has also been said: ma is relative, in the sense of alladhi (which), and the estimate is: "I disbelieved in the idol which you associated with me," so the returning pronoun was omitted. It has also been said: ﴿min qabl﴾ is connected to ﴿kafartu﴾, and ma is in the sense of alladhi: "I disbelieved before, when I refused to prostrate to Adam, in that which you associated with me, namely God, glorified and exalted be He." One says: "I associated Zayd," and when the hamzat al-naql (causative hamza) is added, one says: "I made Zayd associate ʿAmr," i.e., I made him a partner for him. However, this view entails applying ma to God, the Exalted, and the more correct view regarding ma is that it is not applied to any individual of those who have knowledge. al-Zamakhshari said: "Similar to this ma, meaning in its application to God, is the ma in their saying: ﴿Subḥāna mā sakhkhara lanā kunna﴾ (Glory be to Him who subjected these to us)." Whoever prohibits this takes Subḥān as a proper name for the meaning of glorification, just as barra is used as a proper name for piety. The ma is a temporal verbal-masdariyya, and this would be a statement by Iblis confessing his former disbelief against himself, meaning: "My sin came before your sin." ﴿Fa-lā istikhāra ʿindī anna al-ẓālimīna lahum ʿadhābun alīm﴾ (So there is no fault in me, that the wrongdoers have a painful punishment): the apparent view is that this is part of Iblis's speech; God related what he will say at that time, so that it would be a warning to the listeners, that they should consider their end and prepare for what is inevitable, and that they should imagine in themselves that situation in which Satan will say what he says, so that they may fear, act to deliver themselves from it, and be saved. It has also been said: it is from the speech of the guardians of Hell on that day. It has also been said: it is from the speech of God, the Exalted. Abu ʿAbdillah al-Razi has a discussion here about Satan and the angels, which can be found in his tafsir.

﴿Wa-udkhila alladhīna āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāti jannātin tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhāru khālidīna fīhā bi-idhni rabbihim taḥiyyatuhum fīhā salām﴾ (And those who believed and did righteous deeds will be admitted into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein by the permission of their Lord; their greeting therein will be "Peace"): when He gathered both groups in His saying: ﴿Wa-barazū lillāhi jamīʿan﴾ ("And they will all come forth before God") [Ibrahim 14:21], and mentioned some of the states of the disbelievers, He mentioned what the affair of the believers culminated in, namely their admission into Paradise. The majority of readers recited ﴿wa-udkhila﴾ as a past passive verb. al-Hasan and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd recited ﴿wa-udkhilu﴾ with the first-person hamza, the present tense of adkhala, meaning: "And I will admit [them]." According to the majority's reading, the agent may be the angels. The apparent sense is that ﴿bi-idhni rabbihim﴾ is connected to ﴿udkhila﴾. al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: with what is it connected, in the other reading, and your saying 'and I will admit them' [with the phrase] 'by the permission of their Lord' is not a complete statement?" I answer: "The correct way in this reading is that the phrase ﴿bi-idhni rabbihim﴾ is connected to what follows it, meaning: ﴿taḥiyyatuhum fīhā salām﴾ (their greeting therein is 'Peace') by the permission of their Lord; i.e., the angels greet them by the permission of their Lord." End of quote. The apparent meaning of his statement is that ﴿bi-idhni rabbihim﴾ is the object-complement of ﴿taḥiyyatuhum﴾, and that is why he said: "i.e., the angels greet them by the permission of their Lord." This is not permissible, because it entails placing the complement of a verbal noun (masdar) that is dissolved into a masdariyya particle and verb before it, which is not allowed. Abu al-Fadl ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Ahmad al-Razi al-Hasan said: "Udkhilu" with a raised lam, in the future tense, by God's report about Himself, so that the phrase "by the permission of their Lord" becomes more gentle toward them and more tender to them. The explanation of ﴿taḥiyyatuhum fīhā salām﴾ was given at the beginning of Surat Yunus.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verses 24–27:

﴿Have you not considered how Allah presents a parable: a good word is like a good tree, whose root is firmly fixed and whose branches reach into the sky,﴾ ﴿giving its fruit at every time by the permission of its Lord. Allah presents parables for the people that perhaps they may remember.﴾ ﴿And the parable of an evil word is like an evil tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability.﴾ ﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe with the firm word in the worldly life and in the Hereafter, and Allah leaves astray the wrongdoers, and Allah does what He wills.﴾

The discussion of (ḍaraba, "struck") together with (al-mathal, "the parable") has already occurred at the beginning of al-Baqarah, so that discussion suffices here. However, the exegetes have offered certain analyses here. Al-Ḥawfī, al-Mahdawī and Abu al-Baqā' parsed (mathalan) as an object of (ḍaraba), and (kalimatan) as a substitute (badal) for (mathalan). Their parsing is a derivative one, based on the premise that (ḍaraba mathalan) does not transitively take a single object. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said, and al-Zamakhsharī permitted it: (mathalan) is the object of (ḍaraba), and (kalimatan) is the first object, deriving from the view that it, together with (al-mathal), is transitive to two objects, because it carries the sense of (jaʿala, "made"). On this view, (ka-shajaratin) is the predicate of an elided subject, meaning: he made the good word a parable, i.e., the word is like a good tree. On the substitution view, (ka-shajaratin) is an adjective (naʿt) of (al-kalimah). Al-Zamakhsharī also permitted, and began with it, that (kalimatan) be in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: he made a good word, like a good tree; this is an explanation of His saying ﴿Allah struck a parable﴾, as when you say: "The prince honoured Zayd, clothed him in a robe, and mounted him on a horse." End of quote. In this there is a strained supposition of an implied element for which there is no necessity.

It was read irregularly (shādhdh) as (kalimatun ṭayyibatun) with the nominative. Abu al-Baqā' said: "on the basis of it being the subject (mubtada'), and (ka-shajaratin) is its predicate." End of quote. It may also be the predicate of an elided subject, the estimate being: it, i.e., the parable, is a good word like a tree; (ka-shajaratin) is an adjective of (kalimatin).

The "good word" (al-kalimah al-ṭayyibah) is: there is no god but Allah, said Ibn ʿAbbās; or faith, said Mujāhid and Ibn Jurayj; or the believer himself, said ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī and al-Rabīʿ; or all his acts of obedience, or the Qur'an, said al-Aṣamm; or the call to Islam, said Ibn Bahr; or praise of Allah, or glorification and declaring Him free of imperfection (tasbīḥ and tanzīh). The "good tree" is: the believer, said Ibn ʿAbbās; or the coconut palm (jawzat al-Hind), said ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās; or a tree in Paradise, also said by Ibn ʿAbbās; or the date palm, and most of the interpreters hold this view. It is the view of Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Anas, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Ibn Zayd. It is explicitly reported in a ḥadīth from Ibn ʿUmar, which al-Dāraquṭnī transmitted from him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited, and mentioned the verse, then said: 'Do you know what it is?' It came to my mind that it is the date palm," and so on. Abu al-ʿĀliyah said: "I came to Anas ibn Mālik, and a tray with fresh dates was brought. Anas said: 'Eat, O Abu al-ʿĀliyah, for it is the good tree which Allah mentioned in His Book.' Then he said: 'A ṣāʿ of unripe dates was brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he recited this verse.'" In al-Tirmidhī, from the ḥadīth of Anas, there is something similar. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Every fruit-bearing tree with good fruit, like the date palm, the fig tree, the vine, the pomegranate, and others." End of quote.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) likened the believer who recites the Qur'an to the citron (utrujjah), so it is not far-fetched that he is likened also to its tree. Its root is firmly fixed: i.e., in the earth, striking its roots into it. Anas ibn Mālik recited (kashajaratin ṭayyibatin thābitun aṣluhā), where the adjective is applied to the tree verbally, though in reality it belongs to the (sababī, the causal noun, i.e., the root). The reading of the majority attributes firmness to the root explicitly and in meaning, and in it there is a fine division, since it says: its root is firmly fixed and its branch is in the sky. By "branch" it means its highest part and top, even though the thing compared has many branches; this is from the category of being satisfied with the generic noun (al-iktifāʾ bi-lafẓ al-jins). The meaning of "in the sky" is the direction of height and ascent, not a canopy. In a ḥadīth: "Allah created Adam, his height was sixty cubits in the sky." When the good word was likened to the good tree, the word's root is firmly fixed in the hearts of the people of faith, and what issues from it of pure deeds and righteous actions is its branch, rising to the sky to Allah, the Exalted: ﴿To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deed raises it﴾ [Fāṭir: 10]. What follows from that deed, which is Allah's reward, is its fruit. He described this tree with four attributes. The first is His saying: good (ṭayyibah), i.e., of noble origin. The basic meaning of the tree is that it has pleasure in eating. The poet said:

*"Good in its lineage, easy, and for them there are paths, if you wish, through a rugged wilderness."*

That is, their courtyard is easy and good. The second: the firmness of its root, which indicates its establishment and that winds do not snap it; it is slow to perish, and what is like this produces joy in finding it. The third: the height of its branches, which indicates the tree's establishment and the firmness of its roots, and its distance from the impurities of the earth, and its purity from defects. The fourth: the continuance of the existence of its fruit and its presence at all times. The word (ḥīn) in the language means a portion of time. The poet said:

*"The healers feared it because of the badness of its poison; it releases it for a time and then takes it back for a time."*

The meaning: it gives its fruit every time Allah has appointed for it. Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, and al-Ḥasan said: that is, every year. For this reason, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, al-Ḥakam, Ḥammād, and a group of jurists said: whoever swears not to do something for a (ḥīn), he does not do it for a year, and they cited this verse as evidence. It was said: eight months, said ʿAlī and Mujāhid; six months, which is the period the fruit remains on it. Ibn al-Musayyab said: (ḥīn) is two months, because the date palm remains bearing fruit for two months. It was said: it is never without fruit, bearing in every month, and this is the coconut palm. Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Rabīʿ also said: every ḥīn, that is every morning and evening, whenever its fruit is desired, and this is derived from the view that it is a tree in Paradise. The remembrance hoped for through striking a parable is comprehension and conceiving of the meanings perceived by the intellect. When these are displayed through sensible things, the senses, the imagination and the estimative faculty do not dispute them, the intelligible fits the sensible, and understanding and reaching the sought goal are achieved.

The evil word (al-kalimah al-khabīthah) is, according to the majority, the word of disbelief (kufr). Masrūq said: it is lying, and said: it is what draws on the call to disbelief and what the disbeliever attributes to himself. It was said: every speech that Allah, the Exalted, does not approve of. Ubayy read: (wa-ḍaraba Allāhu mathalan kalimatan khabīthah), and it was read: (wa-mathala kalimatin) with the accusative on (mathala), in coordination with ﴿a good word﴾.

The evil tree (al-shajarah al-khabīthah) is the colocynth tree (shajarat al-ḥanẓal), said most of the scholars: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Anas ibn Mālik, and it was transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Zajjāj and a group said: the garlic tree. It was said: the kashūth tree, which is a tree with no leaves and no root; he said: it is kashūth, with no root and no fruit. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: these views are objected to, since all of these are from the herbs (najm) and not from trees, and Allah, the Exalted, only likened [it] to a tree, so these are not called a tree except figuratively. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning garlic and onion: "Whoever eats from this tree..." It was said: the ṭuḥlubah (a moss or lichen). It was said: the truffle (kamʾah). It was said: every tree whose fruit is not good. From Ibn ʿAbbās: it is the disbeliever. From him also: a tree that was not created on the earth. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: (p-423) "In my view the evident meaning is that the comparison was made with an unspecified tree, which, if these attributes are found in it, is like the thorny trees (ʿiḍāh) or the poison tree and the like, when it is uprooted, i.e., pulled out by its roots, and remains in the utmost weakness and frailty, so that the least wind overturns it. The disbeliever thinks he has something in his hand, but it does not stay firm, and it does not benefit him, like this tree which the ignorant person, from a distance, supposes to be something beneficial, while it is evil in its fruit and not beneficial." End of quote.

(Uprooted from the surface of the earth) is the counterpart of His saying (its root is firmly fixed), i.e., no root or stem has become established for it in the earth; it is only sprouting on the face of the earth. (Having no stability) means having no settledness. It is said: (qarra al-shayʾu qarāran), meaning the thing was established, it firmly stayed. The word that is not supported by proof is likened to this tree; it does not remain, but vanishes soon because of its falsehood. The firm word is that which has been established by proof and demonstration in the heart of its holder, took root in it, and his soul is at rest with it.

Their being made firm by it in the world is that, if they were tempted away from their religion in the world, they would stand firm in it and would not slip, as happened to the people of the trench (aṣḥāb al-Ukhdūd), those who were sawn with saws, and whose flesh was scraped with iron combs, as Jurjīs, Shamʿūn and Bilāl were firm, until Bilāl was tortured on the hot sand while saying: "One! One!" Their being made firm in the Hereafter is that when they are questioned at the gathering of witnesses about their belief, they do not stammer, they are not confounded, and the terrors of the Gathering do not bewilder them. (Those who believe) is general, from Adam to the Day of Resurrection. Ṭāwūs, Qatādah and most scholars said: their being made firm in the world is the duration of a person's life, and in the Hereafter it is the time of his questioning in his grave; al-Ṭabarī preferred this view. Al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib and a group said: "in the worldly life" is the time of questioning in the grave, which al-Barāʾ transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), and "in the Hereafter" is the Day of Resurrection at the Presentation. It was said: the meaning of their being made firm in the worldly life and in the Hereafter is that they live upon faith and are gathered upon it. It was said: being made firm in the worldly life is victory and triumph, and in the Hereafter is Paradise and reward. What is authentically reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the ḥadīth of al-Barāʾ concerning his recitation, when the believer is threatened in his grave and is questioned and bears witness to the testimony of sincerity, of His saying ﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe﴾, the verse, does not make clear that (the worldly life) means the life of a person, and that the Hereafter is the grave, nor that the worldly life is in the grave and the Hereafter is the Day of Resurrection; rather the wording is open to these possibilities.

The meaning of (yuthabbitu, "keeps firm") is that He makes them abide upon it and protects them from slipping. From it is the saying of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥah:

*"So may Allah keep firm what He gave you of goodness, a firmness like that of Moses, and victory like that of those who were given victory."*

The evident view is that ﴿with the firm word﴾ is connected to His saying (yuthabbitu). It was also said it is connected to (āmanū, "believed"). The questioning of the servant in his grave is the belief of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah, the orthodox majority).

﴿And Allah leaves astray the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., the disbelievers, because they are contrasted with the believers. Their being led astray in the world is that they do not stand firm in the situations of trials, their feet slip, and this is the bewilderment which overtakes them, since they do not hold to any proof. In the Hereafter it is their confusion in their answer. Since the comparison of the good word was mentioned before the comparison of the evil word, the one to whom the good word is attributed was mentioned first, and the one to whom the evil word is attributed followed. When He mentioned what He did to each of the two categories, He stated that there is no objection possible regarding what He specifically assigned to each of them, since that falls under His will, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed Allah does what He wills﴾, He is not questioned about what He does. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "And Allah does what He wills," i.e., the direction of wisdom, because the will of Allah follows wisdom, in making the believers firm, supporting them, and protecting them when they stand firm and resolve, and in leading the wrongdoers astray and forsaking them and leaving them to their own affairs when they slip. End of quote. In this there is a hidden trace of Mu'tazilism (dasīsat al-i'tizāl).

The evil word (al-kalimah al-khabīthah) is, according to the majority, the word of disbelief (kufr). Masrūq said: it is lying, and said: it is what draws on the call to disbelief and what the disbeliever attributes to himself. It was said: every speech that Allah, the Exalted, does not approve of. Ubayy read: (wa-ḍaraba Allāhu mathalan kalimatan khabīthah), and it was read: (wa-mathala kalimatin) with the accusative on (mathala), in coordination with ﴿a good word﴾.

The evil tree (al-shajarah al-khabīthah) is the colocynth tree (shajarat al-ḥanẓal), said most of the scholars: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Anas ibn Mālik, and it was transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Zajjāj and a group said: the garlic tree. It was said: the kashūth tree, which is a tree with no leaves and no root; he said: it is kashūth, with no root and no fruit. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: these views are objected to, since all of these are from the herbs (najm) and not from trees, and Allah, the Exalted, only likened [it] to a tree, so these are not called a tree except figuratively. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning garlic and onion: "Whoever eats from this tree..." It was said: the ṭuḥlubah (a moss or lichen). It was said: the truffle (kamʾah). It was said: every tree whose fruit is not good. From Ibn ʿAbbās: it is the disbeliever. From him also: a tree that was not created on the earth. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: (p-423) "In my view the evident meaning is that the comparison was made with an unspecified tree, which, if these attributes are found in it, is like the thorny trees (ʿiḍāh) or the poison tree and the like, when it is uprooted, i.e., pulled out by its roots, and remains in the utmost weakness and frailty, so that the least wind overturns it. The disbeliever thinks he has something in his hand, but it does not stay firm, and it does not benefit him, like this tree which the ignorant person, from a distance, supposes to be something beneficial, while it is evil in its fruit and not beneficial." End of quote.

(Uprooted from the surface of the earth) is the counterpart of His saying (its root is firmly fixed), i.e., no root or stem has become established for it in the earth; it is only sprouting on the face of the earth. (Having no stability) means having no settledness. It is said: (qarra al-shayʾu qarāran), meaning the thing was established, it firmly stayed. The word that is not supported by proof is likened to this tree; it does not remain, but vanishes soon because of its falsehood. The firm word is that which has been established by proof and demonstration in the heart of its holder, took root in it, and his soul is at rest with it.

Their being made firm by it in the world is that, if they were tempted away from their religion in the world, they would stand firm in it and would not slip, as happened to the people of the trench (aṣḥāb al-Ukhdūd), those who were sawn with saws, and whose flesh was scraped with iron combs, as Jurjīs, Shamʿūn and Bilāl were firm, until Bilāl was tortured on the hot sand while saying: "One! One!" Their being made firm in the Hereafter is that when they are questioned at the gathering of witnesses about their belief, they do not stammer, they are not confounded, and the terrors of the Gathering do not bewilder them. (Those who believe) is general, from Adam to the Day of Resurrection. Ṭāwūs, Qatādah and most scholars said: their being made firm in the world is the duration of a person's life, and in the Hereafter it is the time of his questioning in his grave; al-Ṭabarī preferred this view. Al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib and a group said: "in the worldly life" is the time of questioning in the grave, which al-Barāʾ transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), and "in the Hereafter" is the Day of Resurrection at the Presentation. It was said: the meaning of their being made firm in the worldly life and in the Hereafter is that they live upon faith and are gathered upon it. It was said: being made firm in the worldly life is victory and triumph, and in the Hereafter is Paradise and reward. What is authentically reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the ḥadīth of al-Barāʾ concerning his recitation, when the believer is threatened in his grave and is questioned and bears witness to the testimony of sincerity, of His saying ﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe﴾, the verse, does not make clear that (the worldly life) means the life of a person, and that the Hereafter is the grave, nor that the worldly life is in the grave and the Hereafter is the Day of Resurrection; rather the wording is open to these possibilities.

The meaning of (yuthabbitu, "keeps firm") is that He makes them abide upon it and protects them from slipping. From it is the saying of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥah:

*"So may Allah keep firm what He gave you of goodness, a firmness like that of Moses, and victory like that of those who were given victory."*

The evident view is that ﴿with the firm word﴾ is connected to His saying (yuthabbitu). It was also said it is connected to (āmanū, "believed"). The questioning of the servant in his grave is the belief of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah, the orthodox majority).

﴿And Allah leaves astray the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., the disbelievers, because they are contrasted with the believers. Their being led astray in the world is that they do not stand firm in the situations of trials, their feet slip, and this is the bewilderment which overtakes them, since they do not hold to any proof. In the Hereafter it is their confusion in their answer. Since the comparison of the good word was mentioned before the comparison of the evil word, the one to whom the good word is attributed was mentioned first, and the one to whom the evil word is attributed followed. When He mentioned what He did to each of the two categories, He stated that there is no objection possible regarding what He specifically assigned to each of them, since that falls under His will, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed Allah does what He wills﴾, He is not questioned about what He does. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "And Allah does what He wills," i.e., the direction of wisdom, because the will of Allah follows wisdom, in making the believers firm, supporting them, and protecting them when they stand firm and resolve, and in leading the wrongdoers astray and forsaking them and leaving them to their own affairs when they slip. End of quote. In this there is a hidden trace of Mu'tazilism (dasīsat al-i'tizāl).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verses 28–30:

﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the favor of Allah for disbelief and settled their people in the abode of ruin?﴾ ﴿[They will enter] Hell, which they will burn, and wretched is the place of settlement.﴾ ﴿And they set up rivals to Allah to lead [others] astray from His way. Say, "Enjoy yourselves, for indeed your destination is the Fire."﴾: When He mentioned the state of the believers and their guidance, and the state of the disbelievers and their misguidance, He mentioned the cause of their misguidance. "Those who exchanged" apparently refers generally to all the polytheists; this is the view of al-Hasan (al-Hasan al-Basri), who said they exchanged the faith for disbelief. Mujahid said: they are the people of Mecca. Allah had blessed them by sending a Messenger from among them who taught them the matter of their religion and honored them with it, settled them in His sanctuary, and made them the custodians of His House. So they put disbelief in place of the thanks due for this blessing. Ibn Abbas asked Umar about them, and he said: "They are the Bedouin of Quraysh, my maternal uncles," meaning the Banu Makhzum, "and they were uprooted at Badr." "And your paternal uncles," meaning the Banu Umayya, "and they were given enjoyment for a time." Something similar is related from Ali. Qatada said: they are the leaders of the polytheists on the Day of Badr. From Ali: they are the Quraysh who formed factions on the Day of Badr, and on the view that they are Quraysh, [this includes] a group of the Companions and the Successors. Also from Ali: they are the hypocrites of Quraysh, whom Allah blessed by making them show the banner of Islam, whereby He protected their blood, their property and their offspring, but then they returned to disbelief. From Ibn Abbas: [the verse was revealed] concerning Jabala ibn al-Ayham. He does not mean that it was revealed concerning him, because the revelation of the verse came before his story, and his story took place during the caliphate of Umar. Rather, Ibn Abbas means that it applies to whoever does an act of the same kind until the Day of Resurrection.

"The favor of Allah" is governed by an omitted genitive modifier (ḥadhf muḍāf), meaning: they exchanged the thanks for the favor of Allah. This is like His saying: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 82], meaning the thanks for your provision. It is as if thanks were obligatory upon them, so they put disbelief in its place, and they made denial in place of their thanks. Al-Zamakhshari said: "There is another interpretation, namely that they exchanged the very favor for disbelief, so that disbelief became for them in place of the favor. They are the people of Mecca, whom Allah settled in His sanctuary, made the custodians of His House, and honored with Muhammad (ﷺ). Yet they disbelieved the favor of Allah, in place of the great thanks that He required of them. Or Allah gave them favor and abundance because of their two journeys (of trade), but they were ungrateful for His favor, so Allah struck them with drought for seven years. Thus disbelief came to them in place of the favor, and disbelief remained as a collar around their necks." End of quotation. "The favor of Allah" is the second object (al-maf'ūl al-thānī), because it is the element that the preposition (ḥarf al-jarr) enters, meaning: "in exchange for the favor of Allah." "Disbelief" (kufran) is the first object (al-maf'ūl al-awwal). This is like His saying: ﴿Those, Allah will change their evil deeds into good deeds﴾ [al-Furqan: 70], meaning: He will change their evil deeds for good deeds. So the accusative noun is what is obtained, and the noun in the genitive with the preposition "bi," or the accusative noun with the preposition dropped, is what is given up. This is the usage of the Arabs, and it is contrary to what common people and many who claim to be scholars understand. We have clarified this matter in His saying in al-Baqarah: ﴿Whoever exchanges disbelief for faith﴾ [al-Baqarah: 108]. If you posit an omitted genitive modifier, namely "thanks for the favor of Allah," then it is this noun that the "bi" entered and was then dropped. If no omitted modifier is posited, then "bi" entered upon "favor" and was then dropped.

"And they settled their people," meaning: those who followed them in disbelief.

Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' claimed that "kufran" is the second object of "baddalū," but this is not correct, because "baddala" belongs to the same class as "ikhtāra" (to choose). The one that the preposition directly governs is the second object, and the one that the verb reaches directly, without the mediation of a preposition, is the first object.

Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' parsed "Jahannam" as a substitute (badal) for "dār al-bawār," while al-Zamakhshari parsed it as an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān). On this view the settling takes place in the Hereafter. "The abode of ruin" is Jahannam, as Ibn Zayd said. It is also said, from Ali, that it refers to the Day of Badr, and from Ata ibn Yasar: [the verse] was revealed concerning the slain of Badr. Then "the abode of ruin" means destruction in this world, like the well of Badr and other places where they were killed. On this view, Ibn Atiyya and Abu al-Baqa' parsed "Jahannam" as an accusative in the construction of occupation (al-ishtighāl), meaning: "they will burn Jahannam, they will burn it." The reading of Ibn Abi Ablah supports this interpretation: "Jahannamu" with the nominative, which allows that "Jahannam" is nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject. This interpretation is preferable, because the accusative under the construction of occupation is less preferred, since nothing preceding it favors it or makes it equally likely. The majority of readers read it in the accusative. They would not have read it with a less preferred or equally likely form, since "Zaydun dacatuhu" is more eloquent than "Zaydan dacatuhu." Therefore its nominative in the reading of Ibn Abi Ablah, as the predicate of an omitted subject, is preferred. On the interpretation of the construction of occupation, "yaslawnahā" has no place in the grammatical structure. On the first interpretation they allowed that it could be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "Jahannam," or from "dār al-bawār," or from "their people." The word that is praised or condemned (al-makhṣūṣ bi-l-dhamm) is omitted, its implied sense being: "and wretched is the place of settlement, it," meaning: Jahannam.

"And they set up rivals to Allah" means: they added to their disbelief the ingratitude of setting up rivals to Allah. These rivals are the idols they took as gods besides Allah.

Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read "liyuḍillū" here with a fatḥa on the yāʾ, and in al-Ḥajj, Luqman and al-Rum as "li-yuḍilla." The rest of the seven read it with a ḍamma. Apparently the lām is the lām of becoming and outcome (lām al-ṣayrūra wa-l-ma'āl). Since the result of taking rivals as gods was misguidance or leading astray, it functions in the manner of the lām of cause in your saying: "I came to you so that you would honor me," by way of analogy. It is also said: the reading with fatḥa does not allow the lām to be the lām of consequence, whereas with ḍamma it allows the meaning of consequence. The cause and the command to enjoy are a command of threat and warning, in the manner of His saying: ﴿Do what you will﴾ [Fussilat: 40]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Enjoy yourselves" is an announcement that, because they are immersed in enjoying the present and know nothing else and desire nothing else, they are commanded to do so by a commander obeyed, from whom they cannot escape and whose command they cannot oppose, nor can they have any other command for themselves. This commander is the commander of desire. The meaning is: if you persist in what you are upon of obeying the command of desire, then indeed your destination is the Fire. It is also permissible that the meaning is abandonment and leaving to oneself, like His saying: ﴿Say, "Enjoy your disbelief a little; indeed you are of the companions of the Fire"﴾ [al-Zumar: 8]. End of quotation.

"Your destination" (maṣīrakum) is a verbal noun of the complete verb ṣāra, meaning "to return." The predicate of "inna" is His saying "to the Fire." Here "ṣāra" does not mean "to move," which is why it is followed by "ilā." The meaning would be "indeed your movement to the Fire," because otherwise "inna" would be left without a predicate, and one should not claim that it is omitted, so that the sense would be "indeed your destination to the Fire is certain or existing." This is because omitting the predicate in such a construction is rare, and it is most often omitted when the subject of "inna" is indefinite and the predicate is a prepositional phrase. Al-Hawfi also permitted that "ilā al-nār" be linked to "maṣīrakum," in which case the predicate is omitted.
