Then "the abode of ruin" means destruction in this world, like the well of Badr and other places where they were killed. On this view, Ibn Atiyya and Abu al-Baqa' parsed "Jahannam" as an accusative in the construction of occupation (al-ishtighāl), meaning: "they will burn Jahannam, they will burn it." The reading of Ibn Abi Ablah supports this interpretation: "Jahannamu" with the nominative, which allows that "Jahannam" is nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject. This interpretation is preferable, because the accusative under the construction of occupation is less preferred, since nothing preceding it favors it or makes it equally likely. The majority of readers read it in the accusative. They would not have read it with a less preferred or equally likely form, since "Zaydun dacatuhu" is more eloquent than "Zaydan dacatuhu." Therefore its nominative in the reading of Ibn Abi Ablah, as the predicate of an omitted subject, is preferred. On the interpretation of the construction of occupation, "yaslawnahā" has no place in the grammatical structure. On the first interpretation they allowed that it could be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "Jahannam," or from "dār al-bawār," or from "their people." The word that is praised or condemned (al-makhṣūṣ bi-l-dhamm) is omitted, its implied sense being: "and wretched is the place of settlement, it," meaning: Jahannam.

"And they set up rivals to Allah" means: they added to their disbelief the ingratitude of setting up rivals to Allah. These rivals are the idols they took as gods besides Allah.

Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read "liyuḍillū" here with a fatḥa on the yāʾ, and in al-Ḥajj, Luqman and al-Rum as "li-yuḍilla." The rest of the seven read it with a ḍamma. Apparently the lām is the lām of becoming and outcome (lām al-ṣayrūra wa-l-ma'āl). Since the result of taking rivals as gods was misguidance or leading astray, it functions in the manner of the lām of cause in your saying: "I came to you so that you would honor me," by way of analogy. It is also said: the reading with fatḥa does not allow the lām to be the lām of consequence, whereas with ḍamma it allows the meaning of consequence. The cause and the command to enjoy are a command of threat and warning, in the manner of His saying: ﴿Do what you will﴾ [Fussilat: 40]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Enjoy yourselves" is an announcement that, because they are immersed in enjoying the present and know nothing else and desire nothing else, they are commanded to do so by a commander obeyed, from whom they cannot escape and whose command they cannot oppose, nor can they have any other command for themselves. This commander is the commander of desire. The meaning is: if you persist in what you are upon of obeying the command of desire, then indeed your destination is the Fire. It is also permissible that the meaning is abandonment and leaving to oneself, like His saying: ﴿Say, "Enjoy your disbelief a little; indeed you are of the companions of the Fire"﴾ [al-Zumar: 8]. End of quotation.

"Your destination" (maṣīrakum) is a verbal noun of the complete verb ṣāra, meaning "to return." The predicate of "inna" is His saying "to the Fire." Here "ṣāra" does not mean "to move," which is why it is followed by "ilā." The meaning would be "indeed your movement to the Fire," because otherwise "inna" would be left without a predicate, and one should not claim that it is omitted, so that the sense would be "indeed your destination to the Fire is certain or existing." This is because omitting the predicate in such a construction is rare, and it is most often omitted when the subject of "inna" is indefinite and the predicate is a prepositional phrase. Al-Hawfi also permitted that "ilā al-nār" be linked to "maṣīrakum," in which case the predicate is omitted.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verses 31–36 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Tell My servants who have believed to establish prayer and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and publicly, before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship.﴾ ﴿It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth and sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you. And He has subjected for you the ships to sail through the sea by His command, and He has subjected for you the rivers.﴾ ﴿And He has subjected for you the sun and the moon, both constant [in their courses], and He has subjected for you the night and the day.﴾ ﴿And He gave you of all you asked of Him. And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it. Indeed, mankind is [generally]壮 unjust and ungrateful.﴾: When the Exalted mentioned the state of the disbelievers and their ingratitude for His favor, and their setting up rivals to Him, and [after] threatening them, He commanded the believers to adhere to obedience and to be watchful over their own souls, and to uphold the two pillars of Islam, the prayer (al-salah) and the zakat (almsgiving), before the coming of the Day of Resurrection. The object of "qul" (say) is omitted, its estimated form being: "Establish the prayer, they will establish [it]." "Yuqimu" (they establish) is jussive, in response to the imperative; this is the view of al-Akhfash and al-Mazini. It was refuted on the ground that it does not follow from "qul" that [the believers] "yuqimu," and this refutation was itself rejected, on the ground that it is the command to the believers to establish [prayer], not to the disbelievers, and the believers, whenever the Messenger commands them to do something, do it without fail.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: It is possible that "yuqimu" is the response to the imperative whose meaning is given to us by His saying "qul," by taking "qul" in this verse to mean "convey" and "deliver the Shariah": "they will establish the prayer." End of quote. This is close to what came before, except that in the earlier view the object of the saying is "aqimu" (establish), whereas in this view the Shariah is the object, on the estimate "convey the Shariah." Al-Kisa'i, al-Zajjaj and a group held that the object of "qul" is His saying "yuqimu," which is a jussive imperative with a deleted lam of command, following the line of the poet:

"Muhammad, let yourself be ransomed by every soul."

Sibawayh recited it, but said that this is permissible only in poetry. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding this view: The deletion of the lam is permitted because the imperative "qul" is a substitute for it. Had it been said, "yuqimu al-salah wa yunfiqu" as a beginning with the lam deleted, it would not have been permitted. End of quote. Al-Mubarrad held that the estimate is: "Say to them, 'Establish,' they will establish," so that "yuqimu," which is explicit, is the response to the deleted "aqimu." It was said: this is corrupt for two reasons. First: the response to a conditional differs from the condition either in the verb, or in the subject, or in both. When it is identical in both, it is an error, as in your saying, "Stand, he will stand," and the estimate on this view would be: "Establish, they will establish." Second: the estimated command is addressed in the second person, while "yuqimu" is in the third person, which is an error when the subject is one. It was also said: the estimate is "Say to them: 'Establish, they will establish,'" as Sibawayh said, as reported by Ibn ʿAtiyyah. Al-Farra' said: the response to the imperative carries an estimated condition; you say, "Obey Allah, He will admit you to Paradise," meaning: "If you obey Him, He will admit you to Paradise." The difference between this view and the one before it is that in this one the condition is estimated after the imperative verb, whereas in the previous one the imperative carries the meaning of the condition. It was also said: it is a present-tense verb in the form of a report, turned away from the form of the imperative, and the meaning is "Establish." This was said by Abu ʿAli and a group. It was refuted on the ground that if it were a present-tense verb in the form of a report with imperative meaning, it would retain its nunation (i.e., its indicative ending with the nun), as in His saying, "Shall I direct you to a trade?" [al-Saff: 10], then "You believe" [al-Saff: 11], meaning "Believe." Abu ʿAli justified this by saying that since it has the meaning of the imperative it was built, meaning on the deletion of the nun, because the intended meaning is "Establish"; this is like the declinable noun being built in the vocative in your saying "Ya Zayd," meaning on a damma, since it was likened to "qabl" and "baʿd." End of quote.

The object of the saying, whether pronounced or estimated, in all these analyses is the command to establish the prayer and to spend, except in Ibn ʿAtiyyah's view where its object is the Shariah, which is more general, since "qul" was estimated to mean "convey and deliver the Shariah." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: It appears that what is said is the verse that follows, namely His saying, "It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth." End of quote. This view, that the object of the saying is His saying, "It is Allah who..." to the end of the verse, separates the speech, contrary to the order of the construction, and makes His saying, "establish the prayer," a detached statement cut off from the saying and its object, or a response separated by it from the saying and its object. It does not follow that it is a response, because His saying, "It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth," does not call for establishing the prayer and spending except by a very distant estimate.

The word "al-salah" may be taken in a general sense, meaning every obligatory and voluntary prayer, or it may be taken to mean the five prayers, and Ibn ʿAbbas explained it thus. He explained "al-infaq" (spending) as the zakat of wealth. The grammatical analysis of "sirran wa ʿalaniyah" (secretly and publicly) was discussed earlier, and explained at the end of al-Baqarah.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: "al-bay'" here means "al-badhl" (giving in exchange for something), and "al-khilal" means "al-mukhallah" (friendship), which is a verbal noun from "khalaltu khilalan wa mukhallatan," and it means companionship. End of quote. By "al-badhl" he means exchange for something. Imru' al-Qays said:

"I turned my desire away from them out of fear of destruction, and I am not one who dislikes friendship, nor one who says [it is useless]."

The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 14, verses 31–36 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Akhfash said: *al-khilal* is the plural of *khallah*. The disagreement over the reading of ﴿there is no trade in it, nor friendship﴾ with a *fatha* or with a *raf'* (*la bay'un fihi wa la khilalun*) has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah. The "day" here is the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask) how does the command to spend match the description of the day as one "in which there is no trade and no friendship"? (I answer): It is because people give away their wealth in contracts of exchange, handing over something in return in order to receive its equivalent. They also give gifts in acts of generosity and in exchanging gifts between friends, so that they may receive in return their like or something better. But spending purely for the sake of God, as in His saying: ﴿And no one has a favour from him to be repaid﴾ [al-Layl: 19], ﴿except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Layl: 20], is not done except by sincere believers. So they send ahead (their spending) so that they may take its reward on a day in which there is no trade and no friendship, meaning: no benefit is gained there through buying and selling, nor through friendship, nor through what they spent of their wealth in exchanges and generous acts. Rather, benefit there is gained only through spending for the sake of God. End of quote.

When God, the Exalted, had extended His discourse describing the conditions of the happy and the wretched, and since happiness is attained through knowledge of God and His attributes, while wretchedness comes through ignorance, He concluded this description with the proofs that indicate the existence of the Creator and the perfection of His knowledge and power. So He said: ﴿God is the One who created the heavens and the earth﴾, and He mentioned ten kinds of proofs. He first mentioned His originating and bringing into being the heavens and the earth, then followed it with the remaining proofs, presenting them in independent clauses, so as to show and alert that each clause is independent in its indication. He did not make their complements into coordinated items joined to a single noun (in the manner of *'atf al-mufrad 'ala al-mufrad*). ﴿Allah﴾ is in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), and ﴿alladhi﴾ (who) is its predicate (*khabar*).

Ibn Atiyya said: Whoever is informed of this sentence and it is firmly established in his soul, he believes, prays and spends. End of quote. This refers to what was mentioned earlier, that the object of "Say" (*qul*) is His saying: ﴿God is the One who created the heavens and the earth﴾, and so on. It is as if He is saying: "They should establish the prayer," as an answer to His saying: "Say to My servants: God is the One who created the heavens and the earth."

The apparent meaning is that the object of *akhraja* (He brought forth) is ﴿provision for you﴾, and *min* (from) is partitive (*li-l-tab'id*). Since it precedes the indefinite noun, it stands in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and the meaning is: "Provision is some of the fruits of the trees, and what is not provision also comes out of them, such as that which is purely harmful." It is also permissible for *min* to be explanatory (*li-bayan al-jins*, specifying the kind); this was stated by Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari, as if He had said: "He brought forth by it provision for you, which is the fruits." But this is not good, because *min* which is explanatory of the kind comes only after a vague term that it specifies.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: It is permissible that ﴿of the fruits﴾ be the object of *akhraja*, and *rizqan* (provision) be a circumstantial clause from the object, or be in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*) from *akhraja*, because it carries the meaning of *rizq*. It has been said that *min* is superfluous (*za'idah*), but this is not permissible according to the majority of the Basran grammarians (the grammarians of the school of Basra), because what precedes it must be a complete clause and what follows it a definite noun. It is permissible according to al-Akhfash.

*Al-fulk* here is a plural of *fulk* (ship), and for this reason He said: (p-428) ﴿so that it may run﴾. The meaning of ﴿by His command﴾ refers back to the command subsisting in His essence. Al-Zamakhshari said: (It refers to) His saying "Be," and the subjugation of the ships includes the subjugation of the seas and the subjugation of the winds. As for the subjugation of the rivers, it is through their flowing and through their being channelled for benefit.

﴿Constant﴾ (*da'ibayn*) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause. The meaning is: they both continue steadily in their course and in their giving light, and in their setting right what they set right of the earth, of bodies, and of plants. From Muqatil ibn Hibban, who traced it back to Ibn Abbas, that he said: its meaning is "constant in obedience to God." Ibn Atiyya said: This is a statement which, if what is meant is that obedience is submission on their part in being subjected, then this exists in His saying: ﴿subjected﴾; and if what is meant is that it is an intended obedience like the worship of humans, then this is good. And God knows best. End of quote.

The subjugation of the night and the day means that they follow each other, one after the other, for sleep and for livelihood. The speculative theologians (*al-mutakallimun*) said: the subjugation of the night and the day is figurative, because they are accidents (*a'rad*), and accidents cannot be subjected.

When God mentioned those great blessings, He mentioned that He did not limit Himself to them, and said: ﴿And He gave you of all that you asked of Him﴾. The address is to the human species in general; that is, a human has been given of everything that it is in his nature to ask for and to benefit from. This does not apply to each and every individual person, but these blessings are distributed among humans, so it is said: according to this whole, you were given such-and-such, by way of affirming the blessing.

Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Muhammad ibn Ali, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, Amr ibn Qa'id, Qatada, Salam, Ya'qub, and Nafi' in one narration read ﴿of all﴾ with tanwin (*min kullin*), meaning: of all these created things that have been mentioned. *Ma* (what) is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*) functioning as the second object; that is, "what it is in his nature to ask for," meaning to seek benefit from it. It has been said that *ma* is negative, and the second object is ﴿of all﴾, like His saying: ﴿and she was given of everything﴾ [al-Naml: 23], meaning: "not those who asked Him." He informed them of the abundance of His blessing upon them with blessings they did not ask for, and He did not mention what they did ask for. The negated clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. Al-Zamakhshari began with this opinion, and Ibn Atiyya repeated it, saying: it is the explanation of al-Dahhak.

This interpretation shows that it contradicts the reading of the majority, ﴿of all that you asked of Him﴾ with the genitive construction (*idafah*), because in that reading, according to this analysis, *ma* is negative, and so they did not ask Him. But in this reading they did ask Him, and *ma* means "that which" (*alladhi*). It has been permitted that it be a verbal (infinitival) relative (*masdariyyah*), and the verbal noun would then carry the meaning of the object.

When al-Zamakhshari sensed the apparent contradiction between this reading and that one, on the supposition that *ma* is negative, he said: It is permissible that *ma* be a relative pronoun, with ﴿And He gave you of all﴾ meaning: that which you needed, and your conditions and livelihoods could not be set right except by it, so it is as if you asked for it, or requested it with the tongue of circumstance. Thus he interpreted "you asked for it" as "what you needed."

The pronoun in ﴿you asked Him﴾: if *ma* is verbal, it refers back to God, the Exalted, and the verbal noun is used to mean the thing asked for. If *ma* is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," the pronoun refers back to it, and the implied sense is: "of all that which you asked Him for." It is not permissible for it to refer back to God. The connecting pronoun linking the relative clause to the relative pronoun is omitted, because if you consider it attached, the sense would be "*ma sa'altumuhu*" (you asked it), which is not permissible; or if you consider it detached, the sense would be "*ma sa'altumuhu iyyahu*" (you asked it of Him), and a detached pronoun may not be omitted.

Here, the word ﴿blessing﴾ (*ni'mah*): al-Wahidi said: It is a noun placed in the position of a verbal noun. One says *an'ama in'aman* and *ni'mah* (he bestowed a blessing), and the noun is placed in the position of the act of bestowing, just as one says *anfaqtu infaqan* and *nafaqah* (I spent). For this reason it is not made plural, because it carries the meaning of a verbal noun. End of quote.

What appears clear is that *ni'mah* refers to the thing bestowed, and that it is a collective noun (*ism jins*), not meant as a single item but as a plural, as if it were said: ﴿And if you count the blessing of God﴾. The meaning of ﴿you cannot count it﴾ is: you cannot enumerate it, nor are you able to count it. This applies when they wish to count it in summary. As for detailed enumeration, no one is capable of it, and none knows it except God.

Abu al-Darda' said: Whoever does not see the blessing of God upon him except in his food and drink, his knowledge is slight, and his punishment is near.

What is meant by "the human" here is the species; that is, these qualities are found in him, namely: wrongdoing and disbelief. He wrongs the blessing by neglecting to give thanks for it, and he disbelieves in it by denying it. It has been said: He is a wrongdoer in hardship, so he complains and despairs; a disbeliever in blessing, so he hoards and withholds.

In Surat al-Nahl: ﴿And if you count the blessing of God, you cannot enumerate it. Indeed God is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 18]. The difference between the two endings is this: here, His saying preceded: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the blessing of God for disbelief﴾ [Ibrahim: 28], and after it: ﴿and they set up rivals to God﴾ [Ibrahim: 30]. So this was an explicit reference to their evil deeds of ingratitude for the blessing and of wrongdoing, which is polytheism through the setting up of rivals. It was fitting to conclude by condemning the one who committed that, so He said: ﴿Indeed, the human is greatly wrongdoing and greatly disbelieving﴾.

As for in al-Nahl: when He mentioned a number of acts of grace and extended His description of them, and said: ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17], meaning: the One who brought into being these blessings mentioned earlier is not like one who has no power to create or to produce anything of them, He mentioned, among His acts of grace, that He is described by forgiveness and mercy, as an encouragement to return to Him. And these two attributes are His, just as the attribute of creating is His. In this there is encouragement for whoever believes in Him. It also moves from the worship of the created to the worship of the Creator, who forgives His servant's past lapse and shows him mercy. Furthermore, since He mentioned that God, the Exalted, is the One who bestows blessings upon the human, He mentioned what proceeds from the Benefactor and from the kind of the one benefited. From the Benefactor came what is suitable to the state of giving, namely forgiveness and mercy, since without these two He would not have bestowed blessings. And from the kind of the one benefited came what is suitable to the state of being blessed, namely wrongdoing and ingratitude. So it is as if it were said: if wrongdoing proceeds from the human, then God is Most Forgiving; or if ingratitude for a blessing proceeds from him, then God is Most Merciful, because He knows the human's weakness and deficiency.

The claim that this verse is abrogated (*mansukhah*) by the verse of al-Nahl is not to be given attention. al-Sakhawi reported this from Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verses 31–36 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Tell My servants who have believed to establish prayer and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and publicly, before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship.﴾ ﴿It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth and sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you. And He has subjected for you the ships to sail through the sea by His command, and He has subjected for you the rivers.﴾ ﴿And He has subjected for you the sun and the moon, both constant [in their courses], and He has subjected for you the night and the day.﴾ ﴿And He gave you of all you asked of Him. And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it. Indeed, mankind is [generally]壮 unjust and ungrateful.﴾: When the Exalted mentioned the state of the disbelievers and their ingratitude for His favor, and their setting up rivals to Him, and [after] threatening them, He commanded the believers to adhere to obedience and to be watchful over their own souls, and to uphold the two pillars of Islam, the prayer (al-salah) and the zakat (almsgiving), before the coming of the Day of Resurrection. The object of "qul" (say) is omitted, its estimated form being: "Establish the prayer, they will establish [it]." "Yuqimu" (they establish) is jussive, in response to the imperative; this is the view of al-Akhfash and al-Mazini. It was refuted on the ground that it does not follow from "qul" that [the believers] "yuqimu," and this refutation was itself rejected, on the ground that it is the command to the believers to establish [prayer], not to the disbelievers, and the believers, whenever the Messenger commands them to do something, do it without fail.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: It is possible that "yuqimu" is the response to the imperative whose meaning is given to us by His saying "qul," by taking "qul" in this verse to mean "convey" and "deliver the Shariah": "they will establish the prayer." End of quote. This is close to what came before, except that in the earlier view the object of the saying is "aqimu" (establish), whereas in this view the Shariah is the object, on the estimate "convey the Shariah." Al-Kisa'i, al-Zajjaj and a group held that the object of "qul" is His saying "yuqimu," which is a jussive imperative with a deleted lam of command, following the line of the poet:

"Muhammad, let yourself be ransomed by every soul."

Sibawayh recited it, but said that this is permissible only in poetry. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding this view: The deletion of the lam is permitted because the imperative "qul" is a substitute for it. Had it been said, "yuqimu al-salah wa yunfiqu" as a beginning with the lam deleted, it would not have been permitted. End of quote. Al-Mubarrad held that the estimate is: "Say to them, 'Establish,' they will establish," so that "yuqimu," which is explicit, is the response to the deleted "aqimu." It was said: this is corrupt for two reasons. First: the response to a conditional differs from the condition either in the verb, or in the subject, or in both. When it is identical in both, it is an error, as in your saying, "Stand, he will stand," and the estimate on this view would be: "Establish, they will establish." Second: the estimated command is addressed in the second person, while "yuqimu" is in the third person, which is an error when the subject is one. It was also said: the estimate is "Say to them: 'Establish, they will establish,'" as Sibawayh said, as reported by Ibn ʿAtiyyah. Al-Farra' said: the response to the imperative carries an estimated condition; you say, "Obey Allah, He will admit you to Paradise," meaning: "If you obey Him, He will admit you to Paradise." The difference between this view and the one before it is that in this one the condition is estimated after the imperative verb, whereas in the previous one the imperative carries the meaning of the condition. It was also said: it is a present-tense verb in the form of a report, turned away from the form of the imperative, and the meaning is "Establish." This was said by Abu ʿAli and a group. It was refuted on the ground that if it were a present-tense verb in the form of a report with imperative meaning, it would retain its nunation (i.e., its indicative ending with the nun), as in His saying, "Shall I direct you to a trade?" [al-Saff: 10], then "You believe" [al-Saff: 11], meaning "Believe." Abu ʿAli justified this by saying that since it has the meaning of the imperative it was built, meaning on the deletion of the nun, because the intended meaning is "Establish"; this is like the declinable noun being built in the vocative in your saying "Ya Zayd," meaning on a damma, since it was likened to "qabl" and "baʿd." End of quote.

The object of the saying, whether pronounced or estimated, in all these analyses is the command to establish the prayer and to spend, except in Ibn ʿAtiyyah's view where its object is the Shariah, which is more general, since "qul" was estimated to mean "convey and deliver the Shariah." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: It appears that what is said is the verse that follows, namely His saying, "It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth." End of quote. This view, that the object of the saying is His saying, "It is Allah who..." to the end of the verse, separates the speech, contrary to the order of the construction, and makes His saying, "establish the prayer," a detached statement cut off from the saying and its object, or a response separated by it from the saying and its object. It does not follow that it is a response, because His saying, "It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth," does not call for establishing the prayer and spending except by a very distant estimate.

The word "al-salah" may be taken in a general sense, meaning every obligatory and voluntary prayer, or it may be taken to mean the five prayers, and Ibn ʿAbbas explained it thus. He explained "al-infaq" (spending) as the zakat of wealth. The grammatical analysis of "sirran wa ʿalaniyah" (secretly and publicly) was discussed earlier, and explained at the end of al-Baqarah.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: "al-bay'" here means "al-badhl" (giving in exchange for something), and "al-khilal" means "al-mukhallah" (friendship), which is a verbal noun from "khalaltu khilalan wa mukhallatan," and it means companionship. End of quote. By "al-badhl" he means exchange for something. Imru' al-Qays said:

"I turned my desire away from them out of fear of destruction, and I am not one who dislikes friendship, nor one who says [it is useless]."

The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 14, verses 31–36 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Akhfash said: *al-khilal* is the plural of *khallah*. The disagreement over the reading of ﴿there is no trade in it, nor friendship﴾ with a *fatha* or with a *raf'* (*la bay'un fihi wa la khilalun*) has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah. The "day" here is the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask) how does the command to spend match the description of the day as one "in which there is no trade and no friendship"? (I answer): It is because people give away their wealth in contracts of exchange, handing over something in return in order to receive its equivalent. They also give gifts in acts of generosity and in exchanging gifts between friends, so that they may receive in return their like or something better. But spending purely for the sake of God, as in His saying: ﴿And no one has a favour from him to be repaid﴾ [al-Layl: 19], ﴿except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Layl: 20], is not done except by sincere believers. So they send ahead (their spending) so that they may take its reward on a day in which there is no trade and no friendship, meaning: no benefit is gained there through buying and selling, nor through friendship, nor through what they spent of their wealth in exchanges and generous acts. Rather, benefit there is gained only through spending for the sake of God. End of quote.

When God, the Exalted, had extended His discourse describing the conditions of the happy and the wretched, and since happiness is attained through knowledge of God and His attributes, while wretchedness comes through ignorance, He concluded this description with the proofs that indicate the existence of the Creator and the perfection of His knowledge and power. So He said: ﴿God is the One who created the heavens and the earth﴾, and He mentioned ten kinds of proofs. He first mentioned His originating and bringing into being the heavens and the earth, then followed it with the remaining proofs, presenting them in independent clauses, so as to show and alert that each clause is independent in its indication. He did not make their complements into coordinated items joined to a single noun (in the manner of *'atf al-mufrad 'ala al-mufrad*). ﴿Allah﴾ is in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), and ﴿alladhi﴾ (who) is its predicate (*khabar*).

Ibn Atiyya said: Whoever is informed of this sentence and it is firmly established in his soul, he believes, prays and spends. End of quote. This refers to what was mentioned earlier, that the object of "Say" (*qul*) is His saying: ﴿God is the One who created the heavens and the earth﴾, and so on. It is as if He is saying: "They should establish the prayer," as an answer to His saying: "Say to My servants: God is the One who created the heavens and the earth."

The apparent meaning is that the object of *akhraja* (He brought forth) is ﴿provision for you﴾, and *min* (from) is partitive (*li-l-tab'id*). Since it precedes the indefinite noun, it stands in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and the meaning is: "Provision is some of the fruits of the trees, and what is not provision also comes out of them, such as that which is purely harmful." It is also permissible for *min* to be explanatory (*li-bayan al-jins*, specifying the kind); this was stated by Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari, as if He had said: "He brought forth by it provision for you, which is the fruits." But this is not good, because *min* which is explanatory of the kind comes only after a vague term that it specifies.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: It is permissible that ﴿of the fruits﴾ be the object of *akhraja*, and *rizqan* (provision) be a circumstantial clause from the object, or be in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*) from *akhraja*, because it carries the meaning of *rizq*. It has been said that *min* is superfluous (*za'idah*), but this is not permissible according to the majority of the Basran grammarians (the grammarians of the school of Basra), because what precedes it must be a complete clause and what follows it a definite noun. It is permissible according to al-Akhfash.

*Al-fulk* here is a plural of *fulk* (ship), and for this reason He said: (p-428) ﴿so that it may run﴾. The meaning of ﴿by His command﴾ refers back to the command subsisting in His essence. Al-Zamakhshari said: (It refers to) His saying "Be," and the subjugation of the ships includes the subjugation of the seas and the subjugation of the winds. As for the subjugation of the rivers, it is through their flowing and through their being channelled for benefit.

﴿Constant﴾ (*da'ibayn*) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause. The meaning is: they both continue steadily in their course and in their giving light, and in their setting right what they set right of the earth, of bodies, and of plants. From Muqatil ibn Hibban, who traced it back to Ibn Abbas, that he said: its meaning is "constant in obedience to God." Ibn Atiyya said: This is a statement which, if what is meant is that obedience is submission on their part in being subjected, then this exists in His saying: ﴿subjected﴾; and if what is meant is that it is an intended obedience like the worship of humans, then this is good. And God knows best. End of quote.

The subjugation of the night and the day means that they follow each other, one after the other, for sleep and for livelihood. The speculative theologians (*al-mutakallimun*) said: the subjugation of the night and the day is figurative, because they are accidents (*a'rad*), and accidents cannot be subjected.

When God mentioned those great blessings, He mentioned that He did not limit Himself to them, and said: ﴿And He gave you of all that you asked of Him﴾. The address is to the human species in general; that is, a human has been given of everything that it is in his nature to ask for and to benefit from. This does not apply to each and every individual person, but these blessings are distributed among humans, so it is said: according to this whole, you were given such-and-such, by way of affirming the blessing.

Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Muhammad ibn Ali, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, Amr ibn Qa'id, Qatada, Salam, Ya'qub, and Nafi' in one narration read ﴿of all﴾ with tanwin (*min kullin*), meaning: of all these created things that have been mentioned. *Ma* (what) is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*) functioning as the second object; that is, "what it is in his nature to ask for," meaning to seek benefit from it. It has been said that *ma* is negative, and the second object is ﴿of all﴾, like His saying: ﴿and she was given of everything﴾ [al-Naml: 23], meaning: "not those who asked Him." He informed them of the abundance of His blessing upon them with blessings they did not ask for, and He did not mention what they did ask for. The negated clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. Al-Zamakhshari began with this opinion, and Ibn Atiyya repeated it, saying: it is the explanation of al-Dahhak.

This interpretation shows that it contradicts the reading of the majority, ﴿of all that you asked of Him﴾ with the genitive construction (*idafah*), because in that reading, according to this analysis, *ma* is negative, and so they did not ask Him. But in this reading they did ask Him, and *ma* means "that which" (*alladhi*). It has been permitted that it be a verbal (infinitival) relative (*masdariyyah*), and the verbal noun would then carry the meaning of the object.

When al-Zamakhshari sensed the apparent contradiction between this reading and that one, on the supposition that *ma* is negative, he said: It is permissible that *ma* be a relative pronoun, with ﴿And He gave you of all﴾ meaning: that which you needed, and your conditions and livelihoods could not be set right except by it, so it is as if you asked for it, or requested it with the tongue of circumstance. Thus he interpreted "you asked for it" as "what you needed."

The pronoun in ﴿you asked Him﴾: if *ma* is verbal, it refers back to God, the Exalted, and the verbal noun is used to mean the thing asked for. If *ma* is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," the pronoun refers back to it, and the implied sense is: "of all that which you asked Him for." It is not permissible for it to refer back to God. The connecting pronoun linking the relative clause to the relative pronoun is omitted, because if you consider it attached, the sense would be "*ma sa'altumuhu*" (you asked it), which is not permissible; or if you consider it detached, the sense would be "*ma sa'altumuhu iyyahu*" (you asked it of Him), and a detached pronoun may not be omitted.

Here, the word ﴿blessing﴾ (*ni'mah*): al-Wahidi said: It is a noun placed in the position of a verbal noun. One says *an'ama in'aman* and *ni'mah* (he bestowed a blessing), and the noun is placed in the position of the act of bestowing, just as one says *anfaqtu infaqan* and *nafaqah* (I spent). For this reason it is not made plural, because it carries the meaning of a verbal noun. End of quote.

What appears clear is that *ni'mah* refers to the thing bestowed, and that it is a collective noun (*ism jins*), not meant as a single item but as a plural, as if it were said: ﴿And if you count the blessing of God﴾. The meaning of ﴿you cannot count it﴾ is: you cannot enumerate it, nor are you able to count it. This applies when they wish to count it in summary. As for detailed enumeration, no one is capable of it, and none knows it except God.

Abu al-Darda' said: Whoever does not see the blessing of God upon him except in his food and drink, his knowledge is slight, and his punishment is near.

What is meant by "the human" here is the species; that is, these qualities are found in him, namely: wrongdoing and disbelief. He wrongs the blessing by neglecting to give thanks for it, and he disbelieves in it by denying it. It has been said: He is a wrongdoer in hardship, so he complains and despairs; a disbeliever in blessing, so he hoards and withholds.

In Surat al-Nahl: ﴿And if you count the blessing of God, you cannot enumerate it. Indeed God is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 18]. The difference between the two endings is this: here, His saying preceded: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the blessing of God for disbelief﴾ [Ibrahim: 28], and after it: ﴿and they set up rivals to God﴾ [Ibrahim: 30]. So this was an explicit reference to their evil deeds of ingratitude for the blessing and of wrongdoing, which is polytheism through the setting up of rivals. It was fitting to conclude by condemning the one who committed that, so He said: ﴿Indeed, the human is greatly wrongdoing and greatly disbelieving﴾.

As for in al-Nahl: when He mentioned a number of acts of grace and extended His description of them, and said: ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17], meaning: the One who brought into being these blessings mentioned earlier is not like one who has no power to create or to produce anything of them, He mentioned, among His acts of grace, that He is described by forgiveness and mercy, as an encouragement to return to Him. And these two attributes are His, just as the attribute of creating is His. In this there is encouragement for whoever believes in Him. It also moves from the worship of the created to the worship of the Creator, who forgives His servant's past lapse and shows him mercy. Furthermore, since He mentioned that God, the Exalted, is the One who bestows blessings upon the human, He mentioned what proceeds from the Benefactor and from the kind of the one benefited. From the Benefactor came what is suitable to the state of giving, namely forgiveness and mercy, since without these two He would not have bestowed blessings. And from the kind of the one benefited came what is suitable to the state of being blessed, namely wrongdoing and ingratitude. So it is as if it were said: if wrongdoing proceeds from the human, then God is Most Forgiving; or if ingratitude for a blessing proceeds from him, then God is Most Merciful, because He knows the human's weakness and deficiency.

The claim that this verse is abrogated (*mansukhah*) by the verse of al-Nahl is not to be given attention. al-Sakhawi reported this from Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verses 31–36 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Tell My servants who have believed to establish prayer and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and publicly, before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship.﴾ ﴿It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth and sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you. And He has subjected for you the ships to sail through the sea by His command, and He has subjected for you the rivers.﴾ ﴿And He has subjected for you the sun and the moon, both constant [in their courses], and He has subjected for you the night and the day.﴾ ﴿And He gave you of all you asked of Him. And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it. Indeed, mankind is [generally]壮 unjust and ungrateful.﴾: When the Exalted mentioned the state of the disbelievers and their ingratitude for His favor, and their setting up rivals to Him, and [after] threatening them, He commanded the believers to adhere to obedience and to be watchful over their own souls, and to uphold the two pillars of Islam, the prayer (al-salah) and the zakat (almsgiving), before the coming of the Day of Resurrection. The object of "qul" (say) is omitted, its estimated form being: "Establish the prayer, they will establish [it]." "Yuqimu" (they establish) is jussive, in response to the imperative; this is the view of al-Akhfash and al-Mazini. It was refuted on the ground that it does not follow from "qul" that [the believers] "yuqimu," and this refutation was itself rejected, on the ground that it is the command to the believers to establish [prayer], not to the disbelievers, and the believers, whenever the Messenger commands them to do something, do it without fail.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: It is possible that "yuqimu" is the response to the imperative whose meaning is given to us by His saying "qul," by taking "qul" in this verse to mean "convey" and "deliver the Shariah": "they will establish the prayer." End of quote. This is close to what came before, except that in the earlier view the object of the saying is "aqimu" (establish), whereas in this view the Shariah is the object, on the estimate "convey the Shariah." Al-Kisa'i, al-Zajjaj and a group held that the object of "qul" is His saying "yuqimu," which is a jussive imperative with a deleted lam of command, following the line of the poet:

"Muhammad, let yourself be ransomed by every soul."

Sibawayh recited it, but said that this is permissible only in poetry. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding this view: The deletion of the lam is permitted because the imperative "qul" is a substitute for it. Had it been said, "yuqimu al-salah wa yunfiqu" as a beginning with the lam deleted, it would not have been permitted. End of quote. Al-Mubarrad held that the estimate is: "Say to them, 'Establish,' they will establish," so that "yuqimu," which is explicit, is the response to the deleted "aqimu." It was said: this is corrupt for two reasons. First: the response to a conditional differs from the condition either in the verb, or in the subject, or in both. When it is identical in both, it is an error, as in your saying, "Stand, he will stand," and the estimate on this view would be: "Establish, they will establish." Second: the estimated command is addressed in the second person, while "yuqimu" is in the third person, which is an error when the subject is one. It was also said: the estimate is "Say to them: 'Establish, they will establish,'" as Sibawayh said, as reported by Ibn ʿAtiyyah. Al-Farra' said: the response to the imperative carries an estimated condition; you say, "Obey Allah, He will admit you to Paradise," meaning: "If you obey Him, He will admit you to Paradise." The difference between this view and the one before it is that in this one the condition is estimated after the imperative verb, whereas in the previous one the imperative carries the meaning of the condition. It was also said: it is a present-tense verb in the form of a report, turned away from the form of the imperative, and the meaning is "Establish." This was said by Abu ʿAli and a group. It was refuted on the ground that if it were a present-tense verb in the form of a report with imperative meaning, it would retain its nunation (i.e., its indicative ending with the nun), as in His saying, "Shall I direct you to a trade?" [al-Saff: 10], then "You believe" [al-Saff: 11], meaning "Believe." Abu ʿAli justified this by saying that since it has the meaning of the imperative it was built, meaning on the deletion of the nun, because the intended meaning is "Establish"; this is like the declinable noun being built in the vocative in your saying "Ya Zayd," meaning on a damma, since it was likened to "qabl" and "baʿd." End of quote.

The object of the saying, whether pronounced or estimated, in all these analyses is the command to establish the prayer and to spend, except in Ibn ʿAtiyyah's view where its object is the Shariah, which is more general, since "qul" was estimated to mean "convey and deliver the Shariah." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: It appears that what is said is the verse that follows, namely His saying, "It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth." End of quote. This view, that the object of the saying is His saying, "It is Allah who..." to the end of the verse, separates the speech, contrary to the order of the construction, and makes His saying, "establish the prayer," a detached statement cut off from the saying and its object, or a response separated by it from the saying and its object. It does not follow that it is a response, because His saying, "It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth," does not call for establishing the prayer and spending except by a very distant estimate.

The word "al-salah" may be taken in a general sense, meaning every obligatory and voluntary prayer, or it may be taken to mean the five prayers, and Ibn ʿAbbas explained it thus. He explained "al-infaq" (spending) as the zakat of wealth. The grammatical analysis of "sirran wa ʿalaniyah" (secretly and publicly) was discussed earlier, and explained at the end of al-Baqarah.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: "al-bay'" here means "al-badhl" (giving in exchange for something), and "al-khilal" means "al-mukhallah" (friendship), which is a verbal noun from "khalaltu khilalan wa mukhallatan," and it means companionship. End of quote. By "al-badhl" he means exchange for something. Imru' al-Qays said:

"I turned my desire away from them out of fear of destruction, and I am not one who dislikes friendship, nor one who says [it is useless]."

When God mentioned those great blessings, He mentioned that He did not limit Himself to them, and said: ﴿And He gave you of all that you asked of Him﴾. Here, the word ﴿blessing﴾ (*ni'mah*): al-Wahidi said: It is a noun placed in the position of a verbal noun. And these two attributes are His, just as the attribute of creating is His. In this there is encouragement for whoever believes in Him. It also moves from the worship of the created to the worship of the Creator, who forgives His servant's past lapse and shows him mercy. Furthermore, since He mentioned that God, the Exalted, is the One who bestows blessings upon the human, He mentioned what proceeds from the Benefactor and from the kind of the one benefited. From the Benefactor came what is suitable to the state of giving, namely forgiveness and mercy, since without these two He would not have bestowed blessings. And from the kind of the one benefited came what is suitable to the state of being blessed, namely wrongdoing and ingratitude. So it is as if it were said: if wrongdoing proceeds from the human, then God is Most Forgiving; or if ingratitude for a blessing proceeds from him, then God is Most Merciful, because He knows the human's weakness and deficiency.

The claim that this verse is abrogated (*mansukhah*) by the verse of al-Nahl is not to be given attention. al-Sakhawi reported this from Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verses 31–36 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Tell My servants who have believed to establish prayer and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and publicly, before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship.﴾ ﴿It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth and sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you. And He has subjected for you the ships to sail through the sea by His command, and He has subjected for you the rivers.﴾ ﴿And He has subjected for you the sun and the moon, both constant [in their courses], and He has subjected for you the night and the day.﴾ ﴿And He gave you of all you asked of Him. And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it. Indeed, mankind is [generally]壮 unjust and ungrateful.﴾: When the Exalted mentioned the state of the disbelievers and their ingratitude for His favor, and their setting up rivals to Him, and [after] threatening them, He commanded the believers to adhere to obedience and to be watchful over their own souls, and to uphold the two pillars of Islam, the prayer (al-salah) and the zakat (almsgiving), before the coming of the Day of Resurrection. The object of "qul" (say) is omitted, its estimated form being: "Establish the prayer, they will establish [it]." "Yuqimu" (they establish) is jussive, in response to the imperative; this is the view of al-Akhfash and al-Mazini. It was refuted on the ground that it does not follow from "qul" that [the believers] "yuqimu," and this refutation was itself rejected, on the ground that it is the command to the believers to establish [prayer], not to the disbelievers, and the believers, whenever the Messenger commands them to do something, do it without fail.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: It is possible that "yuqimu" is the response to the imperative whose meaning is given to us by His saying "qul," by taking "qul" in this verse to mean "convey" and "deliver the Shariah": "they will establish the prayer." End of quote. This is close to what came before, except that in the earlier view the object of the saying is "aqimu" (establish), whereas in this view the Shariah is the object, on the estimate "convey the Shariah." Al-Kisa'i, al-Zajjaj and a group held that the object of "qul" is His saying "yuqimu," which is a jussive imperative with a deleted lam of command, following the line of the poet:

"Muhammad, let yourself be ransomed by every soul."

Sibawayh recited it, but said that this is permissible only in poetry. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding this view: The deletion of the lam is permitted because the imperative "qul" is a substitute for it. Had it been said, "yuqimu al-salah wa yunfiqu" as a beginning with the lam deleted, it would not have been permitted. End of quote. Al-Mubarrad held that the estimate is: "Say to them, 'Establish,' they will establish," so that "yuqimu," which is explicit, is the response to the deleted "aqimu." It was said: this is corrupt for two reasons. First: the response to a conditional differs from the condition either in the verb, or in the subject, or in both. When it is identical in both, it is an error, as in your saying, "Stand, he will stand," and the estimate on this view would be: "Establish, they will establish." Second: the estimated command is addressed in the second person, while "yuqimu" is in the third person, which is an error when the subject is one. It was also said: the estimate is "Say to them: 'Establish, they will establish,'" as Sibawayh said, as reported by Ibn ʿAtiyyah. Al-Farra' said: the response to the imperative carries an estimated condition; you say, "Obey Allah, He will admit you to Paradise," meaning: "If you obey Him, He will admit you to Paradise." The difference between this view and the one before it is that in this one the condition is estimated after the imperative verb, whereas in the previous one the imperative carries the meaning of the condition. It was also said: it is a present-tense verb in the form of a report, turned away from the form of the imperative, and the meaning is "Establish." This was said by Abu ʿAli and a group. It was refuted on the ground that if it were a present-tense verb in the form of a report with imperative meaning, it would retain its nunation (i.e., its indicative ending with the nun), as in His saying, "Shall I direct you to a trade?" [al-Saff: 10], then "You believe" [al-Saff: 11], meaning "Believe." Abu ʿAli justified this by saying that since it has the meaning of the imperative it was built, meaning on the deletion of the nun, because the intended meaning is "Establish"; this is like the declinable noun being built in the vocative in your saying "Ya Zayd," meaning on a damma, since it was likened to "qabl" and "baʿd." End of quote.

The object of the saying, whether pronounced or estimated, in all these analyses is the command to establish the prayer and to spend, except in Ibn ʿAtiyyah's view where its object is the Shariah, which is more general, since "qul" was estimated to mean "convey and deliver the Shariah." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: It appears that what is said is the verse that follows, namely His saying, "It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth." End of quote. This view, that the object of the saying is His saying, "It is Allah who..." to the end of the verse, separates the speech, contrary to the order of the construction, and makes His saying, "establish the prayer," a detached statement cut off from the saying and its object, or a response separated by it from the saying and its object. It does not follow that it is a response, because His saying, "It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth," does not call for establishing the prayer and spending except by a very distant estimate.

The word "al-salah" may be taken in a general sense, meaning every obligatory and voluntary prayer, or it may be taken to mean the five prayers, and Ibn ʿAbbas explained it thus. He explained "al-infaq" (spending) as the zakat of wealth. The grammatical analysis of "sirran wa ʿalaniyah" (secretly and publicly) was discussed earlier, and explained at the end of al-Baqarah.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: "al-bay'" here means "al-badhl" (giving in exchange for something), and "al-khilal" means "al-mukhallah" (friendship), which is a verbal noun from "khalaltu khilalan wa mukhallatan," and it means companionship. End of quote. By "al-badhl" he means exchange for something. Imru' al-Qays said:

"I turned my desire away from them out of fear of destruction, and I am not one who dislikes friendship, nor one who says [it is useless]."

The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 14, verses 31–36 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Akhfash said: *al-khilal* is the plural of *khallah*. The disagreement over the reading of ﴿there is no trade in it, nor friendship﴾ with a *fatha* or with a *raf'* (*la bay'un fihi wa la khilalun*) has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah. The "day" here is the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask) how does the command to spend match the description of the day as one "in which there is no trade and no friendship"? (I answer): It is because people give away their wealth in contracts of exchange, handing over something in return in order to receive its equivalent. They also give gifts in acts of generosity and in exchanging gifts between friends, so that they may receive in return their like or something better. But spending purely for the sake of God, as in His saying: ﴿And no one has a favour from him to be repaid﴾ [al-Layl: 19], ﴿except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Layl: 20], is not done except by sincere believers. So they send ahead (their spending) so that they may take its reward on a day in which there is no trade and no friendship, meaning: no benefit is gained there through buying and selling, nor through friendship, nor through what they spent of their wealth in exchanges and generous acts. Rather, benefit there is gained only through spending for the sake of God. End of quote.

When God, the Exalted, had extended His discourse describing the conditions of the happy and the wretched, and since happiness is attained through knowledge of God and His attributes, while wretchedness comes through ignorance, He concluded this description with the proofs that indicate the existence of the Creator and the perfection of His knowledge and power. So He said: ﴿God is the One who created the heavens and the earth﴾, and He mentioned ten kinds of proofs. He first mentioned His originating and bringing into being the heavens and the earth, then followed it with the remaining proofs, presenting them in independent clauses, so as to show and alert that each clause is independent in its indication. He did not make their complements into coordinated items joined to a single noun (in the manner of *'atf al-mufrad 'ala al-mufrad*). ﴿Allah﴾ is in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), and ﴿alladhi﴾ (who) is its predicate (*khabar*).

Ibn Atiyya said: Whoever is informed of this sentence and it is firmly established in his soul, he believes, prays and spends. End of quote. This refers to what was mentioned earlier, that the object of "Say" (*qul*) is His saying: ﴿God is the One who created the heavens and the earth﴾, and so on. It is as if He is saying: "They should establish the prayer," as an answer to His saying: "Say to My servants: God is the One who created the heavens and the earth."

The apparent meaning is that the object of *akhraja* (He brought forth) is ﴿provision for you﴾, and *min* (from) is partitive (*li-l-tab'id*). Since it precedes the indefinite noun, it stands in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and the meaning is: "Provision is some of the fruits of the trees, and what is not provision also comes out of them, such as that which is purely harmful." It is also permissible for *min* to be explanatory (*li-bayan al-jins*, specifying the kind); this was stated by Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari, as if He had said: "He brought forth by it provision for you, which is the fruits." But this is not good, because *min* which is explanatory of the kind comes only after a vague term that it specifies.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: It is permissible that ﴿of the fruits﴾ be the object of *akhraja*, and *rizqan* (provision) be a circumstantial clause from the object, or be in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*) from *akhraja*, because it carries the meaning of *rizq*. It has been said that *min* is superfluous (*za'idah*), but this is not permissible according to the majority of the Basran grammarians (the grammarians of the school of Basra), because what precedes it must be a complete clause and what follows it a definite noun. It is permissible according to al-Akhfash.

*Al-fulk* here is a plural of *fulk* (ship), and for this reason He said: (p-428) ﴿so that it may run﴾. The meaning of ﴿by His command﴾ refers back to the command subsisting in His essence. Al-Zamakhshari said: (It refers to) His saying "Be," and the subjugation of the ships includes the subjugation of the seas and the subjugation of the winds. As for the subjugation of the rivers, it is through their flowing and through their being channelled for benefit.

﴿Constant﴾ (*da'ibayn*) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause. The meaning is: they both continue steadily in their course and in their giving light, and in their setting right what they set right of the earth, of bodies, and of plants. From Muqatil ibn Hibban, who traced it back to Ibn Abbas, that he said: its meaning is "constant in obedience to God." Ibn Atiyya said: This is a statement which, if what is meant is that obedience is submission on their part in being subjected, then this exists in His saying: ﴿subjected﴾; and if what is meant is that it is an intended obedience like the worship of humans, then this is good. And God knows best. End of quote.

The subjugation of the night and the day means that they follow each other, one after the other, for sleep and for livelihood. The speculative theologians (*al-mutakallimun*) said: the subjugation of the night and the day is figurative, because they are accidents (*a'rad*), and accidents cannot be subjected.

When God mentioned those great blessings, He mentioned that He did not limit Himself to them, and said: ﴿And He gave you of all that you asked of Him﴾. The address is to the human species in general; that is, a human has been given of everything that it is in his nature to ask for and to benefit from. This does not apply to each and every individual person, but these blessings are distributed among humans, so it is said: according to this whole, you were given such-and-such, by way of affirming the blessing.

Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Muhammad ibn Ali, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, Amr ibn Qa'id, Qatada, Salam, Ya'qub, and Nafi' in one narration read ﴿of all﴾ with tanwin (*min kullin*), meaning: of all these created things that have been mentioned. *Ma* (what) is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*) functioning as the second object; that is, "what it is in his nature to ask for," meaning to seek benefit from it. It has been said that *ma* is negative, and the second object is ﴿of all﴾, like His saying: ﴿and she was given of everything﴾ [al-Naml: 23], meaning: "not those who asked Him." He informed them of the abundance of His blessing upon them with blessings they did not ask for, and He did not mention what they did ask for. The negated clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. Al-Zamakhshari began with this opinion, and Ibn Atiyya repeated it, saying: it is the explanation of al-Dahhak.

This interpretation shows that it contradicts the reading of the majority, ﴿of all that you asked of Him﴾ with the genitive construction (*idafah*), because in that reading, according to this analysis, *ma* is negative, and so they did not ask Him. But in this reading they did ask Him, and *ma* means "that which" (*alladhi*). It has been permitted that it be a verbal (infinitival) relative (*masdariyyah*), and the verbal noun would then carry the meaning of the object.

When al-Zamakhshari sensed the apparent contradiction between this reading and that one, on the supposition that *ma* is negative, he said: It is permissible that *ma* be a relative pronoun, with ﴿And He gave you of all﴾ meaning: that which you needed, and your conditions and livelihoods could not be set right except by it, so it is as if you asked for it, or requested it with the tongue of circumstance. Thus he interpreted "you asked for it" as "what you needed."

The pronoun in ﴿you asked Him﴾: if *ma* is verbal, it refers back to God, the Exalted, and the verbal noun is used to mean the thing asked for. If *ma* is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," the pronoun refers back to it, and the implied sense is: "of all that which you asked Him for." It is not permissible for it to refer back to God. The connecting pronoun linking the relative clause to the relative pronoun is omitted, because if you consider it attached, the sense would be "*ma sa'altumuhu*" (you asked it), which is not permissible; or if you consider it detached, the sense would be "*ma sa'altumuhu iyyahu*" (you asked it of Him), and a detached pronoun may not be omitted.

Here, the word ﴿blessing﴾ (*ni'mah*): al-Wahidi said: It is a noun placed in the position of a verbal noun. One says *an'ama in'aman* and *ni'mah* (he bestowed a blessing), and the noun is placed in the position of the act of bestowing, just as one says *anfaqtu infaqan* and *nafaqah* (I spent). For this reason it is not made plural, because it carries the meaning of a verbal noun. End of quote.

What appears clear is that *ni'mah* refers to the thing bestowed, and that it is a collective noun (*ism jins*), not meant as a single item but as a plural, as if it were said: ﴿And if you count the blessing of God﴾. The meaning of ﴿you cannot count it﴾ is: you cannot enumerate it, nor are you able to count it. This applies when they wish to count it in summary. As for detailed enumeration, no one is capable of it, and none knows it except God.

Abu al-Darda' said: Whoever does not see the blessing of God upon him except in his food and drink, his knowledge is slight, and his punishment is near.

What is meant by "the human" here is the species; that is, these qualities are found in him, namely: wrongdoing and disbelief. He wrongs the blessing by neglecting to give thanks for it, and he disbelieves in it by denying it. It has been said: He is a wrongdoer in hardship, so he complains and despairs; a disbeliever in blessing, so he hoards and withholds.

In Surat al-Nahl: ﴿And if you count the blessing of God, you cannot enumerate it. Indeed God is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 18]. The difference between the two endings is this: here, His saying preceded: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the blessing of God for disbelief﴾ [Ibrahim: 28], and after it: ﴿and they set up rivals to God﴾ [Ibrahim: 30]. So this was an explicit reference to their evil deeds of ingratitude for the blessing and of wrongdoing, which is polytheism through the setting up of rivals. It was fitting to conclude by condemning the one who committed that, so He said: ﴿Indeed, the human is greatly wrongdoing and greatly disbelieving﴾.

As for in al-Nahl: when He mentioned a number of acts of grace and extended His description of them, and said: ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17], meaning: the One who brought into being these blessings mentioned earlier is not like one who has no power to create or to produce anything of them, He mentioned, among His acts of grace, that He is described by forgiveness and mercy, as an encouragement to return to Him. And these two attributes are His, just as the attribute of creating is His. In this there is encouragement for whoever believes in Him. It also moves from the worship of the created to the worship of the Creator, who forgives His servant's past lapse and shows him mercy. Furthermore, since He mentioned that God, the Exalted, is the One who bestows blessings upon the human, He mentioned what proceeds from the Benefactor and from the kind of the one benefited. From the Benefactor came what is suitable to the state of giving, namely forgiveness and mercy, since without these two He would not have bestowed blessings. And from the kind of the one benefited came what is suitable to the state of being blessed, namely wrongdoing and ingratitude. So it is as if it were said: if wrongdoing proceeds from the human, then God is Most Forgiving; or if ingratitude for a blessing proceeds from him, then God is Most Merciful, because He knows the human's weakness and deficiency.

The claim that this verse is abrogated (*mansukhah*) by the verse of al-Nahl is not to be given attention. al-Sakhawi reported this from Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam.

It is also permissible for *min* to be explanatory (*li-bayan al-jins*, specifying the kind); this was stated by Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari, as if He had said: "He brought forth by it provision for you, which is the fruits." But this is not good, because *min* which is explanatory of the kind comes only after a vague term that it specifies.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: It is permissible that ﴿of the fruits﴾ be the object of *akhraja*, and *rizqan* (provision) be a circumstantial clause from the object, or be in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*) from *akhraja*, because it carries the meaning of *rizq*. It has been said that *min* is superfluous (*za'idah*), but this is not permissible according to the majority of the Basran grammarians (the grammarians of the school of Basra), because what precedes it must be a complete clause and what follows it a definite noun. It is permissible according to al-Akhfash.

*Al-fulk* here is a plural of *fulk* (ship), and for this reason He said: (p-428) ﴿so that it may run﴾. The meaning of ﴿by His command﴾ refers back to the command subsisting in His essence. Al-Zamakhshari said: (It refers to) His saying "Be," and the subjugation of the ships includes the subjugation of the seas and the subjugation of the winds. As for the subjugation of the rivers, it is through their flowing and through their being channelled for benefit.

﴿Constant﴾ (*da'ibayn*) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause. The meaning is: they both continue steadily in their course and in their giving light, and in their setting right what they set right of the earth, of bodies, and of plants. From Muqatil ibn Hibban, who traced it back to Ibn Abbas, that he said: its meaning is "constant in obedience to God." Ibn Atiyya said: This is a statement which, if what is meant is that obedience is submission on their part in being subjected, then this exists in His saying: ﴿subjected﴾; and if what is meant is that it is an intended obedience like the worship of humans, then this is good. And God knows best. End of quote.

The subjugation of the night and the day means that they follow each other, one after the other, for sleep and for livelihood. The speculative theologians (*al-mutakallimun*) said: the subjugation of the night and the day is figurative, because they are accidents (*a'rad*), and accidents cannot be subjected.

When God mentioned those great blessings, He mentioned that He did not limit Himself to them, and said: ﴿And He gave you of all that you asked of Him﴾. The address is to the human species in general; that is, a human has been given of everything that it is in his nature to ask for and to benefit from. This does not apply to each and every individual person, but these blessings are distributed among humans, so it is said: according to this whole, you were given such-and-such, by way of affirming the blessing.

Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Muhammad ibn Ali, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, Amr ibn Qa'id, Qatada, Salam, Ya'qub, and Nafi' in one narration read ﴿of all﴾ with tanwin (*min kullin*), meaning: of all these created things that have been mentioned. *Ma* (what) is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*) functioning as the second object; that is, "what it is in his nature to ask for," meaning to seek benefit from it. It has been said that *ma* is negative, and the second object is ﴿of all﴾, like His saying: ﴿and she was given of everything﴾ [al-Naml: 23], meaning: "not those who asked Him." He informed them of the abundance of His blessing upon them with blessings they did not ask for, and He did not mention what they did ask for. The negated clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. Al-Zamakhshari began with this opinion, and Ibn Atiyya repeated it, saying: it is the explanation of al-Dahhak.

This interpretation shows that it contradicts the reading of the majority, ﴿of all that you asked of Him﴾ with the genitive construction (*idafah*), because in that reading, according to this analysis, *ma* is negative, and so they did not ask Him. But in this reading they did ask Him, and *ma* means "that which" (*alladhi*). It has been permitted that it be a verbal (infinitival) relative (*masdariyyah*), and the verbal noun would then carry the meaning of the object.

When al-Zamakhshari sensed the apparent contradiction between this reading and that one, on the supposition that *ma* is negative, he said: It is permissible that *ma* be a relative pronoun, with ﴿And He gave you of all﴾ meaning: that which you needed, and your conditions and livelihoods could not be set right except by it, so it is as if you asked for it, or requested it with the tongue of circumstance. Thus he interpreted "you asked for it" as "what you needed."

The pronoun in ﴿you asked Him﴾: if *ma* is verbal, it refers back to God, the Exalted, and the verbal noun is used to mean the thing asked for. If *ma* is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," the pronoun refers back to it, and the implied sense is: "of all that which you asked Him for." It is not permissible for it to refer back to God. The connecting pronoun linking the relative clause to the relative pronoun is omitted, because if you consider it attached, the sense would be "*ma sa'altumuhu*" (you asked it), which is not permissible; or if you consider it detached, the sense would be "*ma sa'altumuhu iyyahu*" (you asked it of Him), and a detached pronoun may not be omitted.

Here, the word ﴿blessing﴾ (*ni'mah*): al-Wahidi said: It is a noun placed in the position of a verbal noun. One says *an'ama in'aman* and *ni'mah* (he bestowed a blessing), and the noun is placed in the position of the act of bestowing, just as one says *anfaqtu infaqan* and *nafaqah* (I spent). For this reason it is not made plural, because it carries the meaning of a verbal noun. End of quote.

What appears clear is that *ni'mah* refers to the thing bestowed, and that it is a collective noun (*ism jins*), not meant as a single item but as a plural, as if it were said: ﴿And if you count the blessing of God﴾. The meaning of ﴿you cannot count it﴾ is: you cannot enumerate it, nor are you able to count it. This applies when they wish to count it in summary. As for detailed enumeration, no one is capable of it, and none knows it except God.

Abu al-Darda' said: Whoever does not see the blessing of God upon him except in his food and drink, his knowledge is slight, and his punishment is near.

What is meant by "the human" here is the species; that is, these qualities are found in him, namely: wrongdoing and disbelief. He wrongs the blessing by neglecting to give thanks for it, and he disbelieves in it by denying it. It has been said: He is a wrongdoer in hardship, so he complains and despairs; a disbeliever in blessing, so he hoards and withholds.

In Surat al-Nahl: ﴿And if you count the blessing of God, you cannot enumerate it. Indeed God is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 18]. The difference between the two endings is this: here, His saying preceded: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the blessing of God for disbelief﴾ [Ibrahim: 28], and after it: ﴿and they set up rivals to God﴾ [Ibrahim: 30]. So this was an explicit reference to their evil deeds of ingratitude for the blessing and of wrongdoing, which is polytheism through the setting up of rivals. It was fitting to conclude by condemning the one who committed that, so He said: ﴿Indeed, the human is greatly wrongdoing and greatly disbelieving﴾.

As for in al-Nahl: when He mentioned a number of acts of grace and extended His description of them, and said: ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17], meaning: the One who brought into being these blessings mentioned earlier is not like one who has no power to create or to produce anything of them, He mentioned, among His acts of grace, that He is described by forgiveness and mercy, as an encouragement to return to Him. And these two attributes are His, just as the attribute of creating is His. In this there is encouragement for whoever believes in Him. It also moves from the worship of the created to the worship of the Creator, who forgives His servant's past lapse and shows him mercy. Furthermore, since He mentioned that God, the Exalted, is the One who bestows blessings upon the human, He mentioned what proceeds from the Benefactor and from the kind of the one benefited. From the Benefactor came what is suitable to the state of giving, namely forgiveness and mercy, since without these two He would not have bestowed blessings. And from the kind of the one benefited came what is suitable to the state of being blessed, namely wrongdoing and ingratitude. So it is as if it were said: if wrongdoing proceeds from the human, then God is Most Forgiving; or if ingratitude for a blessing proceeds from him, then God is Most Merciful, because He knows the human's weakness and deficiency.

The claim that this verse is abrogated (*mansukhah*) by the verse of al-Nahl is not to be given attention. al-Sakhawi reported this from Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verses 31–36 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Tell My servants who have believed to establish prayer and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and publicly, before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship.﴾ ﴿It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth and sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you. And He has subjected for you the ships to sail through the sea by His command, and He has subjected for you the rivers.﴾ ﴿And He has subjected for you the sun and the moon, both constant [in their courses], and He has subjected for you the night and the day.﴾ ﴿And He gave you of all you asked of Him. And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it. Indeed, mankind is [generally]壮 unjust and ungrateful.﴾: When the Exalted mentioned the state of the disbelievers and their ingratitude for His favor, and their setting up rivals to Him, and [after] threatening them, He commanded the believers to adhere to obedience and to be watchful over their own souls, and to uphold the two pillars of Islam, the prayer (al-salah) and the zakat (almsgiving), before the coming of the Day of Resurrection. The object of "qul" (say) is omitted, its estimated form being: "Establish the prayer, they will establish [it]." "Yuqimu" (they establish) is jussive, in response to the imperative; this is the view of al-Akhfash and al-Mazini. It was refuted on the ground that it does not follow from "qul" that [the believers] "yuqimu," and this refutation was itself rejected, on the ground that it is the command to the believers to establish [prayer], not to the disbelievers, and the believers, whenever the Messenger commands them to do something, do it without fail.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: It is possible that "yuqimu" is the response to the imperative whose meaning is given to us by His saying "qul," by taking "qul" in this verse to mean "convey" and "deliver the Shariah": "they will establish the prayer." End of quote.
