It became *a'fidah* (with the first *hamzah* and the second), then the silent *hamzah* was changed to an *alif*, just as they said for *a'ra'm*: *a'ram*. So its pattern is *a'filah*.

It was also recited *afidatan* on the pattern of *fa'ilatan* (fi'lah), so it is possible that it is the plural of *fu'ad*, by dropping the *hamzah* and moving its vowel to the consonant before it, which is the *fa'*, although easing it between two positions is the preferred form. It is also possible that it is an active participle of *afida*, as you say *fariha*, *fahuwa fari-h* (he is happy).

Umm al-Haytham recited *uf'udatan* with a *kasrah* on the *waw* in place of the *hamzah*. The author of *al-Lawami'* said: It is the plural of *wafd* (delegation), and the reading is good, but I do not know this woman. Rather, Abu Hatim mentioned her. End of quote.

He changed the *hamzah* in *fu'ad* after a *dammah*, as it was changed in *jawn*, then he made it plural and retained it in the plural as it was retained in the singular. It is the plural of *wafd*, as the author of *al-Lawami'* said, and the original form would be *awfadah*, with metathesis. The plural of *fa'l* on the pattern of *af'ilah* is irregular, like *najd* and *anjidah*, and *wahy* and *awhiyah*.

Umm al-Haytham was a woman from whom something of the dialects of the Arabs was transmitted.

Zayd ibn 'Ali recited *ifadatun* on the pattern of *ishara*. It appears that the *hamzah* is a substitute for a *kasrah* on the *waw*, as they said *ishah* for *wishah* (sash), so the pattern is *fi'alah*, meaning: make those who are *wifadah* (delegation). It is also permissible that it is the verbal noun of *afada*, *ifadah*, or people of *ifadah*, meaning those who bring benefit and from whom benefit is gained.

The majority read ﴿tahwi ilayhim﴾, meaning they hasten toward them and fly toward them out of longing and yearning. Since *tahwi* was used with the meaning of *tamil* (incline), it was made to take *ila*, although its original construction is with *lam*. The poet said:

*Until when the hand of the youth fell upon her, she flew, and in his hand some of her feathers remained.*

An example of what is in the verse is the poet's saying:

*She hastens toward Makkah seeking guidance; the believer among the jinn is not like its disbelievers.*

Maslamah ibn 'Abd Allah recited *tuhwa* with a *dammah* on the *ta'*, in the passive voice, from *ahwa*, which is the causative of *hawa* (intransitive), with the causative *hamzah*. As if it were said: he hastens with them toward them.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Muhammad ibn 'Ali, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, and Mujahid recited *tahwa* as the imperfect of *hawa* meaning "to love." Since it was used with the meaning of yearning and inclining, it was made to take *ila*.

﴿And provide them with fruits﴾: along with their residents, in a valley where nothing of them grows, by bringing them from the lands, like His words: ﴿to which the fruits of everything are brought﴾ (28:57). It is narrated from Muslim ibn Muhammad al-Ta'ifi that when he, peace be upon him, supplicated that Allah provide the residents of Makkah with fruits, Allah sent Jibril, peace be upon him, who tore off a piece with his wing from Palestine. It was also said: from al-Urdunn. He brought it and circled it around the House seven times, and placed it near Makkah, and this is al-Ta'if. It was named after this story, and it is the place of the Thaqif, and it has trees and fruits. Something similar was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿That they may be grateful﴾: Al-Zamakhshari said: The blessing is that they are provided with all kinds of fruits present in a valley with no vegetation, no tree, and no water. Indeed, Allah the Mighty and Majestic answered Ibrahim's supplication and made it a secure sanctuary, to which the fruits of everything are brought as provision from Us. Then He favored it in the existence of varieties of fruits in it over every fertile region, over the most fertile and fruitful lands, and in whichever land of the East and West you see the wonder that Allah shows you in a valley without cultivation. This is the gathering of early and various fruits of different seasons—spring, summer, and autumn—in a single day, and that is not strange among His signs.

﴿Our Lord, You surely know what we conceal and what we reveal, and nothing is hidden from Allah on earth or in heaven.﴾ ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has given me in old age Isma'il and Ishaq. Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication.﴾ ﴿My Lord, make me one who establishes prayer, and from my offspring; our Lord, and accept my supplication.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the day the reckoning is established.﴾

He repeated the call for humble supplication and reliance. There is no apparent difference between the annexation of *Rabb* to the first-person singular pronoun (*rabbi*) and its annexation to the first-person plural pronoun (*rabbana*).

"What we conceal and what we reveal" is general, covering what they conceal and what they reveal. It was also said: what we conceal of grief over the separation that occurred between us, and what we reveal of weeping and supplication. It was also said: what we conceal of the sorrow of parting, and what we reveal of what passed between him and Hajar when she said to him at the farewell: "To whom are you leaving us?" He said: "To Allah I leave you." She said: "Did Allah command you with this?" He said: "Yes." She said: "Then we are not worried; You have left us to a sufficient one."

The apparent meaning is that His words, ﴿nothing is hidden from Allah on earth or in heaven﴾, are part of Ibrahim's speech, since what precedes and follows it is Ibrahim's speech. When He mentioned that "what is hidden" is general, He and what He referred to by "what is hidden" completed all things, and that they are not hidden from Him, Exalted is He.

It was also said that ﴿and nothing is hidden﴾ is part of the speech of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, confirming Ibrahim, peace be upon him, like His saying, ﴿and thus they do﴾ (27:34).

The apparent meaning is that these sentences which Ibrahim, peace be upon him, spoke were not said by him at one time. Rather, Allah related what he said at different times. This is shown by the fact that Ishaq did not exist at the time of his supplication, since he left Hajar and the infant in Makkah. So the apparent meaning is that his praise of Allah for granting him two sons was after Ishaq's existence.

"In old age" indicates old age in general, and he did not specify the period in which his two sons were granted to him. It is narrated that Isma'il was born to him when he was ninety-nine years old, and Ishaq was born to him when he was one hundred and twelve years old. It was also said: Isma'il at sixty-four, and Ishaq at ninety. It is narrated from Ibn Jubayr: he was not granted a child except after one hundred and seventeen years.

He mentioned the state of old age because the favor in it, in granting a child, is greater, since old age is the time when one despairs of children, and something coming after despair is sweeter to the soul and more delightful to it.

"In old age" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), because he said, "and I am old." "Upon" (*'ala*) retains its basic sense of elevation, but it is metaphorical, since old age is an abstract meaning that is gradually acquired; it is as if when he grew old and aged he became elevated over old age.

Al-Zamakhshari said: *'ala* in His words ﴿in old age﴾ means *ma'a* (with), as in the poet's saying:

*Indeed, despite what you see of my old age, I know where the shoulder is eaten (i.e., where the best of food is).*

And he used "Hearer of supplication" as a metaphor for answering and accepting it. Ibrahim had asked God to grant him a son, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me [a son] from among the righteous﴾ [al-Saffat: 100]. So he praised God for what He had given him of offspring and honored him by answering his supplication. The apparent reading is that *sami'* (hearer) is annexed to its object (*idafa* of the *mif'al* pattern to the object), so the construction is an annexation of the object ("*idafat min nasb*," an annexation in which the noun is the object of the first). This would be evidence for the operation of *fa'il*, the intensive form (*fa'il* of intensity) on the object, as Sibawayh held, although the majority of the Basran grammarians disagreed with him, and the Kufans also disagreed about it. The same applies to the remaining five intensive patterns: *fa'ul*, *fa'\u0101l*, *mif'\u0101l*, and *fa'il*, which is discussed in the science of grammar (*nahw*). It is possible to say that this is not an annexation of object, so that its operation would not be required; rather it is an annexation like the annexation of the active participle, as in: "This is the hitter of Zayd yesterday." Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that it be an annexation of *fa'il* (intensive form) to its agent, and that the supplication of God be made *sami'* by way of metaphorical attribution, meaning: the hearing of God. End of quote. But this is remote, because it entails that it belongs to the category of the attributive adjective (*sifa mushabbaha*), and the attribute is transitive, which is not permitted except according to Abu Ali al-Farisi, where no ambiguity arises. Here, however, ambiguity arises, since the apparent reading is that it is the annexation of the pattern to the object, not its annexation to the agent. Al-Farisi permitted this only in cases like: "Zayd is the oppressor of slaves," when it is known that he has oppressive slaves.

His supplication that God make him one who establishes the prayer, while he himself establishes it, is only intended to mean persistence (*dayumah*).

As for "and from my offspring" (*min dhurriyyati*), the *min* is partitive (*lil-tab'id*), because he was informed that among his offspring there would be someone who is a disbeliever, or someone who neglects its establishment even if he is a believer.

Talha and al-A'mash read: *du'a'u rabbana* (without a *ya'*). Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read it with a silent *ya'* in pausal pronunciation (*wasl*), and some of them affirmed it in pause (*waqf*). Warsh reported from Nafi' its affirmation in continuous recitation (*wasl*).

The apparent reading is that Ibrahim asked forgiveness for his two parents, who were close to him. His mother was a believer, and his father had not despaired of his faith, and the enmity of God had not become clear to him. This accords if we say that these supplications were made at different times, so he gathered here several matters for which he had supplicated. It was also said that he meant his mother and Nuh (peace be upon him). It was said that he meant Adam and Eve. The more evident view is the first opinion. His supplication for his father's forgiveness has come explicitly in His words: ﴿And forgive my father, for he was of those who go astray﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 86]. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): How was it permissible for him to seek forgiveness for his parents when they were disbelievers? (I answer): That is among the permissible things of reason, and its impermissibility is known only through revelation (*tawqif*). End of quote. He agrees in this with the People of the Sunna and differs from the doctrine of the Mu'tazila.

Al-Husayn ibn Ali, Muhammad, and Zayd read: *rabbana* in the indicative (*'ala al-khabar*). Ibn Ya'mar, al-Zuhri, and al-Nakha'i read: *wa-li-waladayya* without an *alif* and with a *fatha* on the *lam*, meaning Isma'il and Ishaq. 'Asim al-Jahdari rejected this reading and said: in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is: *wa-li-abawayya* (my two parents). It is reported from Yahya ibn Ya'mar: *wa-li-wuldayya* with a *damma* on the *waw* and a silent *lam*. This allows that it is the plural of *walad*, like *asad* (lions) to *asad* (lion), and that he supplicated for his descendants; and that it is a dialectal form for *walad* (child). The poet said:

*Fa-layta Ziyadan kana fi batni ummihi*
*wa-layta Ziyadan kana waladu himar*

(Would that Ziyad had been in his mother's womb, and would that Ziyad had been the offspring of a donkey.)

Just as they said: *al-'adam* and *al-'udm* (both meaning lack). Ibn Jubayr read: *wa-li-walidi* with a silent *ya'*, in the singular, like His words: ﴿And forgive my father﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 86]. The "establishment of the reckoning" (*qiyam al-hisab*) is a metaphor for its occurrence and its being fixed, just as one says: "war has risen on its shank" (*qamat al-harb 'ala saq*). Or it is by omission of a modifier, meaning: the people of the reckoning, as the poet said:

(p-435)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verses 37–43 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And when Abraham said: "My Lord, make this town secure, and keep me and my sons far from worshipping idols."﴾ [Ibrahim: 35] ﴿"My Lord, they have led many of the people astray. Whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ [Ibrahim: 36]

Connection of this verse to what precedes it: when Allah mentioned the reproach directed at those who exchanged the blessing of Allah for disbelief and set up rivals (andad) to Allah, namely the Quraysh and the Arabs who followed them, who took gods besides Allah, and when one of Allah's blessings upon them was His settling them in His sanctuary (haram), He followed this with the mention of their forefather Abraham. He (may the blessings of God be upon him) asked Allah to make Makkah secure, and asked that He keep his sons away from worshipping idols. He settled them and his offspring in His House so that they would worship Him alone with the worship that is most noble, which is prayer (salah), so that they would reflect on the religion of their forefather, and realise that it opposes what they had committed of idol worship, so that they would be restrained and turn back from it. The discussion of His saying here "this town" (al-balad) with the definite article was already covered, while in al-Baqarah it is indefinite.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Here he asked, in the first case, that Allah make it among the towns whose people are safe and do not fear, and in the second case, that it move out of a state of fear it was in to its opposite, safety, as if he said: "It is a fearful town, so make it secure." End of quote. Abraham first prayed for what is in obedience to Allah, namely that the place of the worshipper be safe, where he is not afraid, so that he can worship Allah. Then he prayed a second time that he and his sons be kept away from worshipping idols. The meaning of "keep me and my sons" (wajnubni wa-baniya) is: keep me and them persevering in avoiding the worship of idols. By "my sons" he meant his offspring from his own loins. Allah answered him by making the sanctuary secure, and none of his direct descendants from his own loins worshipped an idol. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, when asked how the Arabs worshipped idols, said: None of the descendants of Isma'il worshipped an idol, and they were eight tribes. They only had stones which they set up and called "a stone" (hajar), so wherever they set up a stone it had the meaning of a house (bayt), and they would circle around that stone and call it "the circling stone" (al-Duwar). End of quote.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: This supplication of the Friend (al-Khalil, peace be upon him) implies his extreme fear for himself, and if one who is in his rank fears that he might worship an idol, then how about others? But this verse should be taken as an example in fear and in seeking a good end. He repeated the call (nida') to win the favour of his Lord, and he mentioned the reason for his request, that he and his sons be kept away from worshipping idols, in His saying: ﴿They have led many of the people astray﴾ [Ibrahim: 36], since he had witnessed his father and his people worshipping idols. The meaning of "they have led astray" (adlalna): we were a cause of the misguidance of many people. The meaning is that they went astray by worshipping them, just as you say: "their trial is the world", that is, they were tempted by it and deceived because of it.

Al-Jahdari and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read: "wa-ajnibni" from ajnaba. He used the feminine form for the idols because it is the plural of what does not reason (ma la ya'qil), and he reports about it using the reports of the feminine, as you say: "al-ajdha' inkasarat" (the trunks were broken). The report about it is a report about the plural of rational male beings, with the waw, and it is a figurative usage (majaz), like His saying: ﴿They have indeed gone far astray﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67]. (Majaz: figurative or metaphorical usage.)

"Whoever follows me": that is, upon my religion and what I am upon. "Then he is of me": he made this because of the very close association and attachment to him, like his (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever cheats us is not of us," meaning not one of the believers. This points to the gravity of cheating, to the degree that it strips the cheater of faith. The meaning is that cheating is not among the characteristics of the people of faith.

"And whoever disobeys me": here there is a semantic antithesis (tibaq ma'nawi), because following is obedience. (Tibaq: antithesis, the juxtaposition of opposites.) His saying: ﴿then indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim: 36].

Muqatil said: "And whoever disobeys me," meaning they oppose shirk. Al-Zamakhshari said: You forgive me what has passed of disobedience when it becomes clear to me and I begin obedience anew. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The apparent meaning of "whoever disobeys me" is disbelief, because it parallels His saying "whoever follows me is of me". If this is so, then His saying "then indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful" means: when they believe. For he meant that Allah forgives every disbeliever, but the manner of expression he used was due to his habit of disciplining himself with good speech, pleasant utterance, and fine courtesy (ﷺ). Likewise, the Prophet of Allah 'Isa (peace be upon him) said: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 118].

**Abu Hayyan on Surah Ibrahim, verses 37–43 (part 2 of 3)**

﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without cultivation, by Your Sacred House, our Lord, that they may establish prayer. So make hearts among people incline toward them, and provide them with fruits, that they may be grateful.﴾ He repeated the call (ya Rabbana) out of eagerness for a response and to show humility and reliance upon Allah the Exalted. He used the first-person plural pronoun because the subject had already been mentioned. He mentioned his sons in his words, "and keep me and my sons away" (verse 35). "Some of my offspring" refers to Isma'il and those born from him. This is because when Hajar gave birth to Isma'il, Sarah became jealous of her. It is narrated that he rode the Buraq, along with Hajar and the infant, and came in one day from al-Sham to Makkah. He settled there, left his son and his maidservant there, and rode back the same day. All of this was by revelation from Allah the Exalted. When he was appointed (to this task), he supplicated with what is contained in this verse. As for how Hajar remained there and what happened to her and to Isma'il in that place, it is found in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, in the books of biography (al-siyar), and elsewhere.

The word "min" (some of) is partitive (lil-tab'id), because Ishaq was in al-Sham. The valley is the area between two mountains, and it is not a requirement for it to have water. He said "without cultivation" because he knew that Allah would not abandon Hajar and her son in that valley, and that He would provide them with water. He looked at the far-reaching outcome, so he said "without cultivation." Had he not known this from Allah the Exalted, he would have said "without water," according to the condition of the valley at that time.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It may be said that the negation of it being a place of cultivation entails the negation of water, since cultivation cannot exist except where water is found. So he negated what results from water, which is cultivation, due to the negation of its cause, which is water.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "In a valley" is the valley of Makkah. "Without cultivation" means that there is never any cultivation in it at all, like His words, ﴿an Arabic Qur'an, without crookedness﴾ (39:28), meaning there is no crookedness in it at all; there is nothing in it but straightness, nothing else. End of quote.

He used *qatt*, which is an adverb that is only used with the past tense, as the governed element of his saying "lā yakūnu" (there is not), though it is not in the past tense. It is in the place of *abadan* (never), which is used with non-past forms (the future).

Apparently, His words "by Your Sacred House" require that the House existed at the time of the supplication. The earlier discussion has preceded this, and the discussion about the House and when it was established has been covered in al-Baqarah and Ali 'Imran. It is described as "sacred" (al-muharram) because it was made inviolable against the Flood, meaning it was prevented from it, just as it is called "ancient" ('atiq) because it was freed from (being taken by tyrants) and so no one took control over it; or because it has always been mighty and protected from tyrants; or because it is respected and its violation is not permitted.

"That they may establish" (li-yuqimu) is connected to "I have settled." "Our Lord" is a parenthetical supplication. The meaning is: this glorious House is never free from worship. It was also said that the lam is the lam of command, meaning he supplicated for them to establish prayer.

Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi said: The lam is connected to His words, ﴿keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ (14:35), "that they may establish prayer." End of quote. This is very far-fetched.

He singled out prayer (al-salah) from among the other acts of worship because it is the most excellent of them, or because it is the cause of every good. His words "that they may establish" use the plural pronoun, indicating that Allah informed him that this child would have descendants there and would have offspring.

*Af'idatan* is the plural of *fu'ad*, meaning hearts. The heart is called *fu'ad* because of its *'it'ad* (being heated/burning), derived from *fa'ada*, and from it comes *al-mufta'ad*, which is the place where fire is kindled where meat is roasted.

Mu'arrij said: *al-af'idah* means the portion of people (in the dialect of the Quraysh), and Ibn Bahr went this way.

Mujahid said: If Ibrahim, peace be upon him, had said *af'idat al-nas* (hearts of people), Persia and Rome would have crowded around the House.

Ibn Jubayr said: The Jews and Christians would have made pilgrimage to it.

The apparent meaning is that "min" is partitive, since the sense is: hearts of (some) people. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible for "min" to be for origin (ibtida'), as when you say, "the heart from me is sick," meaning "my heart." So it is as if it were said: hearts of people. He made the annexed noun indefinite in this example to match the indefiniteness of *af'idah*, because in the verse it is indefinite, so that it encompasses some of the hearts. End of quote.

It does not appear that it is for the beginning of the limit (ibtida' al-ghayah), because there is no action for us in which a starting point leads to an endpoint, since it is not valid to say, as a starting point, "making hearts from people." Rather, the apparent meaning of "min" is partitive.

Hisham read *af'idatan* with a *ya'* after the *hamzah* (af'iyatan). This was explicitly stated by al-Hulwani on his authority. This is explained as *ishba'* (prolonging a vowel), but since *ishba'* occurs only in poetic necessity, some scholars took this reading to mean that Hisham recited with easing the *hamzah* like a *ya'*, so the narrator described it as with a *ya'*. Whoever misunderstood it thought it was a *ya'* after the *hamzah*, but what was meant was a *ya'* in place of the *hamzah*. He said: So this distortion is of the same kind as the distortion attributed to those who narrated from Abu 'Amr: *bari'ukum* and *ya'murukum* and similar, with the vowel of the grammatical case being silenced, and that was (merely) *ikhtilas* (rapid, slurred pronunciation).

Abu 'Amr al-Dani, the memorizer, said: What the proponent of this view mentioned is not relied upon, because the transmitters from Hisham and Abu 'Amr were among the most knowledgeable people about recitation and its variants, and ignorance does not lead them to be attributed with such a thing.

It was recited *aafidatan* (with a long vowel after the first *alif*) on the pattern of *fa'ilatan*, so it is possible that it is an active participle from *afida*, meaning he drew near, approached, and hastened, i.e., groups that are hastening, or groups that are hastening; or that it is the plural of *fu'ad* in the sense of the form of exchange (metathesis, min bab al-qalb). It became *a'fidah* (with the first *hamzah* and the second), then the silent *hamzah* was changed to an *alif*, just as they said for *a'ra'm*: *a'ram*. So its pattern is *a'filah*.

It was also recited *afidatan* on the pattern of *fa'ilatan* (fi'lah), so it is possible that it is the plural of *fu'ad*, by dropping the *hamzah* and moving its vowel to the consonant before it, which is the *fa'*, although easing it between two positions is the preferred form. It is also possible that it is an active participle of *afida*, as you say *fariha*, *fahuwa fari-h* (he is happy).

Umm al-Haytham recited *uf'udatan* with a *kasrah* on the *waw* in place of the *hamzah*. The author of *al-Lawami'* said: It is the plural of *wafd* (delegation), and the reading is good, but I do not know this woman. Rather, Abu Hatim mentioned her. End of quote.

He changed the *hamzah* in *fu'ad* after a *dammah*, as it was changed in *jawn*, then he made it plural and retained it in the plural as it was retained in the singular. It is the plural of *wafd*, as the author of *al-Lawami'* said, and the original form would be *awfadah*, with metathesis. The plural of *fa'l* on the pattern of *af'ilah* is irregular, like *najd* and *anjidah*, and *wahy* and *awhiyah*.

Umm al-Haytham was a woman from whom something of the dialects of the Arabs was transmitted.

Zayd ibn 'Ali recited *ifadatun* on the pattern of *ishara*. It appears that the *hamzah* is a substitute for a *kasrah* on the *waw*, as they said *ishah* for *wishah* (sash), so the pattern is *fi'alah*, meaning: make those who are *wifadah* (delegation). It is also permissible that it is the verbal noun of *afada*, *ifadah*, or people of *ifadah*, meaning those who bring benefit and from whom benefit is gained.

The majority read ﴿tahwi ilayhim﴾, meaning they hasten toward them and fly toward them out of longing and yearning. Since *tahwi* was used with the meaning of *tamil* (incline), it was made to take *ila*, although its original construction is with *lam*. The poet said:

*Until when the hand of the youth fell upon her, she flew, and in his hand some of her feathers remained.*

An example of what is in the verse is the poet's saying:

*She hastens toward Makkah seeking guidance; the believer among the jinn is not like its disbelievers.*

Maslamah ibn 'Abd Allah recited *tuhwa* with a *dammah* on the *ta'*, in the passive voice, from *ahwa*, which is the causative of *hawa* (intransitive), with the causative *hamzah*. As if it were said: he hastens with them toward them.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Muhammad ibn 'Ali, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, and Mujahid recited *tahwa* as the imperfect of *hawa* meaning "to love." Since it was used with the meaning of yearning and inclining, it was made to take *ila*.

﴿And provide them with fruits﴾: along with their residents, in a valley where nothing of them grows, by bringing them from the lands, like His words: ﴿to which the fruits of everything are brought﴾ (28:57). It is narrated from Muslim ibn Muhammad al-Ta'ifi that when he, peace be upon him, supplicated that Allah provide the residents of Makkah with fruits, Allah sent Jibril, peace be upon him, who tore off a piece with his wing from Palestine. It was also said: from al-Urdunn. He brought it and circled it around the House seven times, and placed it near Makkah, and this is al-Ta'if. It was named after this story, and it is the place of the Thaqif, and it has trees and fruits. Something similar was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿That they may be grateful﴾: Al-Zamakhshari said: The blessing is that they are provided with all kinds of fruits present in a valley with no vegetation, no tree, and no water. Indeed, Allah the Mighty and Majestic answered Ibrahim's supplication and made it a secure sanctuary, to which the fruits of everything are brought as provision from Us. Then He favored it in the existence of varieties of fruits in it over every fertile region, over the most fertile and fruitful lands, and in whichever land of the East and West you see the wonder that Allah shows you in a valley without cultivation. This is the gathering of early and various fruits of different seasons—spring, summer, and autumn—in a single day, and that is not strange among His signs.

﴿Our Lord, You surely know what we conceal and what we reveal, and nothing is hidden from Allah on earth or in heaven.﴾ ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has given me in old age Isma'il and Ishaq. Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication.﴾ ﴿My Lord, make me one who establishes prayer, and from my offspring; our Lord, and accept my supplication.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the day the reckoning is established.﴾

He repeated the call for humble supplication and reliance. There is no apparent difference between the annexation of *Rabb* to the first-person singular pronoun (*rabbi*) and its annexation to the first-person plural pronoun (*rabbana*).

"What we conceal and what we reveal" is general, covering what they conceal and what they reveal. It was also said: what we conceal of grief over the separation that occurred between us, and what we reveal of weeping and supplication. It was also said: what we conceal of the sorrow of parting, and what we reveal of what passed between him and Hajar when she said to him at the farewell: "To whom are you leaving us?" He said: "To Allah I leave you." She said: "Did Allah command you with this?" He said: "Yes." She said: "Then we are not worried; You have left us to a sufficient one."

The apparent meaning is that His words, ﴿nothing is hidden from Allah on earth or in heaven﴾, are part of Ibrahim's speech, since what precedes and follows it is Ibrahim's speech. When He mentioned that "what is hidden" is general, He and what He referred to by "what is hidden" completed all things, and that they are not hidden from Him, Exalted is He.

It was also said that ﴿and nothing is hidden﴾ is part of the speech of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, confirming Ibrahim, peace be upon him, like His saying, ﴿and thus they do﴾ (27:34).

The apparent meaning is that these sentences which Ibrahim, peace be upon him, spoke were not said by him at one time. Rather, Allah related what he said at different times. This is shown by the fact that Ishaq did not exist at the time of his supplication, since he left Hajar and the infant in Makkah. So the apparent meaning is that his praise of Allah for granting him two sons was after Ishaq's existence.

"In old age" indicates old age in general, and he did not specify the period in which his two sons were granted to him. It is narrated that Isma'il was born to him when he was ninety-nine years old, and Ishaq was born to him when he was one hundred and twelve years old. It was also said: Isma'il at sixty-four, and Ishaq at ninety. It is narrated from Ibn Jubayr: he was not granted a child except after one hundred and seventeen years.

He mentioned the state of old age because the favor in it, in granting a child, is greater, since old age is the time when one despairs of children, and something coming after despair is sweeter to the soul and more delightful to it.

"In old age" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), because he said, "and I am old." "Upon" (*'ala*) retains its basic sense of elevation, but it is metaphorical, since old age is an abstract meaning that is gradually acquired; it is as if when he grew old and aged he became elevated over old age.

Al-Zamakhshari said: *'ala* in His words ﴿in old age﴾ means *ma'a* (with), as in the poet's saying:

*Indeed, despite what you see of my old age, I know where the shoulder is eaten (i.e., where the best of food is).*

And he used "Hearer of supplication" as a metaphor for answering and accepting it. Ibrahim had asked God to grant him a son, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me [a son] from among the righteous﴾ [al-Saffat: 100]. So he praised God for what He had given him of offspring and honored him by answering his supplication. The apparent reading is that *sami'* (hearer) is annexed to its object (*idafa* of the *mif'al* pattern to the object), so the construction is an annexation of the object ("*idafat min nasb*," an annexation in which the noun is the object of the first). This would be evidence for the operation of *fa'il*, the intensive form (*fa'il* of intensity) on the object, as Sibawayh held, although the majority of the Basran grammarians disagreed with him, and the Kufans also disagreed about it. The same applies to the remaining five intensive patterns: *fa'ul*, *fa'\u0101l*, *mif'\u0101l*, and *fa'il*, which is discussed in the science of grammar (*nahw*). It is possible to say that this is not an annexation of object, so that its operation would not be required; rather it is an annexation like the annexation of the active participle, as in: "This is the hitter of Zayd yesterday." Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that it be an annexation of *fa'il* (intensive form) to its agent, and that the supplication of God be made *sami'* by way of metaphorical attribution, meaning: the hearing of God. End of quote. But this is remote, because it entails that it belongs to the category of the attributive adjective (*sifa mushabbaha*), and the attribute is transitive, which is not permitted except according to Abu Ali al-Farisi, where no ambiguity arises. Here, however, ambiguity arises, since the apparent reading is that it is the annexation of the pattern to the object, not its annexation to the agent. Al-Farisi permitted this only in cases like: "Zayd is the oppressor of slaves," when it is known that he has oppressive slaves.

His supplication that God make him one who establishes the prayer, while he himself establishes it, is only intended to mean persistence (*dayumah*).

As for "and from my offspring" (*min dhurriyyati*), the *min* is partitive (*lil-tab'id*), because he was informed that among his offspring there would be someone who is a disbeliever, or someone who neglects its establishment even if he is a believer.

Talha and al-A'mash read: *du'a'u rabbana* (without a *ya'*). Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read it with a silent *ya'* in pausal pronunciation (*wasl*), and some of them affirmed it in pause (*waqf*). Warsh reported from Nafi' its affirmation in continuous recitation (*wasl*).

The apparent reading is that Ibrahim asked forgiveness for his two parents, who were close to him. His mother was a believer, and his father had not despaired of his faith, and the enmity of God had not become clear to him. This accords if we say that these supplications were made at different times, so he gathered here several matters for which he had supplicated. It was also said that he meant his mother and Nuh (peace be upon him). It was said that he meant Adam and Eve. The more evident view is the first opinion. His supplication for his father's forgiveness has come explicitly in His words: ﴿And forgive my father, for he was of those who go astray﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 86]. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): How was it permissible for him to seek forgiveness for his parents when they were disbelievers? (I answer): That is among the permissible things of reason, and its impermissibility is known only through revelation (*tawqif*). End of quote. He agrees in this with the People of the Sunna and differs from the doctrine of the Mu'tazila.

Al-Husayn ibn Ali, Muhammad, and Zayd read: *rabbana* in the indicative (*'ala al-khabar*). Ibn Ya'mar, al-Zuhri, and al-Nakha'i read: *wa-li-waladayya* without an *alif* and with a *fatha* on the *lam*, meaning Isma'il and Ishaq. 'Asim al-Jahdari rejected this reading and said: in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is: *wa-li-abawayya* (my two parents). It is reported from Yahya ibn Ya'mar: *wa-li-wuldayya* with a *damma* on the *waw* and a silent *lam*. This allows that it is the plural of *walad*, like *asad* (lions) to *asad* (lion), and that he supplicated for his descendants; and that it is a dialectal form for *walad* (child). The poet said:

*Fa-layta Ziyadan kana fi batni ummihi*
*wa-layta Ziyadan kana waladu himar*

(Would that Ziyad had been in his mother's womb, and would that Ziyad had been the offspring of a donkey.)

Just as they said: *al-'adam* and *al-'udm* (both meaning lack). Ibn Jubayr read: *wa-li-walidi* with a silent *ya'*, in the singular, like His words: ﴿And forgive my father﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 86]. The "establishment of the reckoning" (*qiyam al-hisab*) is a metaphor for its occurrence and its being fixed, just as one says: "war has risen on its shank" (*qamat al-harb 'ala saq*). Or it is by omission of a modifier, meaning: the people of the reckoning, as the poet said:

(p-435)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verses 37–43 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And when Abraham said: "My Lord, make this town secure, and keep me and my sons far from worshipping idols."﴾ [Ibrahim: 35] ﴿"My Lord, they have led many of the people astray. Whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ [Ibrahim: 36]

Connection of this verse to what precedes it: when Allah mentioned the reproach directed at those who exchanged the blessing of Allah for disbelief and set up rivals (andad) to Allah, namely the Quraysh and the Arabs who followed them, who took gods besides Allah, and when one of Allah's blessings upon them was His settling them in His sanctuary (haram), He followed this with the mention of their forefather Abraham. He (may the blessings of God be upon him) asked Allah to make Makkah secure, and asked that He keep his sons away from worshipping idols. He settled them and his offspring in His House so that they would worship Him alone with the worship that is most noble, which is prayer (salah), so that they would reflect on the religion of their forefather, and realise that it opposes what they had committed of idol worship, so that they would be restrained and turn back from it. The discussion of His saying here "this town" (al-balad) with the definite article was already covered, while in al-Baqarah it is indefinite.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Here he asked, in the first case, that Allah make it among the towns whose people are safe and do not fear, and in the second case, that it move out of a state of fear it was in to its opposite, safety, as if he said: "It is a fearful town, so make it secure." End of quote. Abraham first prayed for what is in obedience to Allah, namely that the place of the worshipper be safe, where he is not afraid, so that he can worship Allah. Then he prayed a second time that he and his sons be kept away from worshipping idols. The meaning of "keep me and my sons" (wajnubni wa-baniya) is: keep me and them persevering in avoiding the worship of idols. By "my sons" he meant his offspring from his own loins. Allah answered him by making the sanctuary secure, and none of his direct descendants from his own loins worshipped an idol. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, when asked how the Arabs worshipped idols, said: None of the descendants of Isma'il worshipped an idol, and they were eight tribes. They only had stones which they set up and called "a stone" (hajar), so wherever they set up a stone it had the meaning of a house (bayt), and they would circle around that stone and call it "the circling stone" (al-Duwar). End of quote.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: This supplication of the Friend (al-Khalil, peace be upon him) implies his extreme fear for himself, and if one who is in his rank fears that he might worship an idol, then how about others? But this verse should be taken as an example in fear and in seeking a good end. He repeated the call (nida') to win the favour of his Lord, and he mentioned the reason for his request, that he and his sons be kept away from worshipping idols, in His saying: ﴿They have led many of the people astray﴾ [Ibrahim: 36], since he had witnessed his father and his people worshipping idols. The meaning of "they have led astray" (adlalna): we were a cause of the misguidance of many people. The meaning is that they went astray by worshipping them, just as you say: "their trial is the world", that is, they were tempted by it and deceived because of it.

Al-Jahdari and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read: "wa-ajnibni" from ajnaba. He used the feminine form for the idols because it is the plural of what does not reason (ma la ya'qil), and he reports about it using the reports of the feminine, as you say: "al-ajdha' inkasarat" (the trunks were broken). The report about it is a report about the plural of rational male beings, with the waw, and it is a figurative usage (majaz), like His saying: ﴿They have indeed gone far astray﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67]. (Majaz: figurative or metaphorical usage.)

"Whoever follows me": that is, upon my religion and what I am upon. "Then he is of me": he made this because of the very close association and attachment to him, like his (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever cheats us is not of us," meaning not one of the believers. This points to the gravity of cheating, to the degree that it strips the cheater of faith. The meaning is that cheating is not among the characteristics of the people of faith.

"And whoever disobeys me": here there is a semantic antithesis (tibaq ma'nawi), because following is obedience. (Tibaq: antithesis, the juxtaposition of opposites.) His saying: ﴿then indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim: 36].

Muqatil said: "And whoever disobeys me," meaning they oppose shirk. Al-Zamakhshari said: You forgive me what has passed of disobedience when it becomes clear to me and I begin obedience anew. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The apparent meaning of "whoever disobeys me" is disbelief, because it parallels His saying "whoever follows me is of me". If this is so, then His saying "then indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful" means: when they believe. For he meant that Allah forgives every disbeliever, but the manner of expression he used was due to his habit of disciplining himself with good speech, pleasant utterance, and fine courtesy (ﷺ). Likewise, the Prophet of Allah 'Isa (peace be upon him) said: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 118].

**Abu Hayyan on Surah Ibrahim, verses 37–43 (part 2 of 3)**

﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without cultivation, by Your Sacred House, our Lord, that they may establish prayer. So make hearts among people incline toward them, and provide them with fruits, that they may be grateful.﴾ He repeated the call (ya Rabbana) out of eagerness for a response and to show humility and reliance upon Allah the Exalted. He used the first-person plural pronoun because the subject had already been mentioned. He mentioned his sons in his words, "and keep me and my sons away" (verse 35). "Some of my offspring" refers to Isma'il and those born from him. This is because when Hajar gave birth to Isma'il, Sarah became jealous of her. It is narrated that he rode the Buraq, along with Hajar and the infant, and came in one day from al-Sham to Makkah. He settled there, left his son and his maidservant there, and rode back the same day. All of this was by revelation from Allah the Exalted. When he was appointed (to this task), he supplicated with what is contained in this verse. As for how Hajar remained there and what happened to her and to Isma'il in that place, it is found in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, in the books of biography (al-siyar), and elsewhere.

The word "min" (some of) is partitive (lil-tab'id), because Ishaq was in al-Sham. The valley is the area between two mountains, and it is not a requirement for it to have water. He said "without cultivation" because he knew that Allah would not abandon Hajar and her son in that valley, and that He would provide them with water. He looked at the far-reaching outcome, so he said "without cultivation." Had he not known this from Allah the Exalted, he would have said "without water," according to the condition of the valley at that time.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It may be said that the negation of it being a place of cultivation entails the negation of water, since cultivation cannot exist except where water is found. So he negated what results from water, which is cultivation, due to the negation of its cause, which is water.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "In a valley" is the valley of Makkah. "Without cultivation" means that there is never any cultivation in it at all, like His words, ﴿an Arabic Qur'an, without crookedness﴾ (39:28), meaning there is no crookedness in it at all; there is nothing in it but straightness, nothing else. End of quote.

He used *qatt*, which is an adverb that is only used with the past tense, as the governed element of his saying "lā yakūnu" (there is not), though it is not in the past tense. It is in the place of *abadan* (never), which is used with non-past forms (the future).

Apparently, His words "by Your Sacred House" require that the House existed at the time of the supplication. The earlier discussion has preceded this, and the discussion about the House and when it was established has been covered in al-Baqarah and Ali 'Imran. It is described as "sacred" (al-muharram) because it was made inviolable against the Flood, meaning it was prevented from it, just as it is called "ancient" ('atiq) because it was freed from (being taken by tyrants) and so no one took control over it; or because it has always been mighty and protected from tyrants; or because it is respected and its violation is not permitted.

"That they may establish" (li-yuqimu) is connected to "I have settled." "Our Lord" is a parenthetical supplication. The meaning is: this glorious House is never free from worship. It was also said that the lam is the lam of command, meaning he supplicated for them to establish prayer.

Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi said: The lam is connected to His words, ﴿keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ (14:35), "that they may establish prayer." End of quote. This is very far-fetched.

He singled out prayer (al-salah) from among the other acts of worship because it is the most excellent of them, or because it is the cause of every good. His words "that they may establish" use the plural pronoun, indicating that Allah informed him that this child would have descendants there and would have offspring.

*Af'idatan* is the plural of *fu'ad*, meaning hearts. The heart is called *fu'ad* because of its *'it'ad* (being heated/burning), derived from *fa'ada*, and from it comes *al-mufta'ad*, which is the place where fire is kindled where meat is roasted.

Mu'arrij said: *al-af'idah* means the portion of people (in the dialect of the Quraysh), and Ibn Bahr went this way.

Mujahid said: If Ibrahim, peace be upon him, had said *af'idat al-nas* (hearts of people), Persia and Rome would have crowded around the House.

Ibn Jubayr said: The Jews and Christians would have made pilgrimage to it.

The apparent meaning is that "min" is partitive, since the sense is: hearts of (some) people. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible for "min" to be for origin (ibtida'), as when you say, "the heart from me is sick," meaning "my heart." So it is as if it were said: hearts of people. He made the annexed noun indefinite in this example to match the indefiniteness of *af'idah*, because in the verse it is indefinite, so that it encompasses some of the hearts. End of quote.

It does not appear that it is for the beginning of the limit (ibtida' al-ghayah), because there is no action for us in which a starting point leads to an endpoint, since it is not valid to say, as a starting point, "making hearts from people." Rather, the apparent meaning of "min" is partitive.

Hisham read *af'idatan* with a *ya'* after the *hamzah* (af'iyatan). This was explicitly stated by al-Hulwani on his authority. This is explained as *ishba'* (prolonging a vowel), but since *ishba'* occurs only in poetic necessity, some scholars took this reading to mean that Hisham recited with easing the *hamzah* like a *ya'*, so the narrator described it as with a *ya'*. Whoever misunderstood it thought it was a *ya'* after the *hamzah*, but what was meant was a *ya'* in place of the *hamzah*. He said: So this distortion is of the same kind as the distortion attributed to those who narrated from Abu 'Amr: *bari'ukum* and *ya'murukum* and similar, with the vowel of the grammatical case being silenced, and that was (merely) *ikhtilas* (rapid, slurred pronunciation).

Abu 'Amr al-Dani, the memorizer, said: What the proponent of this view mentioned is not relied upon, because the transmitters from Hisham and Abu 'Amr were among the most knowledgeable people about recitation and its variants, and ignorance does not lead them to be attributed with such a thing.

It was recited *aafidatan* (with a long vowel after the first *alif*) on the pattern of *fa'ilatan*, so it is possible that it is an active participle from *afida*, meaning he drew near, approached, and hastened, i.e., groups that are hastening, or groups that are hastening; or that it is the plural of *fu'ad* in the sense of the form of exchange (metathesis, min bab al-qalb). It became *a'fidah* (with the first *hamzah* and the second), then the silent *hamzah* was changed to an *alif*, just as they said for *a'ra'm*: *a'ram*. So its pattern is *a'filah*.

It was also recited *afidatan* on the pattern of *fa'ilatan* (fi'lah), so it is possible that it is the plural of *fu'ad*, by dropping the *hamzah* and moving its vowel to the consonant before it, which is the *fa'*, although easing it between two positions is the preferred form. It is also possible that it is an active participle of *afida*, as you say *fariha*, *fahuwa fari-h* (he is happy).

Umm al-Haytham recited *uf'udatan* with a *kasrah* on the *waw* in place of the *hamzah*. The author of *al-Lawami'* said: It is the plural of *wafd* (delegation), and the reading is good, but I do not know this woman. Rather, Abu Hatim mentioned her. End of quote.

He changed the *hamzah* in *fu'ad* after a *dammah*, as it was changed in *jawn*, then he made it plural and retained it in the plural as it was retained in the singular. It is the plural of *wafd*, as the author of *al-Lawami'* said, and the original form would be *awfadah*, with metathesis. The plural of *fa'l* on the pattern of *af'ilah* is irregular, like *najd* and *anjidah*, and *wahy* and *awhiyah*.

Umm al-Haytham was a woman from whom something of the dialects of the Arabs was transmitted.

Zayd ibn 'Ali recited *ifadatun* on the pattern of *ishara*. It appears that the *hamzah* is a substitute for a *kasrah* on the *waw*, as they said *ishah* for *wishah* (sash), so the pattern is *fi'alah*, meaning: make those who are *wifadah* (delegation). It is also permissible that it is the verbal noun of *afada*, *ifadah*, or people of *ifadah*, meaning those who bring benefit and from whom benefit is gained.

The majority read ﴿tahwi ilayhim﴾, meaning they hasten toward them and fly toward them out of longing and yearning. Since *tahwi* was used with the meaning of *tamil* (incline), it was made to take *ila*, although its original construction is with *lam*. The poet said:

*Until when the hand of the youth fell upon her, she flew, and in his hand some of her feathers remained.*

An example of what is in the verse is the poet's saying:

*She hastens toward Makkah seeking guidance; the believer among the jinn is not like its disbelievers.*

Maslamah ibn 'Abd Allah recited *tuhwa* with a *dammah* on the *ta'*, in the passive voice, from *ahwa*, which is the causative of *hawa* (intransitive), with the causative *hamzah*. As if it were said: he hastens with them toward them.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Muhammad ibn 'Ali, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, and Mujahid recited *tahwa* as the imperfect of *hawa* meaning "to love." Since it was used with the meaning of yearning and inclining, it was made to take *ila*.

﴿And provide them with fruits﴾: along with their residents, in a valley where nothing of them grows, by bringing them from the lands, like His words: ﴿to which the fruits of everything are brought﴾ (28:57). It is narrated from Muslim ibn Muhammad al-Ta'ifi that when he, peace be upon him, supplicated that Allah provide the residents of Makkah with fruits, Allah sent Jibril, peace be upon him, who tore off a piece with his wing from Palestine. It was also said: from al-Urdunn. He brought it and circled it around the House seven times, and placed it near Makkah, and this is al-Ta'if. It was named after this story, and it is the place of the Thaqif, and it has trees and fruits. Something similar was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿That they may be grateful﴾: Al-Zamakhshari said: The blessing is that they are provided with all kinds of fruits present in a valley with no vegetation, no tree, and no water. Indeed, Allah the Mighty and Majestic answered Ibrahim's supplication and made it a secure sanctuary, to which the fruits of everything are brought as provision from Us. Then He favored it in the existence of varieties of fruits in it over every fertile region, over the most fertile and fruitful lands, and in whichever land of the East and West you see the wonder that Allah shows you in a valley without cultivation. This is the gathering of early and various fruits of different seasons—spring, summer, and autumn—in a single day, and that is not strange among His signs.

﴿Our Lord, You surely know what we conceal and what we reveal, and nothing is hidden from Allah on earth or in heaven.﴾ ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has given me in old age Isma'il and Ishaq. Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication.﴾ ﴿My Lord, make me one who establishes prayer, and from my offspring; our Lord, and accept my supplication.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the day the reckoning is established.﴾

He repeated the call for humble supplication and reliance. There is no apparent difference between the annexation of *Rabb* to the first-person singular pronoun (*rabbi*) and its annexation to the first-person plural pronoun (*rabbana*).

"What we conceal and what we reveal" is general, covering what they conceal and what they reveal. It was also said: what we conceal of grief over the separation that occurred between us, and what we reveal of weeping and supplication. It was also said: what we conceal of the sorrow of parting, and what we reveal of what passed between him and Hajar when she said to him at the farewell: "To whom are you leaving us?" He said: "To Allah I leave you." She said: "Did Allah command you with this?" He said: "Yes." She said: "Then we are not worried; You have left us to a sufficient one."

The apparent meaning is that His words, ﴿nothing is hidden from Allah on earth or in heaven﴾, are part of Ibrahim's speech, since what precedes and follows it is Ibrahim's speech. When He mentioned that "what is hidden" is general, He and what He referred to by "what is hidden" completed all things, and that they are not hidden from Him, Exalted is He.

It was also said that ﴿and nothing is hidden﴾ is part of the speech of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, confirming Ibrahim, peace be upon him, like His saying, ﴿and thus they do﴾ (27:34).

The apparent meaning is that these sentences which Ibrahim, peace be upon him, spoke were not said by him at one time. Rather, Allah related what he said at different times. This is shown by the fact that Ishaq did not exist at the time of his supplication, since he left Hajar and the infant in Makkah. So the apparent meaning is that his praise of Allah for granting him two sons was after Ishaq's existence.

"In old age" indicates old age in general, and he did not specify the period in which his two sons were granted to him. It is narrated that Isma'il was born to him when he was ninety-nine years old, and Ishaq was born to him when he was one hundred and twelve years old. It was also said: Isma'il at sixty-four, and Ishaq at ninety. It is narrated from Ibn Jubayr: he was not granted a child except after one hundred and seventeen years.

He mentioned the state of old age because the favor in it, in granting a child, is greater, since old age is the time when one despairs of children, and something coming after despair is sweeter to the soul and more delightful to it.

"In old age" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), because he said, "and I am old." "Upon" (*'ala*) retains its basic sense of elevation, but it is metaphorical, since old age is an abstract meaning that is gradually acquired; it is as if when he grew old and aged he became elevated over old age.

Al-Zamakhshari said: *'ala* in His words ﴿in old age﴾ means *ma'a* (with), as in the poet's saying:

*Indeed, despite what you see of my old age, I know where the shoulder is eaten (i.e., where the best of food is).*

And he used "Hearer of supplication" as a metaphor for answering and accepting it. Ibrahim had asked God to grant him a son, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me [a son] from among the righteous﴾ [al-Saffat: 100]. So he praised God for what He had given him of offspring and honored him by answering his supplication. The apparent reading is that *sami'* (hearer) is annexed to its object (*idafa* of the *mif'al* pattern to the object), so the construction is an annexation of the object ("*idafat min nasb*," an annexation in which the noun is the object of the first). This would be evidence for the operation of *fa'il*, the intensive form (*fa'il* of intensity) on the object, as Sibawayh held, although the majority of the Basran grammarians disagreed with him, and the Kufans also disagreed about it. The same applies to the remaining five intensive patterns: *fa'ul*, *fa'\u0101l*, *mif'\u0101l*, and *fa'il*, which is discussed in the science of grammar (*nahw*). It is possible to say that this is not an annexation of object, so that its operation would not be required; rather it is an annexation like the annexation of the active participle, as in: "This is the hitter of Zayd yesterday." Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that it be an annexation of *fa'il* (intensive form) to its agent, and that the supplication of God be made *sami'* by way of metaphorical attribution, meaning: the hearing of God. End of quote. But this is remote, because it entails that it belongs to the category of the attributive adjective (*sifa mushabbaha*), and the attribute is transitive, which is not permitted except according to Abu Ali al-Farisi, where no ambiguity arises. Here, however, ambiguity arises, since the apparent reading is that it is the annexation of the pattern to the object, not its annexation to the agent. Al-Farisi permitted this only in cases like: "Zayd is the oppressor of slaves," when it is known that he has oppressive slaves.

His supplication that God make him one who establishes the prayer, while he himself establishes it, is only intended to mean persistence (*dayumah*).

As for "and from my offspring" (*min dhurriyyati*), the *min* is partitive (*lil-tab'id*), because he was informed that among his offspring there would be someone who is a disbeliever, or someone who neglects its establishment even if he is a believer.

Talha and al-A'mash read: *du'a'u rabbana* (without a *ya'*). Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read it with a silent *ya'* in pausal pronunciation (*wasl*), and some of them affirmed it in pause (*waqf*). Warsh reported from Nafi' its affirmation in continuous recitation (*wasl*).

The apparent reading is that Ibrahim asked forgiveness for his two parents, who were close to him. His mother was a believer, and his father had not despaired of his faith, and the enmity of God had not become clear to him. This accords if we say that these supplications were made at different times, so he gathered here several matters for which he had supplicated. It was also said that he meant his mother and Nuh (peace be upon him). It was said that he meant Adam and Eve. The more evident view is the first opinion. His supplication for his father's forgiveness has come explicitly in His words: ﴿And forgive my father, for he was of those who go astray﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 86]. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): How was it permissible for him to seek forgiveness for his parents when they were disbelievers? (I answer): That is among the permissible things of reason, and its impermissibility is known only through revelation (*tawqif*). End of quote. He agrees in this with the People of the Sunna and differs from the doctrine of the Mu'tazila.

Al-Husayn ibn Ali, Muhammad, and Zayd read: *rabbana* in the indicative (*'ala al-khabar*). Ibn Ya'mar, al-Zuhri, and al-Nakha'i read: *wa-li-waladayya* without an *alif* and with a *fatha* on the *lam*, meaning Isma'il and Ishaq. 'Asim al-Jahdari rejected this reading and said: in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is: *wa-li-abawayya* (my two parents). It is reported from Yahya ibn Ya'mar: *wa-li-wuldayya* with a *damma* on the *waw* and a silent *lam*. This allows that it is the plural of *walad*, like *asad* (lions) to *asad* (lion), and that he supplicated for his descendants; and that it is a dialectal form for *walad* (child). The poet said:

*Fa-layta Ziyadan kana fi batni ummihi*
*wa-layta Ziyadan kana waladu himar*

(Would that Ziyad had been in his mother's womb, and would that Ziyad had been the offspring of a donkey.)

Just as they said: *al-'adam* and *al-'udm* (both meaning lack). Ibn Jubayr read: *wa-li-walidi* with a silent *ya'*, in the singular, like His words: ﴿And forgive my father﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 86]. The "establishment of the reckoning" (*qiyam al-hisab*) is a metaphor for its occurrence and its being fixed, just as one says: "war has risen on its shank" (*qamat al-harb 'ala saq*). Or it is by omission of a modifier, meaning: the people of the reckoning, as the poet said:

(p-435)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verses 37–43 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And when Abraham said: "My Lord, make this town secure, and keep me and my sons far from worshipping idols."﴾ [Ibrahim: 35] ﴿"My Lord, they have led many of the people astray. Whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ [Ibrahim: 36]

Connection of this verse to what precedes it: when Allah mentioned the reproach directed at those who exchanged the blessing of Allah for disbelief and set up rivals (andad) to Allah, namely the Quraysh and the Arabs who followed them, who took gods besides Allah, and when one of Allah's blessings upon them was His settling them in His sanctuary (haram), He followed this with the mention of their forefather Abraham. He (may the blessings of God be upon him) asked Allah to make Makkah secure, and asked that He keep his sons away from worshipping idols. He settled them and his offspring in His House so that they would worship Him alone with the worship that is most noble, which is prayer (salah), so that they would reflect on the religion of their forefather, and realise that it opposes what they had committed of idol worship, so that they would be restrained and turn back from it. The discussion of His saying here "this town" (al-balad) with the definite article was already covered, while in al-Baqarah it is indefinite.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Here he asked, in the first case, that Allah make it among the towns whose people are safe and do not fear, and in the second case, that it move out of a state of fear it was in to its opposite, safety, as if he said: "It is a fearful town, so make it secure." End of quote. Abraham first prayed for what is in obedience to Allah, namely that the place of the worshipper be safe, where he is not afraid, so that he can worship Allah. Then he prayed a second time that he and his sons be kept away from worshipping idols. The meaning of "keep me and my sons" (wajnubni wa-baniya) is: keep me and them persevering in avoiding the worship of idols. By "my sons" he meant his offspring from his own loins. Allah answered him by making the sanctuary secure, and none of his direct descendants from his own loins worshipped an idol. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, when asked how the Arabs worshipped idols, said: None of the descendants of Isma'il worshipped an idol, and they were eight tribes. They only had stones which they set up and called "a stone" (hajar), so wherever they set up a stone it had the meaning of a house (bayt), and they would circle around that stone and call it "the circling stone" (al-Duwar). End of quote.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: This supplication of the Friend (al-Khalil, peace be upon him) implies his extreme fear for himself, and if one who is in his rank fears that he might worship an idol, then how about others? But this verse should be taken as an example in fear and in seeking a good end. He repeated the call (nida') to win the favour of his Lord, and he mentioned the reason for his request, that he and his sons be kept away from worshipping idols, in His saying: ﴿They have led many of the people astray﴾ [Ibrahim: 36], since he had witnessed his father and his people worshipping idols. The meaning of "they have led astray" (adlalna): we were a cause of the misguidance of many people. The meaning is that they went astray by worshipping them, just as you say: "their trial is the world", that is, they were tempted by it and deceived because of it.

Al-Jahdari and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read: "wa-ajnibni" from ajnaba. He used the feminine form for the idols because it is the plural of what does not reason (ma la ya'qil), and he reports about it using the reports of the feminine, as you say: "al-ajdha' inkasarat" (the trunks were broken). The report about it is a report about the plural of rational male beings, with the waw, and it is a figurative usage (majaz), like His saying: ﴿They have indeed gone far astray﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67]. (Majaz: figurative or metaphorical usage.)

"Whoever follows me": that is, upon my religion and what I am upon. "Then he is of me": he made this because of the very close association and attachment to him, like his (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever cheats us is not of us," meaning not one of the believers. This points to the gravity of cheating, to the degree that it strips the cheater of faith. The meaning is that cheating is not among the characteristics of the people of faith.

"And whoever disobeys me": here there is a semantic antithesis (tibaq ma'nawi), because following is obedience. (Tibaq: antithesis, the juxtaposition of opposites.) His saying: ﴿then indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim: 36].

Muqatil said: "And whoever disobeys me," meaning they oppose shirk. Al-Zamakhshari said: You forgive me what has passed of disobedience when it becomes clear to me and I begin obedience anew. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The apparent meaning of "whoever disobeys me" is disbelief, because it parallels His saying "whoever follows me is of me". If this is so, then His saying "then indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful" means: when they believe. For he meant that Allah forgives every disbeliever, but the manner of expression he used was due to his habit of disciplining himself with good speech, pleasant utterance, and fine courtesy (ﷺ). Likewise, the Prophet of Allah 'Isa (peace be upon him) said: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 118].

**Abu Hayyan on Surah Ibrahim, verses 37–43 (part 2 of 3)**

﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without cultivation, by Your Sacred House, our Lord, that they may establish prayer. So make hearts among people incline toward them, and provide them with fruits, that they may be grateful.﴾ He repeated the call (ya Rabbana) out of eagerness for a response and to show humility and reliance upon Allah the Exalted. He used the first-person plural pronoun because the subject had already been mentioned. He mentioned his sons in his words, "and keep me and my sons away" (verse 35). "Some of my offspring" refers to Isma'il and those born from him. This is because when Hajar gave birth to Isma'il, Sarah became jealous of her. It is narrated that he rode the Buraq, along with Hajar and the infant, and came in one day from al-Sham to Makkah. He settled there, left his son and his maidservant there, and rode back the same day. All of this was by revelation from Allah the Exalted. When he was appointed (to this task), he supplicated with what is contained in this verse. As for how Hajar remained there and what happened to her and to Isma'il in that place, it is found in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, in the books of biography (al-siyar), and elsewhere.

The word "min" (some of) is partitive (lil-tab'id), because Ishaq was in al-Sham. The valley is the area between two mountains, and it is not a requirement for it to have water. He said "without cultivation" because he knew that Allah would not abandon Hajar and her son in that valley, and that He would provide them with water. He looked at the far-reaching outcome, so he said "without cultivation." Had he not known this from Allah the Exalted, he would have said "without water," according to the condition of the valley at that time.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It may be said that the negation of it being a place of cultivation entails the negation of water, since cultivation cannot exist except where water is found. So he negated what results from water, which is cultivation, due to the negation of its cause, which is water.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "In a valley" is the valley of Makkah. "Without cultivation" means that there is never any cultivation in it at all, like His words, ﴿an Arabic Qur'an, without crookedness﴾ (39:28), meaning there is no crookedness in it at all; there is nothing in it but straightness, nothing else. End of quote.

He used *qatt*, which is an adverb that is only used with the past tense, as the governed element of his saying "lā yakūnu" (there is not), though it is not in the past tense. It is in the place of *abadan* (never), which is used with non-past forms (the future).

Apparently, His words "by Your Sacred House" require that the House existed at the time of the supplication. The earlier discussion has preceded this, and the discussion about the House and when it was established has been covered in al-Baqarah and Ali 'Imran. It is described as "sacred" (al-muharram) because it was made inviolable against the Flood, meaning it was prevented from it, just as it is called "ancient" ('atiq) because it was freed from (being taken by tyrants) and so no one took control over it; or because it has always been mighty and protected from tyrants; or because it is respected and its violation is not permitted.

"That they may establish" (li-yuqimu) is connected to "I have settled." "Our Lord" is a parenthetical supplication. The meaning is: this glorious House is never free from worship. It was also said that the lam is the lam of command, meaning he supplicated for them to establish prayer.

Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi said: The lam is connected to His words, ﴿keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ (14:35), "that they may establish prayer." End of quote. This is very far-fetched.

He singled out prayer (al-salah) from among the other acts of worship because it is the most excellent of them, or because it is the cause of every good. His words "that they may establish" use the plural pronoun, indicating that Allah informed him that this child would have descendants there and would have offspring.

*Af'idatan* is the plural of *fu'ad*, meaning hearts. The heart is called *fu'ad* because of its *'it'ad* (being heated/burning), derived from *fa'ada*, and from it comes *al-mufta'ad*, which is the place where fire is kindled where meat is roasted.

Mu'arrij said: *al-af'idah* means the portion of people (in the dialect of the Quraysh), and Ibn Bahr went this way.

Mujahid said: If Ibrahim, peace be upon him, had said *af'idat al-nas* (hearts of people), Persia and Rome would have crowded around the House.

Ibn Jubayr said: The Jews and Christians would have made pilgrimage to it.

The apparent meaning is that "min" is partitive, since the sense is: hearts of (some) people. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible for "min" to be for origin (ibtida'), as when you say, "the heart from me is sick," meaning "my heart." So it is as if it were said: hearts of people. He made the annexed noun indefinite in this example to match the indefiniteness of *af'idah*, because in the verse it is indefinite, so that it encompasses some of the hearts. End of quote.

It does not appear that it is for the beginning of the limit (ibtida' al-ghayah), because there is no action for us in which a starting point leads to an endpoint, since it is not valid to say, as a starting point, "making hearts from people." Rather, the apparent meaning of "min" is partitive.

Hisham read *af'idatan* with a *ya'* after the *hamzah* (af'iyatan). This was explicitly stated by al-Hulwani on his authority. This is explained as *ishba'* (prolonging a vowel), but since *ishba'* occurs only in poetic necessity, some scholars took this reading to mean that Hisham recited with easing the *hamzah* like a *ya'*, so the narrator described it as with a *ya'*. Whoever misunderstood it thought it was a *ya'* after the *hamzah*, but what was meant was a *ya'* in place of the *hamzah*. He said: So this distortion is of the same kind as the distortion attributed to those who narrated from Abu 'Amr: *bari'ukum* and *ya'murukum* and similar, with the vowel of the grammatical case being silenced, and that was (merely) *ikhtilas* (rapid, slurred pronunciation).

Abu 'Amr al-Dani, the memorizer, said: What the proponent of this view mentioned is not relied upon, because the transmitters from Hisham and Abu 'Amr were among the most knowledgeable people about recitation and its variants, and ignorance does not lead them to be attributed with such a thing.

It was recited *aafidatan* (with a long vowel after the first *alif*) on the pattern of *fa'ilatan*, so it is possible that it is an active participle from *afida*, meaning he drew near, approached, and hastened, i.e., groups that are hastening, or groups that are hastening; or that it is the plural of *fu'ad* in the sense of the form of exchange (metathesis, min bab al-qalb). It became *a'fidah* (with the first *hamzah* and the second), then the silent *hamzah* was changed to an *alif*, just as they said for *a'ra'm*: *a'ram*. So its pattern is *a'filah*.

It was also recited *afidatan* on the pattern of *fa'ilatan* (fi'lah), so it is possible that it is the plural of *fu'ad*, by dropping the *hamzah* and moving its vowel to the consonant before it, which is the *fa'*, although easing it between two positions is the preferred form. It is also possible that it is an active participle of *afida*, as you say *fariha*, *fahuwa fari-h* (he is happy).

Umm al-Haytham recited *uf'udatan* with a *kasrah* on the *waw* in place of the *hamzah*. The author of *al-Lawami'* said: It is the plural of *wafd* (delegation), and the reading is good, but I do not know this woman. Rather, Abu Hatim mentioned her. End of quote.

He changed the *hamzah* in *fu'ad* after a *dammah*, as it was changed in *jawn*, then he made it plural and retained it in the plural as it was retained in the singular. It is the plural of *wafd*, as the author of *al-Lawami'* said, and the original form would be *awfadah*, with metathesis. The plural of *fa'l* on the pattern of *af'ilah* is irregular, like *najd* and *anjidah*, and *wahy* and *awhiyah*.

Umm al-Haytham was a woman from whom something of the dialects of the Arabs was transmitted.

Zayd ibn 'Ali recited *ifadatun* on the pattern of *ishara*. It appears that the *hamzah* is a substitute for a *kasrah* on the *waw*, as they said *ishah* for *wishah* (sash), so the pattern is *fi'alah*, meaning: make those who are *wifadah* (delegation). It is also permissible that it is the verbal noun of *afada*, *ifadah*, or people of *ifadah*, meaning those who bring benefit and from whom benefit is gained.

The majority read ﴿tahwi ilayhim﴾, meaning they hasten toward them and fly toward them out of longing and yearning. Since *tahwi* was used with the meaning of *tamil* (incline), it was made to take *ila*, although its original construction is with *lam*. The poet said:

*Until when the hand of the youth fell upon her, she flew, and in his hand some of her feathers remained.*

An example of what is in the verse is the poet's saying:

*She hastens toward Makkah seeking guidance; the believer among the jinn is not like its disbelievers.*

Maslamah ibn 'Abd Allah recited *tuhwa* with a *dammah* on the *ta'*, in the passive voice, from *ahwa*, which is the causative of *hawa* (intransitive), with the causative *hamzah*. As if it were said: he hastens with them toward them.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Muhammad ibn 'Ali, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, and Mujahid recited *tahwa* as the imperfect of *hawa* meaning "to love." Since it was used with the meaning of yearning and inclining, it was made to take *ila*.

﴿And provide them with fruits﴾: along with their residents, in a valley where nothing of them grows, by bringing them from the lands, like His words: ﴿to which the fruits of everything are brought﴾ (28:57). It is narrated from Muslim ibn Muhammad al-Ta'ifi that when he, peace be upon him, supplicated that Allah provide the residents of Makkah with fruits, Allah sent Jibril, peace be upon him, who tore off a piece with his wing from Palestine. It was also said: from al-Urdunn. He brought it and circled it around the House seven times, and placed it near Makkah, and this is al-Ta'if. It was named after this story, and it is the place of the Thaqif, and it has trees and fruits. Something similar was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿That they may be grateful﴾: Al-Zamakhshari said: The blessing is that they are provided with all kinds of fruits present in a valley with no vegetation, no tree, and no water. Indeed, Allah the Mighty and Majestic answered Ibrahim's supplication and made it a secure sanctuary, to which the fruits of everything are brought as provision from Us. Then He favored it in the existence of varieties of fruits in it over every fertile region, over the most fertile and fruitful lands, and in whichever land of the East and West you see the wonder that Allah shows you in a valley without cultivation. This is the gathering of early and various fruits of different seasons—spring, summer, and autumn—in a single day, and that is not strange among His signs.
