If "inna" and what follows it is a parenthetical clause, it does not matter that it separates the governing word from the governed, or that it is an object of "intiqam" — as al-Zamakhshari, al-Hawfi, and Abu al-Baqa' said, first mentioning it. It was read "nubaddilu" with the nun, "al-ardu" in the accusative, and "al-samawat" coordinated with "al-ard", with "ghayr" elided: that is, "other than the heavens", elided because of what precedes it as an indication. The apparent reading is that it is a new sentence, "wa barazu". Abu al-Baqa' said: it is permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from "al-ard", with "qad" implied with it. The meaning of "li-Allah" is: for the judgment of Allah, or for what He promised of the Garden and the Fire. Zayd ibn 'Ali read "wa-buriz" with a damma on the ba' and a kasra on the ra' shaddah, making it passive for the sake of intensity in relation to the world and its multitude, not in relation to the repetition of the verb.

These two attributes were brought: the One, the one who has no partner in His divinity, and by this He alerts that their gods will profit them nothing on that day; and the Overpowering, who prevails over everything. This is like His saying: ﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is Allah's, the One, the Overpowering﴾ [Ghafir: 16].

﴿And you will see the criminals on that day, when they are bound together in chains.﴾ "Muqarranin" means: shackled in fetters; that is, some of them are linked to others in the shackles and iron collars, or to their devils — each disbeliever with his devil in one fetter — or their hands are joined to their feet, bound. The apparent connection is that "fi al-asfad" is attached to "muqarranin", that is, they are yoked in the fetters. It may also be in the position of a qualifier to "muqarranin", and in the position of a circumstantial clause, so it is attached to an elided word, as if it were said: "settled in the fetters." Al-Hasan said: there is in Hell no valley, no wilderness, no shackle, no chain, except that the name of its owner is written upon it.

Ali, Abu Hurayra, Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrima, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Sirin, and al-Hasan (with a variant from him) read — and Sinan ibn Salama ibn al-Muhnaq, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Qatada, Abu Salih, al-Kalbi, 'Isa al-Hamdani, 'Amr ibn Fa'id, and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read — "min qatir", with fathah on the qaf, kasra on the ta', and tanwin on the ra', the active participle of "anna" being an adjective of "qatir". It was said: it is copper-slag (qasdir), and it was said: copper. From Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: it is not tar (al-qatran), but it is copper, which takes on its color. "Ani" means: the molten, hot one whose heat has reached its extreme. Al-Hasan said: Hell has been kindled over it since it was created, so its heat has become extreme. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, it has come time for them to be punished with it; that is, their punishment with it has arrived. Al-Zamakhshari said: and it is in its nature that the fire kindles in it swiftly, and it may be used as fuel; it is black in color and foul in smell, so the skins of the people of the Fire are smeared with it until its coating becomes for them like the sarabil, which are shirts, so that four things gather upon them: the sting and burning of the tar, the swift spreading of the fire over their skins, the dark color, and the foul smell. Yet the difference between these two tars is like the difference between these two fires. Whatever Allah has promised, or threatened in the Hereafter, between it and what one witnesses of its kind there is an incomparable difference, and it is as if what we have of it are only the names and the named things there; so by His vast generosity we seek refuge from His wrath, and we ask Him for success in what saves us from His punishment; end of quote. Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ali ibn Abi Talib read "min qatran", with fathah on the qaf and sukun on the ta', and it occurs in the poetry of Abu al-Najm, who said:

"They clothed them in tar and coarse garments."

The commentary you have given is the continuation of Abu Hayyan's remarks, so I translate it as it stands:

The majority of readers recited ﴿وتَغْشى وُجُوهَهُمْ﴾ (and the fire will cover their faces) with the accusative (naṣb) case, and it was also read with the nominative (rafʿ). The first reading is like His saying: ﴿واللَّيْلِ إذا يَغْشى﴾ (By the night when it covers) [al-Layl: 1]; so it is in the literal sense of covering (ghashayān). The second is in a figurative sense (tajawwuz), for the arrival of the face at the Fire is made into a covering. It was also read: wa-taghsha wujūhahum, meaning tatagghashsha (wa-tataghashsha, "is covered"), and the faces are singled out here. In His saying: ﴿أفَمَن يَتَّقِي بِوَجْهِهِ سُوءَ العَذابِ يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾ (Is one who shields his face from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection...) [al-Zumar: 24], and ﴿يَوْمَ يُسْحَبُونَ في النّارِ عَلى وُجُوهِهِمْ﴾ (The Day they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces) [al-Qamar: 48], the reason is that the face is the most honoured and noblest place on the outer body, like the heart within it; for this reason He said: ﴿تَطَّلِعُ عَلى الأفْئِدَةِ﴾ (It rises over the hearts) [al-Humazah: 7].

The lām in liyajziya (that He may recompense) is connected to an omitted verb whose estimate is: He does to the criminals what He does, so that He may recompense every soul; that is, every soul that is criminal for what it earned, or every soul, both criminal and obedient, since when He punishes the criminals for their crimes it is known that He rewards the obedient for their obedience; this was said by al-Zamakhshari. It appears that it is connected to His saying "and they came forth" (wa-baraza); that is, all of creation, and "every soul" is general, meaning both obedient and criminal, and the sentence "and you see" (wa-tarā) is parenthetical (muʿtaridah). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the lām is connected to an implied verb whose estimate is: He did this, or He executed this punishment upon the criminals, so that He might recompense the wrongdoer for his wrongdoing; end of quote. The reference of "this" (hādhā) is to what Allah mentioned from His saying: ﴿ولا تَحْسَبَنَّ اللَّهَ غافِلًا﴾ (And do not think that Allah is unaware) [Ibrahim: 42] up to His saying: ﴿سَرِيعُ الحِسابِ﴾ (swift in reckoning). It was also said that the reference is to the Qur'an, and it was said to the surah. The meaning of balāgh (a message) is sufficiency in admonition and reminding, and "that they may be warned by it" (wa-liyunḏharū bihi). Al-Mawardi said: the wāw is extra (zāʾidah). From al-Mubarrad: it is a single coordination (ʿaṭf mufrad); that is, "this is a message and a warning"; end of quote. This is an explanation of meaning, not of grammatical analysis (iʿrāb). It was also said: it is carried over to the meaning; that is, "that they may convey and be warned." It was also said: the lām is the lām of command (lām al-amr). One of them said: this is good were it not for His saying "and that they may be reminded" (wa-liyadhdhakkara), for it is simply in the accusative; end of quote. This does not undermine it, since (wa-liyadhdhakkara) need not be coordinated with the command, but rather a verb is implied for it to depend on. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the meaning is "this is a message for mankind, and it is so that they may be warned by it"; end of quote. So he made it in the place of a nominative predicate of the omitted hūwa. Al-Zamakhshari said: "that they may be warned" (wa-liyunḏharū) is coordinated with an omitted element; that is, "that they may be advised and warned by it through this message"; end of quote. Mujahid and Humayd read it with a dammed tāʾ and a kasra on the dhāl (tunḏharū, "you warn"): the message is general, and the warning is for those addressed. Yahya ibn ʿUmarah, from his father al-Dharrāʿ, and Ahmad ibn Zayd ibn Usayd al-Sulami read: wa-liyanḏharū, with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and the dhāl, the imperfect of nadhara bi-l-shay' (to know of a thing and prepare for it). They said: no verbal noun (maṣdar) is known for this verb, so it is like ʿasā and others of the verbs used without a known root. And "that they may know" (wa-liyaʿlamū): for when they fear what they have been warned of, that moves them to reflect, so they arrive at the Oneness of Allah and devotion to Him alone, since fear is the root of good. And "that those of understanding may be reminded" (wa-liyadhdhakkara): that is, may take heed and review themselves in light of the admonitions they have heard. He attributed remembrance and admonition to those who possess intellect (lubb), because they are the ones in whom remembrance is of benefit. It was also said that this refers to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. The ending of this surah corresponds to its opening, and this is frequent in the surahs of the Qur'an, to the extent that some claimed that His saying "and that they may be warned by it" is coordinated with His saying "to bring forth mankind" (litukhrija al-nās).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verses 44–52 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿On the Day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6].

﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do. He only defers them to a Day when eyes will stare fixedly, hastening forward with raised heads, their gaze not returning to them, and their hearts void﴾ [Ibrahim: 42–43]. The address in His words "and do not think" is to the listener who could conceive such a thought because of his ignorance of Allah's attributes, not to the Messenger, for that is impossible in his regard. In this verse there is a great warning to the wrongdoers and consolation to the oppressed. Talha read *wa-la tahsab* ("and do not think") without the emphatic nun (*nun al-tawkid*), and likewise *fa-la tahsab Allaha mukhlifa wa'dihi* ("so do not think that Allah breaks His promise"). The purpose of the prohibition against thinking that He is "unaware" is to announce that He knows what the wrongdoers do, nothing of it is hidden from Him, and that He will punish them for its little and its much, by way of warning and threat, like His words: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283], meaning a warning. It is also possible that the meaning is: "Do not think that He deals with them as one who is unaware of what they do, but rather as a watcher over them who calls them to account for the smallest and the most trivial." 

As-Sulami, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, al-Mufaddal (from ʿAsim), ʿAbbas ibn al-Fadl, Harun al-Ataki and Yunus ibn Habib (from Abu ʿAmr) read *wa-nu'akhkhiruhum* with the nun of majesty (*nun al-ʿaẓama*), while the majority read it with the *ya'* (*yu'akhkhiruhum*), meaning "Allah defers them."

*Muhti'in* ("hastening forward") means hurrying, as said by Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah, and that is out of humiliation and submission, like the hurrying of a captive or one in fear. Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu al-Duha said: "intensely gazing without blinking." Ibn Zayd said: "not raising their heads." Mujahid said: "extending the gaze to the right." Al-Akhfash said: "approaching in order to listen," and he recited:

*Bi-Dijlata dāruhum wa-laqad arāhum*
*bi-Dijlata muhti'īna ilā al-samāʿ*

(Their home is at the Tigris, and indeed I have seen them at the Tigris hastening toward the hearing.)

Al-Hasan said: "*muqni'i ruʾusihim* (raised heads): the faces of people on that day are toward the sky, and no one looks at anyone else." Ibn Jurayj said: "*hawa'* (void): empty of good, hollow of it." Abu ʿUbayda said: "a hollow with no minds in them." Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: "a ruin, hollow, with no good and no intellect in it." Sufyan said: "empty except from the terror of that Day," like His words: ﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became void﴾ [al-Qasas: 10], meaning "except from the anxiety of Moses." *Hawa'* is a pure simile, since they are not literally air. It may be that the comparison lies in their emptiness of hope and desire for mercy, so they are broken, resembling air in its being free of things and its being torn apart. It may also lie in the agitation of their hearts and their surging in the chests, and that they come and go and reach their throats, so they are in that like air, which is always in agitation. The occurrence of these five attributes in the wrongdoers is before the reckoning, as evidenced by their being mentioned after His words: "the Day when the reckoning is established." It has been said: it is at the response of the caller and the rising from the graves. It has also been said: it is at the going of the blessed to Paradise and the wretched to the Fire.

(p. 436) ﴿And warn mankind of the Day when the punishment comes to them, and those who did wrong will say: "Our Lord, defer us to a near term, we will answer Your call and follow the messengers." Had you not sworn before that there would be no decline for you? And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves, and it became clear to you how We dealt with them, and We set forth parables for you﴾.

This is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ). *Yawm* (Day) is in the accusative as a second object of *andhir* ("warn"), and it cannot be a time-adverb, because that Day is not a time for warning. This Day is the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is: "Warn mankind, the wrongdoers," and his words "those who did wrong will say" make this clear, because believers give good tidings and do not warn. It has also been said: the Day is the day of their destruction by immediate punishment, or the day of their death while being tormented by the severity of the agonies, and meeting the angels without good tidings, like His words: ﴿Had You not deferred me to a near term, I would have given charity﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10]. The meaning of deferment to "a near term" is a return to the world, as said by al-Dahhak, since a respite to a limited period of time is near, as said by al-Suddi. That is, so that they may make up for what they neglected of answering the call and following the messengers.

*Aw lam takunu* ("Had you not…") is governed by an implied verb of saying (*idmar al-qawl*), and the apparent meaning is: "It will be said to them." The speaker is either the angels or Allah the Exalted. They are rebuked by this, and their statement denying resurrection and their swearing to it is recalled, as He the Exalted said: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that Allah will not raise up one who dies﴾ [al-Nahl: 38]. The meaning of *ma lakum min zawal* ("there is no decline for you") is from the earth after death; that is, "we will not be raised from the graves." Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: this statement will be made by them while they are in the Fire, and what follows, "Had you not…," is a reply to them, and its meaning is rebuke and reproach.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Aw lam takunu aqsamtum*" is on the intention of saying, and there are two aspects to this: that they say it out of arrogance and wickedness, and because of the habit of ignorance and folly that overcame them; and that they say it by the tongue of their state, since they built strongly and hoped for long. *Ma lakum* is the answer of the oath. It came in the form of direct address because of His words "you swore"; had it reported the words of the swearers, it would have been said *ma lana min zawal* ("there is no decline for us"). The meaning: "You swore that you would remain in the world and not decline by death and annihilation." It was also said: "you would not move to another abode." Here ends al-Zamakhshari. He made *aw lam takunu* a report of their own words, which contradicts what we have explained, that it is said to them. His statement that they "do not decline by death and annihilation" is not good, because they acknowledge death and annihilation. This is also the statement of Mujahid.

*Wa-sakantum*: if it is from *sukun* (stillness), the meaning is that they settled in it and were at rest, content of soul, following the conduct of those before them in wrongdoing and corruption, not relating to them what befell the wrongdoers before them. If it is from *sukna* (dwelling), then *sukna* derives from *sukun*, which is lingering, and its original construction is with *fi* (in), as one says *aqama fi al-dar* ("he stayed in the house") and *qarra fiha* ("he settled in it"). But when it was applied to a specific kind of dwelling it was used transitively, so one says *sakana al-dar* ("he dwelt the house"), as one says *tabawwa'aha* ("he occupied it"). *Wa-tabayyana lakum*: by report and by observation, what We did to them of destruction and retribution became clear to you.

The majority read *wa-tabayyana* as a past-tense verb, with an implied subject indicated by the context, meaning "it became clear to you, that is, their condition." The subject cannot be *kayfa* ("how"), because *kayfa* only occurs as an interrogative or conditional noun, and neither of these is governed by what precedes it, except for the anomalous reports of *ʿala* ("upon") preceding *kayfa* in the saying "ʿala kayfa tabi'u al-ahmarayn" ("on what terms do you sell the two reds"), and *ila* ("to") in the saying "anzur ila kayfa tasna'" ("I look at how you act"). Here *kayfa* is an interrogative about a state, in a position of the accusative governed by *fa'alna* ("We did").

As-Sulami, as reported from him by Abu ʿAmr al-Dani, read *wa-nubayyinu* with a *damma* on the nun and with the final nun in the nominative, the present tense of *bayyana*, and Sahib al-Lawami transmitted it from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him). This is on the supposition of *wa-nahnu nubayyinu* ("and We make clear"), and the clause is in the circumstantial position (*hali*). Al-Mahdawi said, from as-Sulami, that he read so, except that he made the nun jussive (*jazm*), as a conjunction to *aw lam takunu* ("had you not"), meaning "and We did not make clear." Thus he shares in the affirmation.

﴿And We set forth parables for you﴾, that is, the descriptions of what they did and what was done to them, and these are, in their strangeness, like the parables set forth for every wrongdoer.

﴿They have indeed plotted their plot, but their plot is with Allah, though their plot could move mountains from their places﴾ [Ibrahim: 46]. ﴿So do not think that Allah will break His promise to His messengers. Indeed Allah is Mighty, Owner of retribution﴾ [Ibrahim: 47]. ﴿On the Day when the earth will be replaced by another earth, and the heavens too, and they will come out before Allah, the One, the Irresistible﴾ [Ibrahim: 48]. ﴿And you will see the criminals that Day bound together in shackles﴾ [Ibrahim: 49]. ﴿Their garments of tar, and the Fire covering their faces﴾ [Ibrahim: 50]. ﴿That Allah may recompense every soul for what it earned. Indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ [Ibrahim: 51]. ﴿This is a message for mankind, that they may be warned by it, and that they may know that He is only one God, and that people of understanding may be reminded﴾ [Ibrahim: 52].

(p. 437) The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in *makaru* ("they plotted") refers back to the addressees in His words "Had you not sworn before," meaning they plotted by associating partners with Allah and denying the messengers. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the people of the Messenger, as in His words "and warn mankind," meaning: "your people, O Muhammad, have plotted," and this is what is in His words: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30], and so on. The meaning of *makrihim* ("their plot") is the great plot in which they exhausted their effort. The apparent meaning is that this is an announcement from Allah to His Prophet of what issued from them in the world, and it is not spoken in the Hereafter. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "It is possible that it is something said on the Day of Resurrection to the wrongdoers who dwelt in their dwellings." *Wa-ʿinda Allahi makruhum* ("with Allah is their plot") means the knowledge of their plot, so He is aware of it, and He does not let their intention take effect, nor does He make their hope or the recompense of their plot reach them; and their recompense is His punishment for them. The apparent reading is that *makr* (plot), the verbal noun, is in the genitive by the agent, as it is in the first clause, as if it were said: "with Allah is what they plotted, that is, their plot." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It may also be in the genitive by the object, meaning: 'with Allah is their plot which He plots against them, namely their punishment which they deserve, which will come to them from where they do not perceive and do not expect.'" Here ends al-Zamakhshari. This is not correct unless *makr* transitively takes an object by itself, as he said, since he assumed "He plots against them by it"; but what is preserved is that *makara* does not take a direct object by itself. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30], and you say *zaydun mamkurun bihi* ("Zayd is plotted against by it"), but *zaydun mamkurun bi-sabab kadha* ("Zayd is plotted against because of such-and-such") is not attested.

The majority read *wa-in kana* with the nun. ʿAmr, ʿAli, ʿAbd Allah, Ubayy, Abu Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, Abu Ishaq al-Sabiʿi and Zayd ibn ʿAli read *wa-in kada* ("though it nearly") with a *dal* in place of the nun, *li-tazula* with a *fatha* on the first lam and a *damma* on the second, and this reading is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Ibn Wathhab and al-Kisa'i read the same way, except that they read *wa-in kana* with the nun. On these two readings, *in* is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and the lam is the distinguishing lam (*lam al-fariqa*), according to the school of the Basrans. As for the school of the Kufans, *in* is negative and the lam has the sense of *illa* ("except"). Whoever reads *kada* with the *dal* means: the removal of the mountains is near because of their plot, but the removal does not occur. On the reading *kana* with the nun, the removal of the mountains has occurred, and in that is the magnification of their plot and its intensity, such that the mountains would be removed by it and cut off from their places. It is possible that the meaning of *li-tazula* is that their removal is near, so the meaning becomes the same as the meaning of the reading *kada*. This interpretation is supported by what Abu Hatim mentioned, that in the reading of Ubayy there is: "and had it not been for the word of Allah, the mountains would have been removed from their plot." This reading should be taken as an explanation, because it contradicts the consensus of the written text of the codex (*sawad al-mushaf*).

The majority and the rest of the Seven read *wa-in kana* with the nun, *makruhum li-tazula* with a *kasra* on the lam and a *fatha* on the final one. This reading is reported from ʿAli. The grammatical analysis of it has been disputed. According to al-Hasan and a group, *in* is negative, *kana* is complete (*tamma*), and the meaning is: the belittling of their plot, and that it was not such that the laws and prophethoods and the decrees of Allah, which are like mountains in their firmness and strength, would be removed by it. This interpretation is supported by what is reported from Ibn Masʿud, that he read *wa-ma kana* with the negative *ma*. But this interpretation, and what is reported from Ibn Masʿud of reading *wa-ma* with negation, contradicts the readings previously mentioned, because in those is the magnification of their plot, while in this is its belittling. It is possible, on the supposition that it is negative, that *kana* is defective (*naqisa*), the lam is the lam of denial (*lam al-juhud*), and the predicate of *kana* is subject to the disagreement between the Basrans and the Kufans: is it omitted, or is it the verb which the lam entered upon? And on the basis that *in* is negative and *kana* is defective, with the lam in *li-tazula* attached to a verb in the position of the predicate of *kana*, al-Hawfi has derived it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Even if their scheming was such that the mountains would thereby be moved" — even though their scheming was great and was carried to extremes of severity, the image of the mountains' removal being used as a metaphor for its intensity and gravity; that is, even though their scheming was prepared and ready to remove mountains. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible in my view that this reading means the magnification of their scheming; that is, even though it was severe in what they did, such that great affairs would be removed by it," end of quote. On the explanation of these two, (in) is the lightened form of the heavy (inna), and (kana) is the defective verb. On this explanation the meanings of the readings agree or come close, while on the explanation of negation they conflict, as we mentioned. It was also read (litazula) with the first lam fathah and the second lam naṣb, and this is according to the dialect of those who make the lam of (kay) fathah. What appears is that the removal of the mountains is a figure of speech, struck as a parable for the scheming of Quraysh and its enormity, while mountains do not actually move; this is of the category of exaggeration, hyperbole and extravagance in censuring their scheming.

As for what is reported, that a mountain moved because of the oath of a woman whom her husband had accused, and that whoever swore falsely upon that mountain would die, so he brought her to take the oath, and she schemed by throwing herself from the mount, having promised the man she was accused with that he would be at the place where she fell from the mount; so her husband and that man mounted her, and she swore upon the mountain that no one but they two had touched her; so she descended safe, and the mountain had crumbled by morning, and the woman was from 'Adnan — and what is reported of the story of Nimrod or Bukhtnassar, and their taking eagles and ascending on them toward the heaven, in a long story — these are not to be relied upon. Some interpreters explained that by the mountains he meant Islam and the Qur'an, for their firmness and steadfastness, and by their scheming he meant their disagreement about it, from their saying: this is magic, this is poetry, this is falsehood; these are sayings which the apparent wording rejects, and the story of the eagles is very far-fetched.

The prohibition against thinking (al-husban) is like his saying: ﴿And do not think that Allah is heedless﴾ [Ibrahim: 42], and here "thinking" is applied to a matter that is certain, as the poet said:

"So do not think that I am lost to my fate, for every man will taste the cup of death."

This promise is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers﴾ [Ghafir: 51], ﴿Allah has decreed: I and My messengers will surely prevail﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21]. The majority read "mukhlif" with a genitive attachment to "wa'dihi" and the accusative "rusulahu". Its i'rab (grammatical analysis) was disputed. The majority — al-Farra', Qutrub, al-Hawfi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, and Abu al-Baqa' — said: it is of the type in which the active participle is attached to its second object, as in the saying "hadha mu'ti dirhamin Zaydan" ("this is one who gives a dirham to Zayd"); since it transitively takes two objects, it may be attached to either of them, and the one that comes later is put in the accusative. Some cited as a parallel the poet's verse:

"You see the bull with its head placed in the shade, while the rest of it is exposed to the sun entirely."

Abu al-Baqa' said: it is close to their saying "ya sariqa al-laylati ahla al-dar" ("O thief of the night, the people of the house"). Al-Farra' and Qutrub said: since the verb reaches both objects together, the order of precedence and delay does not matter. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: why was it not said 'mukhlif rusulihi wa'dahu', and why was the second object placed before the first? I answer: he placed the promise first so that it would be known that He does not break His promise at all, in accordance with His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not break the appointment﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31]. Then he said: 'His messengers', to indicate that if He does not break His promise to anyone, and breaking promises is not part of His nature, how would His messengers, who are His chosen and purest, break it?" End of quote. This is an answer according to the Mu'tazilite method, that Allah's promise certainly comes to pass, so whoever He promised the Fire to among the disobedient cannot be forgiven at all. The position of the People of the Sunna is that whatever punishment He promised to disobedient believers is conditional upon His will for its execution. It was also said: "mukhlif" here is transitive to one object, as in His saying: ﴿does not break the appointment﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31], so it is attached to it, and "rusulahu" is governed by "wa'dihi", since it is a verbal noun which may be resolved into a verb with a masdar particle, as if he said: "breaking what He promised His messengers", with "ma" being a verbal particle, not in the sense of "alladhi". A group read "mukhlif wa'dahu rusulihi", with "wa'dahu" in the accusative and "mukhlif" attached to "rusulihi", separating the annexed noun from its annexed-to by the object. This is like the reading "qatlu awladihim shuraka'ihim", which was discussed at length in al-An'am. This reading supports the majority's analysis of the first reading, and that "mukhlif" is transitive there to two objects.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty, none can resist Him, and none can overcome Him, Owner of Retribution against the disbelievers, who does not pardon them.﴾

The substitution (al-tabdil) may occur in the essence, that is, one essence passes away and another comes; from it: ﴿We will substitute for them other skins﴾ [al-Nisa: 56], ﴿and We substituted for them their two gardens with two gardens﴾ [Saba: 16]. It may also occur in the attributes, as when you say: "I changed the ring into a seal," where the essence is not lost but has moved from one form to another. They differed about the substitution here: is it in the essence or in the attributes? Ibn 'Abbas said: it will be stretched as a hide is stretched, and its mountains, hills, trees, and everything in it will be removed, until it becomes level, so that you see in it no crookedness or unevenness; and the heavens will be substituted by the folding up of their sun, the scattering of their stars, their splitting open, and the eclipsing of their moon. Ibn Mas'ud said: the earth will be substituted by another earth like pure silver in which no blood has been shed and no sin has been committed; and he said: upon that earth of silver, and the Garden of gold. Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Ibn Jubayr said: it is an earth of bread from which the believers will eat beneath their feet, and this was reported as a marfu' hadith. It was also said: it will become fire while the Garden is behind it, you see its cups and its maidens. Ubayy said: the heavens will become like leather bags. It was also said: its substitution is its folding up. It was also said: once like molten metal, and once like a rose-red wine like oil-dregs, reported by Ibn al-Anbari. It was also said: by its splitting open, so that it casts no shade.

In a hadith: "Indeed Allah will substitute this earth with another earth white and pure, as if it were a loaf of pure bread." In al-Zamakhshari's book, and from 'Ali: the earth will be substituted by an earth of silver and the heavens by gold. From al-Dahhak: an earth of white silver like scrolls. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is that same earth, but it is changed; and he recited:

"The people are not the people you knew, nor is the abode the abode you knew."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: I heard from Ubayy — may Allah be pleased with him — that he related that the substitution happens to the earth, but it is substituted for each group according to its condition: the believer will be on bread from which he eats according to his need, a group will be on silver if the chain is sound regarding it, and the group of disbelievers will be on fire, and similar things; and all of this falls under Allah's power. In a hadith: "The believers at the time of the substitution will be in the shade of the Throne, and it is also said that at that time they will be on the Bridge (al-Sirat)." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: the intended meaning of the substitution of the earth and the heavens is that He, exalted is He, makes the earth into Hell, and makes the heavens into the Garden; the proof is His saying: ﴿Nay, indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 7] and His saying: ﴿Nay, indeed the record of the righteous is in 'Illiyyin﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 18]; end of quote. His words indicate that the Garden and the Fire are not created, while the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and hadith is that both have been created, and it is established in a hadith that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked upon them both, and he could not have truly looked upon them unless they had been created.

﴿And they will come forth﴾, that is, they will appear, ﴿with no building or fortress to shelter them.﴾ The accusative of "yawm" is that it is a substitute for "yawma ya'tihim", as al-Zamakhshari said, or that it is an object of "mukhlif wa'dihi". "Inna" and what follows it is a parenthetical clause, as al-Hawfi said. Abu al-Baqa' said: it cannot be a temporal adverb governed by "mukhlif" nor by "wa'dihi", because what precedes "an" does not govern what follows it; but it is permitted that something of the meaning of the sentence that governs the adverb be supplied, that is: "He does not break His promise on the day when [the earth] is substituted," end of quote. If "inna" and what follows it is a parenthetical clause, it does not matter that it separates the governing word from the governed, or that it is an object of "intiqam" — as al-Zamakhshari, al-Hawfi, and Abu al-Baqa' said, first mentioning it. It was read "nubaddilu" with the nun, "al-ardu" in the accusative, and "al-samawat" coordinated with "al-ard", with "ghayr" elided: that is, "other than the heavens", elided because of what precedes it as an indication. The apparent reading is that it is a new sentence, "wa barazu". Abu al-Baqa' said: it is permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from "al-ard", with "qad" implied with it. The meaning of "li-Allah" is: for the judgment of Allah, or for what He promised of the Garden and the Fire. Zayd ibn 'Ali read "wa-buriz" with a damma on the ba' and a kasra on the ra' shaddah, making it passive for the sake of intensity in relation to the world and its multitude, not in relation to the repetition of the verb.

These two attributes were brought: the One, the one who has no partner in His divinity, and by this He alerts that their gods will profit them nothing on that day; and the Overpowering, who prevails over everything. This is like His saying: ﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is Allah's, the One, the Overpowering﴾ [Ghafir: 16].

﴿And you will see the criminals on that day, when they are bound together in chains.﴾ "Muqarranin" means: shackled in fetters; that is, some of them are linked to others in the shackles and iron collars, or to their devils — each disbeliever with his devil in one fetter — or their hands are joined to their feet, bound. The apparent connection is that "fi al-asfad" is attached to "muqarranin", that is, they are yoked in the fetters. It may also be in the position of a qualifier to "muqarranin", and in the position of a circumstantial clause, so it is attached to an elided word, as if it were said: "settled in the fetters." Al-Hasan said: there is in Hell no valley, no wilderness, no shackle, no chain, except that the name of its owner is written upon it.

Ali, Abu Hurayra, Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrima, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Sirin, and al-Hasan (with a variant from him) read — and Sinan ibn Salama ibn al-Muhnaq, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Qatada, Abu Salih, al-Kalbi, 'Isa al-Hamdani, 'Amr ibn Fa'id, and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read — "min qatir", with fathah on the qaf, kasra on the ta', and tanwin on the ra', the active participle of "anna" being an adjective of "qatir". It was said: it is copper-slag (qasdir), and it was said: copper. From Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: it is not tar (al-qatran), but it is copper, which takes on its color. "Ani" means: the molten, hot one whose heat has reached its extreme. Al-Hasan said: Hell has been kindled over it since it was created, so its heat has become extreme. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, it has come time for them to be punished with it; that is, their punishment with it has arrived. Al-Zamakhshari said: and it is in its nature that the fire kindles in it swiftly, and it may be used as fuel; it is black in color and foul in smell, so the skins of the people of the Fire are smeared with it until its coating becomes for them like the sarabil, which are shirts, so that four things gather upon them: the sting and burning of the tar, the swift spreading of the fire over their skins, the dark color, and the foul smell. Yet the difference between these two tars is like the difference between these two fires. Whatever Allah has promised, or threatened in the Hereafter, between it and what one witnesses of its kind there is an incomparable difference, and it is as if what we have of it are only the names and the named things there; so by His vast generosity we seek refuge from His wrath, and we ask Him for success in what saves us from His punishment; end of quote. Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ali ibn Abi Talib read "min qatran", with fathah on the qaf and sukun on the ta', and it occurs in the poetry of Abu al-Najm, who said:

"They clothed them in tar and coarse garments."

The commentary you have given is the continuation of Abu Hayyan's remarks, so I translate it as it stands:

The majority of readers recited ﴿وتَغْشى وُجُوهَهُمْ﴾ (and the fire will cover their faces) with the accusative (naṣb) case, and it was also read with the nominative (rafʿ). The first reading is like His saying: ﴿واللَّيْلِ إذا يَغْشى﴾ (By the night when it covers) [al-Layl: 1]; so it is in the literal sense of covering (ghashayān). The second is in a figurative sense (tajawwuz), for the arrival of the face at the Fire is made into a covering. It was also read: wa-taghsha wujūhahum, meaning tatagghashsha (wa-tataghashsha, "is covered"), and the faces are singled out here. In His saying: ﴿أفَمَن يَتَّقِي بِوَجْهِهِ سُوءَ العَذابِ يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾ (Is one who shields his face from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection...) [al-Zumar: 24], and ﴿يَوْمَ يُسْحَبُونَ في النّارِ عَلى وُجُوهِهِمْ﴾ (The Day they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces) [al-Qamar: 48], the reason is that the face is the most honoured and noblest place on the outer body, like the heart within it; for this reason He said: ﴿تَطَّلِعُ عَلى الأفْئِدَةِ﴾ (It rises over the hearts) [al-Humazah: 7].

The lām in liyajziya (that He may recompense) is connected to an omitted verb whose estimate is: He does to the criminals what He does, so that He may recompense every soul; that is, every soul that is criminal for what it earned, or every soul, both criminal and obedient, since when He punishes the criminals for their crimes it is known that He rewards the obedient for their obedience; this was said by al-Zamakhshari. It appears that it is connected to His saying "and they came forth" (wa-baraza); that is, all of creation, and "every soul" is general, meaning both obedient and criminal, and the sentence "and you see" (wa-tarā) is parenthetical (muʿtaridah). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the lām is connected to an implied verb whose estimate is: He did this, or He executed this punishment upon the criminals, so that He might recompense the wrongdoer for his wrongdoing; end of quote. The reference of "this" (hādhā) is to what Allah mentioned from His saying: ﴿ولا تَحْسَبَنَّ اللَّهَ غافِلًا﴾ (And do not think that Allah is unaware) [Ibrahim: 42] up to His saying: ﴿سَرِيعُ الحِسابِ﴾ (swift in reckoning). It was also said that the reference is to the Qur'an, and it was said to the surah. The meaning of balāgh (a message) is sufficiency in admonition and reminding, and "that they may be warned by it" (wa-liyunḏharū bihi). Al-Mawardi said: the wāw is extra (zāʾidah). From al-Mubarrad: it is a single coordination (ʿaṭf mufrad); that is, "this is a message and a warning"; end of quote. This is an explanation of meaning, not of grammatical analysis (iʿrāb). It was also said: it is carried over to the meaning; that is, "that they may convey and be warned." It was also said: the lām is the lām of command (lām al-amr). One of them said: this is good were it not for His saying "and that they may be reminded" (wa-liyadhdhakkara), for it is simply in the accusative; end of quote. This does not undermine it, since (wa-liyadhdhakkara) need not be coordinated with the command, but rather a verb is implied for it to depend on. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the meaning is "this is a message for mankind, and it is so that they may be warned by it"; end of quote. So he made it in the place of a nominative predicate of the omitted hūwa. Al-Zamakhshari said: "that they may be warned" (wa-liyunḏharū) is coordinated with an omitted element; that is, "that they may be advised and warned by it through this message"; end of quote. Mujahid and Humayd read it with a dammed tāʾ and a kasra on the dhāl (tunḏharū, "you warn"): the message is general, and the warning is for those addressed. Yahya ibn ʿUmarah, from his father al-Dharrāʿ, and Ahmad ibn Zayd ibn Usayd al-Sulami read: wa-liyanḏharū, with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and the dhāl, the imperfect of nadhara bi-l-shay' (to know of a thing and prepare for it). They said: no verbal noun (maṣdar) is known for this verb, so it is like ʿasā and others of the verbs used without a known root. And "that they may know" (wa-liyaʿlamū): for when they fear what they have been warned of, that moves them to reflect, so they arrive at the Oneness of Allah and devotion to Him alone, since fear is the root of good. And "that those of understanding may be reminded" (wa-liyadhdhakkara): that is, may take heed and review themselves in light of the admonitions they have heard. He attributed remembrance and admonition to those who possess intellect (lubb), because they are the ones in whom remembrance is of benefit. It was also said that this refers to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. The ending of this surah corresponds to its opening, and this is frequent in the surahs of the Qur'an, to the extent that some claimed that His saying "and that they may be warned by it" is coordinated with His saying "to bring forth mankind" (litukhrija al-nās).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verses 44–52 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿On the Day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6].

﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do. He only defers them to a Day when eyes will stare fixedly, hastening forward with raised heads, their gaze not returning to them, and their hearts void﴾ [Ibrahim: 42–43]. The address in His words "and do not think" is to the listener who could conceive such a thought because of his ignorance of Allah's attributes, not to the Messenger, for that is impossible in his regard. In this verse there is a great warning to the wrongdoers and consolation to the oppressed. Talha read *wa-la tahsab* ("and do not think") without the emphatic nun (*nun al-tawkid*), and likewise *fa-la tahsab Allaha mukhlifa wa'dihi* ("so do not think that Allah breaks His promise"). The purpose of the prohibition against thinking that He is "unaware" is to announce that He knows what the wrongdoers do, nothing of it is hidden from Him, and that He will punish them for its little and its much, by way of warning and threat, like His words: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283], meaning a warning. It is also possible that the meaning is: "Do not think that He deals with them as one who is unaware of what they do, but rather as a watcher over them who calls them to account for the smallest and the most trivial." 

As-Sulami, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, al-Mufaddal (from ʿAsim), ʿAbbas ibn al-Fadl, Harun al-Ataki and Yunus ibn Habib (from Abu ʿAmr) read *wa-nu'akhkhiruhum* with the nun of majesty (*nun al-ʿaẓama*), while the majority read it with the *ya'* (*yu'akhkhiruhum*), meaning "Allah defers them."

*Muhti'in* ("hastening forward") means hurrying, as said by Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah, and that is out of humiliation and submission, like the hurrying of a captive or one in fear. Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu al-Duha said: "intensely gazing without blinking." Ibn Zayd said: "not raising their heads." Mujahid said: "extending the gaze to the right." Al-Akhfash said: "approaching in order to listen," and he recited:

*Bi-Dijlata dāruhum wa-laqad arāhum*
*bi-Dijlata muhti'īna ilā al-samāʿ*

(Their home is at the Tigris, and indeed I have seen them at the Tigris hastening toward the hearing.)

Al-Hasan said: "*muqni'i ruʾusihim* (raised heads): the faces of people on that day are toward the sky, and no one looks at anyone else." Ibn Jurayj said: "*hawa'* (void): empty of good, hollow of it." Abu ʿUbayda said: "a hollow with no minds in them." Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: "a ruin, hollow, with no good and no intellect in it." Sufyan said: "empty except from the terror of that Day," like His words: ﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became void﴾ [al-Qasas: 10], meaning "except from the anxiety of Moses." *Hawa'* is a pure simile, since they are not literally air. It may be that the comparison lies in their emptiness of hope and desire for mercy, so they are broken, resembling air in its being free of things and its being torn apart. It may also lie in the agitation of their hearts and their surging in the chests, and that they come and go and reach their throats, so they are in that like air, which is always in agitation. The occurrence of these five attributes in the wrongdoers is before the reckoning, as evidenced by their being mentioned after His words: "the Day when the reckoning is established." It has been said: it is at the response of the caller and the rising from the graves. It has also been said: it is at the going of the blessed to Paradise and the wretched to the Fire.

(p. 436) ﴿And warn mankind of the Day when the punishment comes to them, and those who did wrong will say: "Our Lord, defer us to a near term, we will answer Your call and follow the messengers." Had you not sworn before that there would be no decline for you? And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves, and it became clear to you how We dealt with them, and We set forth parables for you﴾.

This is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ). *Yawm* (Day) is in the accusative as a second object of *andhir* ("warn"), and it cannot be a time-adverb, because that Day is not a time for warning. This Day is the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is: "Warn mankind, the wrongdoers," and his words "those who did wrong will say" make this clear, because believers give good tidings and do not warn. It has also been said: the Day is the day of their destruction by immediate punishment, or the day of their death while being tormented by the severity of the agonies, and meeting the angels without good tidings, like His words: ﴿Had You not deferred me to a near term, I would have given charity﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10]. The meaning of deferment to "a near term" is a return to the world, as said by al-Dahhak, since a respite to a limited period of time is near, as said by al-Suddi. That is, so that they may make up for what they neglected of answering the call and following the messengers.

*Aw lam takunu* ("Had you not…") is governed by an implied verb of saying (*idmar al-qawl*), and the apparent meaning is: "It will be said to them." The speaker is either the angels or Allah the Exalted. They are rebuked by this, and their statement denying resurrection and their swearing to it is recalled, as He the Exalted said: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that Allah will not raise up one who dies﴾ [al-Nahl: 38]. The meaning of *ma lakum min zawal* ("there is no decline for you") is from the earth after death; that is, "we will not be raised from the graves." Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: this statement will be made by them while they are in the Fire, and what follows, "Had you not…," is a reply to them, and its meaning is rebuke and reproach.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Aw lam takunu aqsamtum*" is on the intention of saying, and there are two aspects to this: that they say it out of arrogance and wickedness, and because of the habit of ignorance and folly that overcame them; and that they say it by the tongue of their state, since they built strongly and hoped for long. *Ma lakum* is the answer of the oath. It came in the form of direct address because of His words "you swore"; had it reported the words of the swearers, it would have been said *ma lana min zawal* ("there is no decline for us"). The meaning: "You swore that you would remain in the world and not decline by death and annihilation." It was also said: "you would not move to another abode." Here ends al-Zamakhshari. He made *aw lam takunu* a report of their own words, which contradicts what we have explained, that it is said to them. His statement that they "do not decline by death and annihilation" is not good, because they acknowledge death and annihilation. This is also the statement of Mujahid.

*Wa-sakantum*: if it is from *sukun* (stillness), the meaning is that they settled in it and were at rest, content of soul, following the conduct of those before them in wrongdoing and corruption, not relating to them what befell the wrongdoers before them. If it is from *sukna* (dwelling), then *sukna* derives from *sukun*, which is lingering, and its original construction is with *fi* (in), as one says *aqama fi al-dar* ("he stayed in the house") and *qarra fiha* ("he settled in it"). But when it was applied to a specific kind of dwelling it was used transitively, so one says *sakana al-dar* ("he dwelt the house"), as one says *tabawwa'aha* ("he occupied it"). *Wa-tabayyana lakum*: by report and by observation, what We did to them of destruction and retribution became clear to you.

The majority read *wa-tabayyana* as a past-tense verb, with an implied subject indicated by the context, meaning "it became clear to you, that is, their condition." The subject cannot be *kayfa* ("how"), because *kayfa* only occurs as an interrogative or conditional noun, and neither of these is governed by what precedes it, except for the anomalous reports of *ʿala* ("upon") preceding *kayfa* in the saying "ʿala kayfa tabi'u al-ahmarayn" ("on what terms do you sell the two reds"), and *ila* ("to") in the saying "anzur ila kayfa tasna'" ("I look at how you act"). Here *kayfa* is an interrogative about a state, in a position of the accusative governed by *fa'alna* ("We did").

As-Sulami, as reported from him by Abu ʿAmr al-Dani, read *wa-nubayyinu* with a *damma* on the nun and with the final nun in the nominative, the present tense of *bayyana*, and Sahib al-Lawami transmitted it from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him). This is on the supposition of *wa-nahnu nubayyinu* ("and We make clear"), and the clause is in the circumstantial position (*hali*). Al-Mahdawi said, from as-Sulami, that he read so, except that he made the nun jussive (*jazm*), as a conjunction to *aw lam takunu* ("had you not"), meaning "and We did not make clear." Thus he shares in the affirmation.

﴿And We set forth parables for you﴾, that is, the descriptions of what they did and what was done to them, and these are, in their strangeness, like the parables set forth for every wrongdoer.

﴿They have indeed plotted their plot, but their plot is with Allah, though their plot could move mountains from their places﴾ [Ibrahim: 46]. ﴿So do not think that Allah will break His promise to His messengers. Indeed Allah is Mighty, Owner of retribution﴾ [Ibrahim: 47]. ﴿On the Day when the earth will be replaced by another earth, and the heavens too, and they will come out before Allah, the One, the Irresistible﴾ [Ibrahim: 48]. ﴿And you will see the criminals that Day bound together in shackles﴾ [Ibrahim: 49]. ﴿Their garments of tar, and the Fire covering their faces﴾ [Ibrahim: 50]. ﴿That Allah may recompense every soul for what it earned. Indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ [Ibrahim: 51]. ﴿This is a message for mankind, that they may be warned by it, and that they may know that He is only one God, and that people of understanding may be reminded﴾ [Ibrahim: 52].

(p. 437) The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in *makaru* ("they plotted") refers back to the addressees in His words "Had you not sworn before," meaning they plotted by associating partners with Allah and denying the messengers. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the people of the Messenger, as in His words "and warn mankind," meaning: "your people, O Muhammad, have plotted," and this is what is in His words: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30], and so on. The meaning of *makrihim* ("their plot") is the great plot in which they exhausted their effort. The apparent meaning is that this is an announcement from Allah to His Prophet of what issued from them in the world, and it is not spoken in the Hereafter. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "It is possible that it is something said on the Day of Resurrection to the wrongdoers who dwelt in their dwellings." *Wa-ʿinda Allahi makruhum* ("with Allah is their plot") means the knowledge of their plot, so He is aware of it, and He does not let their intention take effect, nor does He make their hope or the recompense of their plot reach them; and their recompense is His punishment for them. The apparent reading is that *makr* (plot), the verbal noun, is in the genitive by the agent, as it is in the first clause, as if it were said: "with Allah is what they plotted, that is, their plot." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It may also be in the genitive by the object, meaning: 'with Allah is their plot which He plots against them, namely their punishment which they deserve, which will come to them from where they do not perceive and do not expect.'" Here ends al-Zamakhshari. This is not correct unless *makr* transitively takes an object by itself, as he said, since he assumed "He plots against them by it"; but what is preserved is that *makara* does not take a direct object by itself. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30], and you say *zaydun mamkurun bihi* ("Zayd is plotted against by it"), but *zaydun mamkurun bi-sabab kadha* ("Zayd is plotted against because of such-and-such") is not attested.

The majority read *wa-in kana* with the nun. ʿAmr, ʿAli, ʿAbd Allah, Ubayy, Abu Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, Abu Ishaq al-Sabiʿi and Zayd ibn ʿAli read *wa-in kada* ("though it nearly") with a *dal* in place of the nun, *li-tazula* with a *fatha* on the first lam and a *damma* on the second, and this reading is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Ibn Wathhab and al-Kisa'i read the same way, except that they read *wa-in kana* with the nun. On these two readings, *in* is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and the lam is the distinguishing lam (*lam al-fariqa*), according to the school of the Basrans. As for the school of the Kufans, *in* is negative and the lam has the sense of *illa* ("except"). Whoever reads *kada* with the *dal* means: the removal of the mountains is near because of their plot, but the removal does not occur. On the reading *kana* with the nun, the removal of the mountains has occurred, and in that is the magnification of their plot and its intensity, such that the mountains would be removed by it and cut off from their places. It is possible that the meaning of *li-tazula* is that their removal is near, so the meaning becomes the same as the meaning of the reading *kada*. This interpretation is supported by what Abu Hatim mentioned, that in the reading of Ubayy there is: "and had it not been for the word of Allah, the mountains would have been removed from their plot." This reading should be taken as an explanation, because it contradicts the consensus of the written text of the codex (*sawad al-mushaf*).

The majority and the rest of the Seven read *wa-in kana* with the nun, *makruhum li-tazula* with a *kasra* on the lam and a *fatha* on the final one. This reading is reported from ʿAli. The grammatical analysis of it has been disputed. According to al-Hasan and a group, *in* is negative, *kana* is complete (*tamma*), and the meaning is: the belittling of their plot, and that it was not such that the laws and prophethoods and the decrees of Allah, which are like mountains in their firmness and strength, would be removed by it. This interpretation is supported by what is reported from Ibn Masʿud, that he read *wa-ma kana* with the negative *ma*. But this interpretation, and what is reported from Ibn Masʿud of reading *wa-ma* with negation, contradicts the readings previously mentioned, because in those is the magnification of their plot, while in this is its belittling. It is possible, on the supposition that it is negative, that *kana* is defective (*naqisa*), the lam is the lam of denial (*lam al-juhud*), and the predicate of *kana* is subject to the disagreement between the Basrans and the Kufans: is it omitted, or is it the verb which the lam entered upon? And on the basis that *in* is negative and *kana* is defective, with the lam in *li-tazula* attached to a verb in the position of the predicate of *kana*, al-Hawfi has derived it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Even if their scheming was such that the mountains would thereby be moved" — even though their scheming was great and was carried to extremes of severity, the image of the mountains' removal being used as a metaphor for its intensity and gravity; that is, even though their scheming was prepared and ready to remove mountains. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible in my view that this reading means the magnification of their scheming; that is, even though it was severe in what they did, such that great affairs would be removed by it," end of quote. On the explanation of these two, (in) is the lightened form of the heavy (inna), and (kana) is the defective verb. On this explanation the meanings of the readings agree or come close, while on the explanation of negation they conflict, as we mentioned. It was also read (litazula) with the first lam fathah and the second lam naṣb, and this is according to the dialect of those who make the lam of (kay) fathah. What appears is that the removal of the mountains is a figure of speech, struck as a parable for the scheming of Quraysh and its enormity, while mountains do not actually move; this is of the category of exaggeration, hyperbole and extravagance in censuring their scheming.

As for what is reported, that a mountain moved because of the oath of a woman whom her husband had accused, and that whoever swore falsely upon that mountain would die, so he brought her to take the oath, and she schemed by throwing herself from the mount, having promised the man she was accused with that he would be at the place where she fell from the mount; so her husband and that man mounted her, and she swore upon the mountain that no one but they two had touched her; so she descended safe, and the mountain had crumbled by morning, and the woman was from 'Adnan — and what is reported of the story of Nimrod or Bukhtnassar, and their taking eagles and ascending on them toward the heaven, in a long story — these are not to be relied upon. Some interpreters explained that by the mountains he meant Islam and the Qur'an, for their firmness and steadfastness, and by their scheming he meant their disagreement about it, from their saying: this is magic, this is poetry, this is falsehood; these are sayings which the apparent wording rejects, and the story of the eagles is very far-fetched.

The prohibition against thinking (al-husban) is like his saying: ﴿And do not think that Allah is heedless﴾ [Ibrahim: 42], and here "thinking" is applied to a matter that is certain, as the poet said:

"So do not think that I am lost to my fate, for every man will taste the cup of death."

This promise is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers﴾ [Ghafir: 51], ﴿Allah has decreed: I and My messengers will surely prevail﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21]. The majority read "mukhlif" with a genitive attachment to "wa'dihi" and the accusative "rusulahu". Its i'rab (grammatical analysis) was disputed. The majority — al-Farra', Qutrub, al-Hawfi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, and Abu al-Baqa' — said: it is of the type in which the active participle is attached to its second object, as in the saying "hadha mu'ti dirhamin Zaydan" ("this is one who gives a dirham to Zayd"); since it transitively takes two objects, it may be attached to either of them, and the one that comes later is put in the accusative. Some cited as a parallel the poet's verse:

"You see the bull with its head placed in the shade, while the rest of it is exposed to the sun entirely."

Abu al-Baqa' said: it is close to their saying "ya sariqa al-laylati ahla al-dar" ("O thief of the night, the people of the house"). Al-Farra' and Qutrub said: since the verb reaches both objects together, the order of precedence and delay does not matter. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: why was it not said 'mukhlif rusulihi wa'dahu', and why was the second object placed before the first? I answer: he placed the promise first so that it would be known that He does not break His promise at all, in accordance with His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not break the appointment﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31]. Then he said: 'His messengers', to indicate that if He does not break His promise to anyone, and breaking promises is not part of His nature, how would His messengers, who are His chosen and purest, break it?" End of quote. This is an answer according to the Mu'tazilite method, that Allah's promise certainly comes to pass, so whoever He promised the Fire to among the disobedient cannot be forgiven at all. The position of the People of the Sunna is that whatever punishment He promised to disobedient believers is conditional upon His will for its execution. It was also said: "mukhlif" here is transitive to one object, as in His saying: ﴿does not break the appointment﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31], so it is attached to it, and "rusulahu" is governed by "wa'dihi", since it is a verbal noun which may be resolved into a verb with a masdar particle, as if he said: "breaking what He promised His messengers", with "ma" being a verbal particle, not in the sense of "alladhi". A group read "mukhlif wa'dahu rusulihi", with "wa'dahu" in the accusative and "mukhlif" attached to "rusulihi", separating the annexed noun from its annexed-to by the object. This is like the reading "qatlu awladihim shuraka'ihim", which was discussed at length in al-An'am. This reading supports the majority's analysis of the first reading, and that "mukhlif" is transitive there to two objects.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty, none can resist Him, and none can overcome Him, Owner of Retribution against the disbelievers, who does not pardon them.﴾

The substitution (al-tabdil) may occur in the essence, that is, one essence passes away and another comes; from it: ﴿We will substitute for them other skins﴾ [al-Nisa: 56], ﴿and We substituted for them their two gardens with two gardens﴾ [Saba: 16]. It may also occur in the attributes, as when you say: "I changed the ring into a seal," where the essence is not lost but has moved from one form to another. They differed about the substitution here: is it in the essence or in the attributes? Ibn 'Abbas said: it will be stretched as a hide is stretched, and its mountains, hills, trees, and everything in it will be removed, until it becomes level, so that you see in it no crookedness or unevenness; and the heavens will be substituted by the folding up of their sun, the scattering of their stars, their splitting open, and the eclipsing of their moon. Ibn Mas'ud said: the earth will be substituted by another earth like pure silver in which no blood has been shed and no sin has been committed; and he said: upon that earth of silver, and the Garden of gold. Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Ibn Jubayr said: it is an earth of bread from which the believers will eat beneath their feet, and this was reported as a marfu' hadith. It was also said: it will become fire while the Garden is behind it, you see its cups and its maidens. Ubayy said: the heavens will become like leather bags. It was also said: its substitution is its folding up. It was also said: once like molten metal, and once like a rose-red wine like oil-dregs, reported by Ibn al-Anbari. It was also said: by its splitting open, so that it casts no shade.

In a hadith: "Indeed Allah will substitute this earth with another earth white and pure, as if it were a loaf of pure bread." In al-Zamakhshari's book, and from 'Ali: the earth will be substituted by an earth of silver and the heavens by gold. From al-Dahhak: an earth of white silver like scrolls. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is that same earth, but it is changed; and he recited:

"The people are not the people you knew, nor is the abode the abode you knew."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: I heard from Ubayy — may Allah be pleased with him — that he related that the substitution happens to the earth, but it is substituted for each group according to its condition: the believer will be on bread from which he eats according to his need, a group will be on silver if the chain is sound regarding it, and the group of disbelievers will be on fire, and similar things; and all of this falls under Allah's power. In a hadith: "The believers at the time of the substitution will be in the shade of the Throne, and it is also said that at that time they will be on the Bridge (al-Sirat)." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: the intended meaning of the substitution of the earth and the heavens is that He, exalted is He, makes the earth into Hell, and makes the heavens into the Garden; the proof is His saying: ﴿Nay, indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 7] and His saying: ﴿Nay, indeed the record of the righteous is in 'Illiyyin﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 18]; end of quote. His words indicate that the Garden and the Fire are not created, while the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and hadith is that both have been created, and it is established in a hadith that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked upon them both, and he could not have truly looked upon them unless they had been created.

﴿And they will come forth﴾, that is, they will appear, ﴿with no building or fortress to shelter them.﴾ The accusative of "yawm" is that it is a substitute for "yawma ya'tihim", as al-Zamakhshari said, or that it is an object of "mukhlif wa'dihi". "Inna" and what follows it is a parenthetical clause, as al-Hawfi said. Abu al-Baqa' said: it cannot be a temporal adverb governed by "mukhlif" nor by "wa'dihi", because what precedes "an" does not govern what follows it; but it is permitted that something of the meaning of the sentence that governs the adverb be supplied, that is: "He does not break His promise on the day when [the earth] is substituted," end of quote. If "inna" and what follows it is a parenthetical clause, it does not matter that it separates the governing word from the governed, or that it is an object of "intiqam" — as al-Zamakhshari, al-Hawfi, and Abu al-Baqa' said, first mentioning it. It was read "nubaddilu" with the nun, "al-ardu" in the accusative, and "al-samawat" coordinated with "al-ard", with "ghayr" elided: that is, "other than the heavens", elided because of what precedes it as an indication. The apparent reading is that it is a new sentence, "wa barazu". Abu al-Baqa' said: it is permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from "al-ard", with "qad" implied with it. The meaning of "li-Allah" is: for the judgment of Allah, or for what He promised of the Garden and the Fire. Zayd ibn 'Ali read "wa-buriz" with a damma on the ba' and a kasra on the ra' shaddah, making it passive for the sake of intensity in relation to the world and its multitude, not in relation to the repetition of the verb.

These two attributes were brought: the One, the one who has no partner in His divinity, and by this He alerts that their gods will profit them nothing on that day; and the Overpowering, who prevails over everything. This is like His saying: ﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is Allah's, the One, the Overpowering﴾ [Ghafir: 16].

﴿And you will see the criminals on that day, when they are bound together in chains.﴾ "Muqarranin" means: shackled in fetters; that is, some of them are linked to others in the shackles and iron collars, or to their devils — each disbeliever with his devil in one fetter — or their hands are joined to their feet, bound. The apparent connection is that "fi al-asfad" is attached to "muqarranin", that is, they are yoked in the fetters. It may also be in the position of a qualifier to "muqarranin", and in the position of a circumstantial clause, so it is attached to an elided word, as if it were said: "settled in the fetters." Al-Hasan said: there is in Hell no valley, no wilderness, no shackle, no chain, except that the name of its owner is written upon it.

Ali, Abu Hurayra, Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrima, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Sirin, and al-Hasan (with a variant from him) read — and Sinan ibn Salama ibn al-Muhnaq, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Qatada, Abu Salih, al-Kalbi, 'Isa al-Hamdani, 'Amr ibn Fa'id, and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read — "min qatir", with fathah on the qaf, kasra on the ta', and tanwin on the ra', the active participle of "anna" being an adjective of "qatir". It was said: it is copper-slag (qasdir), and it was said: copper. From Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: it is not tar (al-qatran), but it is copper, which takes on its color. "Ani" means: the molten, hot one whose heat has reached its extreme. Al-Hasan said: Hell has been kindled over it since it was created, so its heat has become extreme. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, it has come time for them to be punished with it; that is, their punishment with it has arrived. Al-Zamakhshari said: and it is in its nature that the fire kindles in it swiftly, and it may be used as fuel; it is black in color and foul in smell, so the skins of the people of the Fire are smeared with it until its coating becomes for them like the sarabil, which are shirts, so that four things gather upon them: the sting and burning of the tar, the swift spreading of the fire over their skins, the dark color, and the foul smell. Yet the difference between these two tars is like the difference between these two fires. Whatever Allah has promised, or threatened in the Hereafter, between it and what one witnesses of its kind there is an incomparable difference, and it is as if what we have of it are only the names and the named things there; so by His vast generosity we seek refuge from His wrath, and we ask Him for success in what saves us from His punishment; end of quote. Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ali ibn Abi Talib read "min qatran", with fathah on the qaf and sukun on the ta', and it occurs in the poetry of Abu al-Najm, who said:

"They clothed them in tar and coarse garments."

The commentary you have given is the continuation of Abu Hayyan's remarks, so I translate it as it stands:

The majority of readers recited ﴿وتَغْشى وُجُوهَهُمْ﴾ (and the fire will cover their faces) with the accusative (naṣb) case, and it was also read with the nominative (rafʿ). The first reading is like His saying: ﴿واللَّيْلِ إذا يَغْشى﴾ (By the night when it covers) [al-Layl: 1]; so it is in the literal sense of covering (ghashayān). The second is in a figurative sense (tajawwuz), for the arrival of the face at the Fire is made into a covering. It was also read: wa-taghsha wujūhahum, meaning tatagghashsha (wa-tataghashsha, "is covered"), and the faces are singled out here. In His saying: ﴿أفَمَن يَتَّقِي بِوَجْهِهِ سُوءَ العَذابِ يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾ (Is one who shields his face from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection...) [al-Zumar: 24], and ﴿يَوْمَ يُسْحَبُونَ في النّارِ عَلى وُجُوهِهِمْ﴾ (The Day they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces) [al-Qamar: 48], the reason is that the face is the most honoured and noblest place on the outer body, like the heart within it; for this reason He said: ﴿تَطَّلِعُ عَلى الأفْئِدَةِ﴾ (It rises over the hearts) [al-Humazah: 7].

The lām in liyajziya (that He may recompense) is connected to an omitted verb whose estimate is: He does to the criminals what He does, so that He may recompense every soul; that is, every soul that is criminal for what it earned, or every soul, both criminal and obedient, since when He punishes the criminals for their crimes it is known that He rewards the obedient for their obedience; this was said by al-Zamakhshari. It appears that it is connected to His saying "and they came forth" (wa-baraza); that is, all of creation, and "every soul" is general, meaning both obedient and criminal, and the sentence "and you see" (wa-tarā) is parenthetical (muʿtaridah). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the lām is connected to an implied verb whose estimate is: He did this, or He executed this punishment upon the criminals, so that He might recompense the wrongdoer for his wrongdoing; end of quote. The reference of "this" (hādhā) is to what Allah mentioned from His saying: ﴿ولا تَحْسَبَنَّ اللَّهَ غافِلًا﴾ (And do not think that Allah is unaware) [Ibrahim: 42] up to His saying: ﴿سَرِيعُ الحِسابِ﴾ (swift in reckoning). It was also said that the reference is to the Qur'an, and it was said to the surah. The meaning of balāgh (a message) is sufficiency in admonition and reminding, and "that they may be warned by it" (wa-liyunḏharū bihi). Al-Mawardi said: the wāw is extra (zāʾidah). From al-Mubarrad: it is a single coordination (ʿaṭf mufrad); that is, "this is a message and a warning"; end of quote. This is an explanation of meaning, not of grammatical analysis (iʿrāb). It was also said: it is carried over to the meaning; that is, "that they may convey and be warned." It was also said: the lām is the lām of command (lām al-amr). One of them said: this is good were it not for His saying "and that they may be reminded" (wa-liyadhdhakkara), for it is simply in the accusative; end of quote. This does not undermine it, since (wa-liyadhdhakkara) need not be coordinated with the command, but rather a verb is implied for it to depend on. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the meaning is "this is a message for mankind, and it is so that they may be warned by it"; end of quote. So he made it in the place of a nominative predicate of the omitted hūwa. Al-Zamakhshari said: "that they may be warned" (wa-liyunḏharū) is coordinated with an omitted element; that is, "that they may be advised and warned by it through this message"; end of quote. Mujahid and Humayd read it with a dammed tāʾ and a kasra on the dhāl (tunḏharū, "you warn"): the message is general, and the warning is for those addressed. Yahya ibn ʿUmarah, from his father al-Dharrāʿ, and Ahmad ibn Zayd ibn Usayd al-Sulami read: wa-liyanḏharū, with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and the dhāl, the imperfect of nadhara bi-l-shay' (to know of a thing and prepare for it). They said: no verbal noun (maṣdar) is known for this verb, so it is like ʿasā and others of the verbs used without a known root. And "that they may know" (wa-liyaʿlamū): for when they fear what they have been warned of, that moves them to reflect, so they arrive at the Oneness of Allah and devotion to Him alone, since fear is the root of good. And "that those of understanding may be reminded" (wa-liyadhdhakkara): that is, may take heed and review themselves in light of the admonitions they have heard. He attributed remembrance and admonition to those who possess intellect (lubb), because they are the ones in whom remembrance is of benefit. It was also said that this refers to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. The ending of this surah corresponds to its opening, and this is frequent in the surahs of the Qur'an, to the extent that some claimed that His saying "and that they may be warned by it" is coordinated with His saying "to bring forth mankind" (litukhrija al-nās).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 14, verses 44–52 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿On the Day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6].

﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do. He only defers them to a Day when eyes will stare fixedly, hastening forward with raised heads, their gaze not returning to them, and their hearts void﴾ [Ibrahim: 42–43]. The address in His words "and do not think" is to the listener who could conceive such a thought because of his ignorance of Allah's attributes, not to the Messenger, for that is impossible in his regard. In this verse there is a great warning to the wrongdoers and consolation to the oppressed. Talha read *wa-la tahsab* ("and do not think") without the emphatic nun (*nun al-tawkid*), and likewise *fa-la tahsab Allaha mukhlifa wa'dihi* ("so do not think that Allah breaks His promise"). The purpose of the prohibition against thinking that He is "unaware" is to announce that He knows what the wrongdoers do, nothing of it is hidden from Him, and that He will punish them for its little and its much, by way of warning and threat, like His words: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283], meaning a warning. It is also possible that the meaning is: "Do not think that He deals with them as one who is unaware of what they do, but rather as a watcher over them who calls them to account for the smallest and the most trivial." 

As-Sulami, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, al-Mufaddal (from ʿAsim), ʿAbbas ibn al-Fadl, Harun al-Ataki and Yunus ibn Habib (from Abu ʿAmr) read *wa-nu'akhkhiruhum* with the nun of majesty (*nun al-ʿaẓama*), while the majority read it with the *ya'* (*yu'akhkhiruhum*), meaning "Allah defers them."

*Muhti'in* ("hastening forward") means hurrying, as said by Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah, and that is out of humiliation and submission, like the hurrying of a captive or one in fear. Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu al-Duha said: "intensely gazing without blinking." Ibn Zayd said: "not raising their heads." Mujahid said: "extending the gaze to the right." Al-Akhfash said: "approaching in order to listen," and he recited:

*Bi-Dijlata dāruhum wa-laqad arāhum*
*bi-Dijlata muhti'īna ilā al-samāʿ*

(Their home is at the Tigris, and indeed I have seen them at the Tigris hastening toward the hearing.)

Al-Hasan said: "*muqni'i ruʾusihim* (raised heads): the faces of people on that day are toward the sky, and no one looks at anyone else." Ibn Jurayj said: "*hawa'* (void): empty of good, hollow of it." Abu ʿUbayda said: "a hollow with no minds in them." Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: "a ruin, hollow, with no good and no intellect in it." Sufyan said: "empty except from the terror of that Day," like His words: ﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became void﴾ [al-Qasas: 10], meaning "except from the anxiety of Moses." *Hawa'* is a pure simile, since they are not literally air. It may be that the comparison lies in their emptiness of hope and desire for mercy, so they are broken, resembling air in its being free of things and its being torn apart. It may also lie in the agitation of their hearts and their surging in the chests, and that they come and go and reach their throats, so they are in that like air, which is always in agitation.
